arguments_petitioner:
Petitioners argue for certain actions related to health and welfare in Srikakulam District. They seek judicial intervention to address specific issues concerning health services and facilities.

To direct the Union and the State Government to undertake periodical national surveys for determining the prevalence rate and new cases detection rate of Uddanam CKD and publish the reports into the public domain. To organize massive awareness campaigns about the signs and symptoms of Uddanam CKD and the free availability of medicines. To ensure that drugs for managing Uddanam CKD and its complications are available free of cost at all Primary Health Centers. To provide treatment at free of cost to all Uddanam CKD cases diagnosed through the general health care system. To organize seminars to hear views and experiences from former patients, families, doctors, social workers, experts, NGOs, and government officials. To ensure that both private and public schools do not discriminate against children from CKD-affected families and provide them free education. To appoint food inspectors to prevent food adulteration. To issue Below Poverty Line (BPL) cards to persons affected with CKD to avail benefits under schemes.

The petitioners seek several reliefs including the construction of super specialty hospitals with adequate dialysis units, formulation of a rehabilitation scheme for CKD affected persons, provision of mobile dialysis units, and framing of separate rules for CKD patients. Additionally, they request a sensitization program to prevent alcohol consumption, use of cashew nut powder in food, and smoking raw tobacco.

The petitioners contend that the disease is intensifying quickly from village to village and it appears more in young male agricultural workers and indigent in rural working population, thereby, 70% of the patients die due to inadequate resources to continue treatment. Due to lack of systematic screening, less number of dialysis centers, expensive treatment in private hospitals, lack of providing free medicines, 80% patients are dying at home due to their non-affordability to costly treatment. The petitioners request to direct the respondents to provide good and adequate health care to the people of Uddanam area and since the governmental agencies are neglecting the CKD sufferers, the petitioners filed the present writ petitions for the welfare and benefit of the residents of Uddanam area.

Petitioner argues that the government has not taken sufficient measures to identify and mitigate the causes of chronic kidney disease in the Uddanam area, despite the high prevalence and significant health impact on the local population.

Mr. Simhachalam Karukola, petitioner-in-person, contended that the State has failed to take necessary action to prevent CKD in the Uddanam area and that the failure to provide effective treatment and preventive measures violates fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Constitution of India and human rights.

Unless stern action is taken to prevent the spread of kidney disease in Uddanam area, it is difficult for the survival of future generations. The State Government is under obligation to take immediate steps to prevent the spread of CKD among the people of Uddanam area to protect the future of the residents. Requested the Court to issue necessary directions to prevent further spread of CKD among the residents of Uddanam area.

The right to health as a fundamental right grew as an offshoot of environmental litigation initiated by environmental activists regarding the environment issues. A pollution free environment as a fundamental right presupposes right to health as a fundamental right.

The Court observed that great achievements and accomplishments in life are possible if one is permitted to lead an acceptably healthy life. Health is life’s grace and efforts are to be made to sustain the same. In a Country like ours, it may not be possible to have sophisticated hospitals but definitely villagers of this Country within their limitations can aspire to have a Primary Health Centre. The Government is required to assist people, and its endeavour should be to see that the people get treatment and lead a healthy life. Healthy society is a collective gain and no Government should make any effort to smother it. Primary concern should be the Primary Health Clinic (hereinafter will be referred as „PHC) and technical fetters cannot be introduced as subterfuges to cause hindrances in the establishment of health centre.

The Supreme Court, while interpreting Article 21 of the Constitution ruled that the expression „life does not connote mere animal existence or continued drudgery through life but includes, inter alia, the opportunities to eliminate sickness and physical disability. In Francis Coralie Mullin v. Union Territory of Delhi6, it was held that, right to life guaranteed in Article 21 of the Constitution in its true meaning includes the basic right to food, clothing and shelter. The Apex Court, in Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal7 while widening the scope of Article 21 and the governments responsibility to provide medical aid to every person in the country, held that in a welfare state, the primary duty of the government is to secure the welfare of the people. Providing adequate medical facilities for the people is an obligation undertaken by the government in a welfare state. The government discharges this obligation by providing medical care to the persons seeking to avail of those facilities. In Unnikrishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh8, it was held that the maintenance and improvement of public health is the duty of the State to fulfill its constitutional obligations cast on it under Article 21 of the Constitution. arguments_respondent:
The respondents, represented by the Union of India, argue against the petitioners' claims, likely defending the current state of health services and policies in the region.

The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued G.O.Ms.No.102, dated 03.09.2019 for establishment of 200 bedded super Specialty Hospital, with Kidney Research Center and Dialysis Unit with an estimated expenditure of Rs.50 Crores (Non-recurring expenditure) and Rs.8.93 Crores per annum (recurring expenditure). In addition to the three existing dialysis centres, two more centres, one at CHC, Palasa and one at CHC, Sompeta are started under national free dialysis Programme and functioning since May' 2017. One more dialysis center was established on 31.01.2019 at CHC Kaviti in Srikakulam district. Nephrologist services are available once in 15 days at all the 6 dialysis centers. A-V fistula facility, to perform dialysis is made available at RIMS/Government General Hospital Srikakulam, free of cost to all the patients requiring dialysis. The Government of A.P is also providing dialysis facility under the State Government sponsored Dr YSR Aarogyasree Scheme.

The respondent also provided statistics from 2003 to 2019 with regard to the measures being adopted for prevention and control of CKDs in Uddanam area. The Government of Andhra Pradesh, inaugurated the CKD Special Mobile Medical Clinics on 19.01.2017 at CHC Sompeta, and explained the details of work undertaken in order to combat CKD in Uddanam area. The Government also established one research centre at Palasa of Uddanam area in collaboration with George Institute for Global Health, New Delhi with the name „STOP CKDu in Andhra Pradesh. District initiatives to stop CKD in Uddanam area: ‚ Awareness camps conducted in 7 mandals, 853 villages in Uddanam area to create awareness among the public of Uddanam area on prevention and control of CKD through public meetings, distribution of pamphlets, display of posters, etc. ‚ As a district initiative, the District Collector, Srikakulam has established 17 laboratories with semi auto analyzers for testing of serium creatin and blood urea levels which are basic tests for assess CKD levels of the Uddanam area public. ‚ PHC Wise tests are conducted in the Uddanam area.

Respondent states that extensive studies and interventions have been undertaken, including mass screenings and referrals to healthcare centers, but the exact cause remains unidentified due to complex factors.

The respondents explained the steps taken by the State Government to control tobacco usage, alcohol consumption, pain killers usage, genetic testing, and early treatment for persons with a family history of CKD. They mentioned the establishment of a Kidney Research Institute and continuous education programs to prevent the spread of CKD.

The State has taken palliative, preventive, and curative steps to address CKD and has provided necessary medical facilities and water to the Uddanam area inhabitants as a measure of prevention. The State contends that it has never violated the fundamental right of residents of Uddanam area guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India and is discharging its constitutional duties under Article 47 of the Constitution of India. Requested to dismiss the writ petition.

The municipal corporation was prosecuted by some citizens for not clearing up the garbage. The corporation took up the plea that it did not have money.

The respondent argued against the petitioner's claims regarding the violation of Article 21 and the enforcement of the right to pollution-free water and air.

Respondent argues that necessary measures have been taken and further actions are being considered.

The State argues that it has taken significant steps towards fulfilling its obligations under the Constitution, including the establishment of healthcare facilities and programs aimed at improving public health.

The respondent acknowledges the importance of health facilities, goods, and services but may argue about the practical implementation and resources required to ensure these standards across all regions, especially in rural areas.

The respondents acknowledge the existence of CKD in the Uddanam area but mention that certain Government Orders were passed for establishing water purifier plants and Reverse Osmosis water plants to supply water to the residents through Kiosks.

The court considers the evidence presented by both parties, including the findings from various studies and expert opinions, and evaluates the government's response to the CKD issue.

The Court needs to examine the issue in two dimensions: (1) Constitutional perspective and (2) Human Rights perspective, to decide whether the State is able to provide adequate health care facilities to prevent and cure CKD in Uddanam area.

Part IV of the Constitution lists the Directive Principles of State Policy. These are the principles which should be followed by the State as the guiding principles while enacting laws and policies but have traditionally been believed not to be enforceable in courts of law. The obligation of the State to provide health care facilities is set out in the „Directive Principles of State Policy.

In CERC vs. Union of India, the Supreme Court was dealing with the rights of workers in asbestos manufacturing and health hazards related to it. The Court was dealing essentially with private employers involved in asbestos mining and industry. To begin with, the Court noted that the right to health and health care of a worker is a component of the fundamental right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. The Court observed that, Article 38(1) lays down the foundation for human rights and enjoins the State to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting, as effectively as it may, a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life.

The court reasoned that the protection of the environment is a duty of citizens and an obligation of the State. Environmental pollution violates Article 21 of the Constitution, and the right to health and medical care is a fundamental right under Article 21.

The right to health to a worker is an integral facet of meaningful right to life to have not only a meaningful existence but also robust health and vigour without which worker would lead life of misery. Lack of health denudes his livelihood. Compelling economic necessity to work in an industry exposed to health hazards due to indigence to bread winning to him and his dependents should not beat the cost of the health and vigour of the workman.

The right to health contains both freedoms and entitlements, including the right to control one's health and body, and the right to be free from interference such as nonconsensual medical treatment. The entitlements include the right to a system of health protection that provides equality of opportunity for people to enjoy the highest attainable level of health.

The court examines the provisions of the Constitution of India and relevant precedents to determine the obligations of the state towards public health and environmental protection.

The Court considered the provisions of the Constitution and the State's actions in providing healthcare services. It noted the importance of ensuring access to healthcare for all citizens, especially those in vulnerable situations.

The court discusses the right to health in all its forms and at all levels, emphasizing the need for functioning public health and health-care facilities, goods, and services. It highlights the importance of non-discrimination, physical accessibility, affordability, and cultural appropriateness.

The court discusses the obligations of the local authorities under the Act No.III of 1939, including the need for a Health Officer, providing drinking water, executing water works, and monitoring water supply. It also mentions the provisions related to food control and the failure of the local authorities to exercise their powers under these provisions.

The documents produced by the respondents are sufficient to conclude that the State intends to provide potable water in Uddanam area to improve their health avoiding silicon deposits in the water. The measures taken by the Medical and Health department, at best, establish the minimum steps taken by the Medical and Health department to treat the patients suffering from CKD in Uddanam area and extend financial aid to the patients at the advanced stage of kidney problem. But these measures are not sufficient to prevent CKD in Uddanam area.

Independent medical research institutes like the George Institute for Global Health, India, also took up research in Uddanam and this phenomenon was discussed and termed 'Uddanam Nephropathy' at the 2013 International Congress of Nephrology held in Hong Kong, but could not suggest the ways and means to prevent CKD in Uddanam area. The suspected causative factors for CKD Uddanam (CKDu) are tobacco usage and regular alcohol consumption, extensive use of pain killers/analgesic medications, family history of CKD, heat stress due to occupational exposure, and silica and fluoride contamination in groundwater.

The court considered the recommendations of the Enquiry Committee and the necessity for efficient bed management and patient care in hospitals.

Providing adequate medical facilities is an essential part of the obligation undertaken by the State in a welfare state. The Government discharges this obligation by running hospitals and health centres. Article 21 imposes an obligation on the State to safeguard right to life of every person. Preservation of human life is thus of paramount importance. Government hospitals run by the state and the medical officers employed therein are duty-bound to extend medical assistance for preserving human life.

Finally it is contended that, the State is taking every step, both to prevent and treat CKD, more particularly in Uddanam area and that there is no negligence on the part of the State and its officials to prevent and cure CKD disease and requested to dismiss the writ petition.

The petition is allowed, directing the government to take further steps to investigate and address the causes of chronic kidney disease in the affected areas.

The court held that the petition is allowed, recognizing the right to pollution-free water and air as an enforceable fundamental right under Article 21.

The court directs the Union of India to take necessary steps to implement the Uddanam Nephropathy Scheme effectively.

The Court ruled that the State must take further steps to fulfill its constitutional obligations regarding healthcare, emphasizing the need for improved public health infrastructure and services.

The Court directed the State to continue the investigation to detect the causative factors for CKD in Uddanam and to provide health care to the residents of Uddanam area for effective control and treatment of the disease.

The petition is allowed. The court directs the establishment of a central Bed Bureau and the upgrading of intermediate hospitals.

The court held that the people affected due to the contaminated water should be treated at the expense of the State. It also added that the State should bear the expenses of any surgery might be required. The State was also directed to closing of hand pumps where the water had excessive amount of fluoride and that a proper and safe drinking water facility should be put in place.

We direct the State and Local governments of Uddanam area to take immediate action to stop effluents from nearby industries into water bodies. Proper medical aid and adequate health care must be provided at Health Centres and hospitals to CKD patients.

The Court finds in favor of the petitioners and directs the Union and State Governments to take necessary measures to ensure non-discrimination against CKD-affected children in schools, appointment of food inspectors to prevent adulteration, and issuance of household supply cards to CKD-affected individuals.

Member Secretary, State Legal Services is hereby directed to get necessary funds from the State by taking appropriate steps and report to Patron-in-Chief from time-to-time. The State may take help from NGOs and industrialist and assist as part of corporate social responsibility, to ensure, protect right to life and adequate health care and to protect human rights of the residents of Uddanam area. Consequently, miscellaneous petitions pending, if any, shall also stand closed.

Versus Union of India, Rep. by its Secretary, Health & Family Welfare Department „A Wing Shastri Bhawan, Rajendra Prasad Road, New Delhi - 110 001 & 22 others. Petitioners argue for certain actions related to health and welfare in Srikakulam District. They seek judicial intervention to address specific issues concerning health services and facilities. The respondents, represented by the Union of India, argue against the petitioners' claims, likely defending the current state of health services and policies in the region.

Mr. Karukola Simhachalam, a practicing Advocate, claiming to be a public spirited person for public good, filed W.P (P.I.L) No.164 of 2019 under Article 226 of the Constitution of India as public interest litigation. Annepu Mahandhata, age 64 years, filed W.P (P.I.L) No.236 of 2021. Both petitions claim identical reliefs, except for additional relief in W.P (P.I.L) No.236 of 2021. To direct the Union and the State Government to undertake periodical national surveys for determining the prevalence rate and new cases detection rate of Uddanam CKD and publish the reports into the public domain. To organize massive awareness campaigns about the signs and symptoms of Uddanam CKD and the free availability of medicines. To ensure that drugs for managing Uddanam CKD and its complications are available free of cost at all Primary Health Centers. To provide treatment at free of cost to all Uddanam CKD cases diagnosed through the general health care system. To organize seminars to hear views and experiences from former patients, families, doctors, social workers, experts, NGOs, and government officials. To ensure that both private and public schools do not discriminate against children from CKD-affected families and provide them free education. To appoint food inspectors to prevent food adulteration. To issue Below Poverty Line (BPL) cards to persons affected with CKD to avail benefits under schemes.

The writ petitioners claim that for the last two decades, lakhs of people in the Uddanam area, Srikakulam District, Andhra Pradesh, have been afflicted by Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) known as Uddanam Nephropathy. The disease has disproportionately affected farmers and agricultural workers. The cause of Uddanam Nephropathy remains unestablished despite studies suggesting potential links to environmental toxins, heat stress, and water contamination. By 2015, it was estimated that more than 4500 people had died, and around 34,000 people were suffering from kidney diseases in this area. The petitioners seek several reliefs including the construction of super specialty hospitals with adequate dialysis units, formulation of a rehabilitation scheme for CKD affected persons, provision of mobile dialysis units, and framing of separate rules for CKD patients. Additionally, they request a sensitization program to prevent alcohol consumption, use of cashew nut powder in food, and smoking raw tobacco.

Few scientific institutions and organizations conducted several tests of blood, urine, water and soil and opined the reason for kidney diseases as high level of silica in water, prolonged dehydration, heat stress, anti-inflammatory drug use, gene mutations, high pesticides use and heavy metals in water. Usage of adulterated local made tea powder with cashew nut seed coat in Uddanam area was also suggested, which residues with high levels of Anacardic acids, which decreases the activity of human kidney. The disease is intensifying quickly from village to village and it appears more in young male agricultural workers and indigent in rural working population. Uddanam area is being de-isolated from the State, as most of the schools in the area do not have minimum primary facilities like supply of drinking water, poor sanitation, good hygienic food. With the World Health Organization identifying this area as one of the three areas burgeoning with kidney cases, vacancies in government offices and schools arose in this area. Many state employees who are working in Uddanam prefer to stay in other parts of the district and are scared to drink water here. The situation has also become difficult for youngsters planning to get married in the future as they have to find a girl from the same village or mandal as no one from other districts want to marry a girl or boy from this area due to the fear that they may also contract the disease in future. The petitioners contend that the disease is intensifying quickly from village to village and it appears more in young male agricultural workers and indigent in rural working population, thereby, 70% of the patients die due to inadequate resources to continue treatment. Due to lack of systematic screening, less number of dialysis centers, expensive treatment in private hospitals, lack of providing free medicines, 80% patients are dying at home due to their non-affordability to costly treatment. The petitioners request to direct the respondents to provide good and adequate health care to the people of Uddanam area and since the governmental agencies are neglecting the CKD sufferers, the petitioners filed the present writ petitions for the welfare and benefit of the residents of Uddanam area. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued G.O.Ms.No.102, dated 03.09.2019 for establishment of 200 bedded super Specialty Hospital, with Kidney Research Center and Dialysis Unit with an estimated expenditure of Rs.50 Crores (Non-recurring expenditure) and Rs.8.93 Crores per annum (recurring expenditure). In addition to the three existing dialysis centres, two more centres, one at CHC, Palasa and one at CHC, Sompeta are started under national free dialysis Programme and functioning since May' 2017. One more dialysis center was established on 31.01.2019 at CHC Kaviti in Srikakulam district. Nephrologist services are available once in 15 days at all the 6 dialysis centers. A-V fistula facility, to perform dialysis is made available at RIMS/Government General Hospital Srikakulam, free of cost to all the patients requiring dialysis. The Government of A.P is also providing dialysis facility under the State Government sponsored Dr YSR Aarogyasree Scheme.

The Government of AP installed 6 RO Mother plants with 135 Dispensary units to provide safe drinking water. An orientation and training program for Medical Officers and staff of 18 primary health centres in Uddanam area on CKD care was conducted. Uddanam groundwater has lower range of total dissolved solids and aluminum concentrations compared to Machilipatnam population. Ground water contamination with phthalates has been observed extensively in Uddanam area. The Government of Andhra Pradesh entered an MOU with the George Institute for Global Health, India, New Delhi in two phases to study CKD prevalence and risk factors. Mass screening was done for the age groups of above 30 years in all the Mandals of Uddanam area from Jan, 2017 to April, 2017. Two Expert teams from Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India and Team constituted by Govt. of AP with ICMR visited Uddanam area in Jan.2018 to study the various aspects of CKD problem. CHCs Sompeta, Palasa, Kaviti, Ichapuram, Barua and Haripuram are provided with Lab Equipment and Reagents for testing CKD. Two more dialysis centres were started under National Free Dialysis Programme and functioning since May'2017. One more dialysis center was established on 31.01.2019 at CHC Kaviti in Srikakulam district.

The Government of Andhra Pradesh determined additional risk factors through detailed evaluation of occupational, dietary, heat exposure and NSAIDs (Non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, like Aspirin, Ibuprofen, Diclofenac, Aceclofenac etc) usage repeat eGFR and Urine PCR estimation for identifying new incident cases of CKD at 6 monthly intervals. Government of Andhra Pradesh, inaugurated the CKD Special Mobile Medical Clinics on 19.01.2017 at CHC Sompeta, and explained the details of work undertaken in order to combat CKD in Uddanam area. The Government of India has deployed a Central Team of Experts under the Chairmanship of Dr. Sanjay Agarwal, HOD, Department of Nephrology, AIIMS, New Delhi with their team visited the Gunupalli Village of Vajrapu Kottur Mandal on 21.01.2017 and interacted with public and examined the CKD Patients. The Government also established one research centre at Palasa of Uddanam area in collaboration with George Institute for Global Health, New Delhi with the name „STOP CKDu in Andhra Pradesh. The respondent also provided statistics from 2003 to 2019 with regard to the measures being adopted for prevention and control of CKDs in Uddanam area. The Government of Andhra Pradesh, inaugurated the CKD Special Mobile Medical Clinics on 19.01.2017 at CHC Sompeta, and explained the details of work undertaken in order to combat CKD in Uddanam area. The Government also established one research centre at Palasa of Uddanam area in collaboration with George Institute for Global Health, New Delhi with the name „STOP CKDu in Andhra Pradesh. District initiatives to stop CKD in Uddanam area: ‚ Awareness camps conducted in 7 mandals, 853 villages in Uddanam area to create awareness among the public of Uddanam area on prevention and control of CKD through public meetings, distribution of pamphlets, display of posters, etc. ‚ As a district initiative, the District Collector, Srikakulam has established 17 laboratories with semi auto analyzers for testing of serium creatin and blood urea levels which are basic tests for assess CKD levels of the Uddanam area public. ‚ PHC Wise tests are conducted in the Uddanam area.

In the year 2003, kidney diseases were noticed in Gunupalli and Matturu of Vajrapu Kothuru Mandal of Srikakulam District, AP. The Medical Officers and Staff of concerned Primary Health Centre detected 25 suspected kidney cases. The Areaal Laboratory, Visakhapatnam examined the water samples of those areas and reported that the water contained Nitrogen Nitrate and recommended frequent and continuation chlorination of water sources. Medical camps were organized at Kavity on 15-12-2006 under the supervision of Dr. Raviraj, Nephrologist, King George Hospital, Visakhapatnam, educating about 63,000 people from 20 villages. At the specialist camp, 610 suspected cases were attended to, out of which 41 cases suffered from kidney diseases. The Specialist Doctors Team under the supervision of Nephrologists of NIMS Hospital, Hyderabad visited Uddanam Area to study the cause of prevalence of Kidney diseases. The water was found to contain silicon which may have caused the Kidney diseases in Uddanam Area of Andhra Pradesh. Further, the teams found the following reasons for the likely cause of Kidney diseases: (a) Personal Dietary Habits like low intake of water, alcoholism, chewing of tobacco products, excess eating of dry fish; (b) frequently inhalation of pesticides and sprays at time of agricultural operations; (c) Irregular and frequent usage of NSAID (Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs), tablets and Analgesic drugs without prescription of qualified Doctors. From the year 2003 to 2013, various organizations including the World Health Organization, the Indian Council for Medical Research, Harvard Medical College, Christian Medical College, King George Medical College, etc., had conducted various studies and tests and also created awareness among the people of the Uddanam area. However, despite the numerous studies and tests, no specific reason or cause could be identified for the CKD. By the year 2017, the Government had identified six Mandals with high prevalence of CKD in the Uddanam area. A total of 167 villages fall within these 6 mandals with a population of 2,67,493

facts_text:
The appellants are before this Court challenging the judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the III Additional District and Sessions Judge, Ballari sitting at Hosapete (for brevity, 'trial Court') in S.C.No.89/2011 dated 28.03.2016.

On 25.07.2010, at about 7.00 p.m., there was a quarrel between PW.13/CW.17-Eshwara Gouda and accused No.3-Kantesh and accused No.1-Kenchanagoudra Basavarajappa for mixing water in the milk. At around 12.00 midnight on the same day, all the accused formed an unlawful assembly in front of the house of the complainant PW.4/CW.1-Kadlenni Basappa, committed rioting by holding sticks, stones, axe, abused them in indecent words, insulted them and provoked them to break the public peace, threatened them with life and criminally trespassed into the house of PW.4/CW.1-Kadlenni Basappa. The deceased Kamaraj @ Honnappa died on 01.08.2010 at 2.20 p.m. due to the said injuries. The complainant PW.4/CW.1-Kadlenni Basappa filed a complaint before PW.20/CW.32-Shadakshari Patil, ASI of Police, Holalu on 26.07.2010 at 1.00 a.m. in the night. The Committal Court took cognizance of the offences. Charges were framed, read over and explained to the accused in a language known to them i.e. Kannada. The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.

The prosecution alleges that the incident occurred inside the house of PW.4/CW.1- Kadlenni Basappa. However, there are no bloodstains in the house as per the spot panchanama, and no scientific examinations were conducted to establish the incident occurred there. The incident allegedly occurred at 10.30 p.m. on the road leading to the grain trashing yard near the house of the complainant. The deceased expired on 01.08.2010.

The prosecution case involves the absence of an independent witness, Kapur Singh, who was present at the scene and could corroborate the testimony of related witnesses. The incident allegedly occurred in a public place

In State of H.P. v. Mast Ram[(2004) 8 SCC 660], it has been stated that there is no set rule that one must react in a particular way, for the natural reaction of man is unpredictable. Everyone reacts in his own way and, hence, natural human behaviour is difficult to prove by credible evidence. It has to be appreciated in the context of given facts and circumstances of the case. Similar view has been reiterated in Lahu Kamlakar Patil and anr. v. State of Maharashtra[AIR 2013 SC (Cri) 441]. Thus, the behaviour of witnesses or their reactions would differ from situation to situation and individual to individual. Expectation of uniformity in the reaction of witnesses would be unrealistic but the court cannot be oblivious of the fact that even taking into account the unpredictability of human conduct and lack of uniformity in human reaction, whether in the circumstances of the case, the behaviour is acceptably natural allowing the variations. In the case at hand, PW-9 was given a threat when her mother was forcibly taken away but she had the courage to walk in the night to her grandmother who was in her mid-fifties. After coming to know about the incident, it defies commonsense that the mother would not tell her other daughter and the son-in-law about the kidnapping of the deceased by her mother-in-law. It is interesting to note that the High Court has ascribed the reason that PW-7 possibly wanted to save the reputation of the deceased-daughter and that is why she did not inform the other daughter and son-in-law. That apart, the fear factor has also been taken into consideration. Definitely, there would have been fear because, as alleged, the mother-in-law had forcibly taken away the deceased, but it is totally contrary to normal behaviour that she would have maintained a sphinx-like silence and not inform others. It is also worthy to note that she did not tell it to anyone for almost two days and it has not been explained why she had thought it apt to search for her daughter without even informing anyone else in the family or in the village or without going to the police station.

PW 7 had witnessed the crime being committed by the accused at about 10.30 p.m. in the night and there was no electricity at the alleged scene of offence. According to PW 7, her husband also witnessed the crime, but they could not identify whether the accused were cutting into pieces the body of a dead person or an alive person. Even after watching the brutal crime, neither PW 7 nor her husband had raised hue and cry in the vicinity which was stated to be thickly populated, but they went to sleep peacefully and thereafter led normal life. There is also no dispute that PW 7 did not identify the respondent herein--Accused 2 and her statement was recorded after a gap of one-and-half months from the date of the incident.

When we look at the medical evidence, the Doctor (PW10) has categorically stated that the weapons were not sent to her. In the chief examination, it was stated that the injuries 1 & 4 on the body of the deceased are possible with chopper and club. But in the cross examination it was deposed that even if a person falls on a sharp object these injuries could happen. According to PW3, the deceased fell into the drain. The other ground is, when the father of A5 gave a complaint against the deceased's family as the police filed 'B form' the same was closed and not filed before the Court. Apart from that, the direction of the Court to seize the gun of the deceased and file a case under the relevant provisions of the Arms Act was not brought to the notice of the Court. Non explanation of injuries on A5 is another major defect.

All the accused persons were armed with sharp weapons. PW 5 Smt Veero stated that Amar Singh, son of Bachan Singh, and Rattan Singh were each armed with a sua, Lakha Singh was armed with a barchi, Harbhajan Singh was armed with a kulhari, and Amar Singh, son of Isher Das, was armed with a kirpan. arguments_petitioner:
By way of the said judgment, the appellants/accused were convicted of the offences punishable under Sections 148, 448, 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal code (for brevity, 'IPC') and they were acquitted for the offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 504, 324, 326, 323, 506 read with Section 149 of IPC.

There are several inconsistencies in the events as narrated by the complainant, as such the evidence of the complainant ought to have been discarded. There is no clear and clinching evidence regarding the incident alleged to have taken place in the evening as also in the night. The prosecution has been unable to prove beyond reasonable doubt the guilt of the accused.

The prosecution has failed to prove the genesis of the incident by relying on cogent and reliable evidence. The prosecution has not examined any independent witnesses. The evidence of all interested witnesses is required to be discarded. There is delay in filing of the FIR and in the FIR being received by the Magistrate. There are material inconsistencies between the complaint and the evidence of PW.4/CW.1-Kadlenni Basappa.

Petitioner argues for the consideration of related witness testimonies despite the absence of an independent witness.

Nine persons including four witnesses belonging to the complainant party received injuries whereas as many as 14 accused persons received injuries including some who even suffered grievous injuries. Admittedly, there was a mob of about 75-100 persons who descended from the hill side to the place of occurrence by pelting stones and a melee followed. Not even a single witness including the injured witnesses could specifically state as to who had caused what injury either to the deceased or to the injured witnesses or to the accused. A very general statement has been made that the accused persons were armed with deadly weapons and caused injuries to the complainant party.

The prosecution argues that despite the lack of immediate reporting and the absence of corroborative evidence, the testimony of PW 7 should be considered reliable and sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused.

Where the evidence of the witnesses for the prosecution is totally inconsistent with the medical evidence or the evidence of the ballistic expert, this is a most fundamental defect in the prosecution case and unless reasonably explained it is sufficient to discredit the entire case. In a case where death is due to injuries or wounds caused by a lethal weapon, it has always been considered to be the duty of the prosecution to prove by expert evidence that it was likely or at least possible for the injuries to have been caused with the weapon with which and in the manner in which they are alleged to have been caused. It is elementary that where the prosecution has a definite or positive case, it is doubtful whether the injuries which are attributed to the appellant were caused by a gun or by a rifle.

The prosecution relied on the evidence of PW 5 Smt Veero, who claimed that the accused inflicted injuries on Piara Singh with their respective weapons. The prosecution also cited the precedent in Ram Narain Singh v. State of Punjab [(1975) 4 SCC 497 : 1975 SCC (Cri) 571 : AIR 1975 SC 1727], stating that if the evidence of the witnesses for the prosecution is totally inconsistent with the medical evidence, it is a fundamental defect in the prosecution case.

PW 25 Mirza Majid Beg and PW 24 Mohamed Shakir slipping away unnoticed by the others particularly after the alleged attack is utterly unbelievable. It appears unreal. They are not strange to expect and they did not render any help for shifting the injured to the hospital nor had the courtesy to go inside the hospital to ascertain the condition and also did not inform the occurrence to the police. The aspect of fear is without any foundation and is not supported by any evidence of act or conduct. This plea does not impress us.

Petitioner's counsel argued that the accused acted in self-defense and that there was insufficient evidence to prove their involvement in the altercation.

PW.4/CW.1-Kadlenni Basappa and PW.6/CW.4-Sangana Basappa argue that the accused, including Kenchanagoudra Basavarajappa, were involved in a violent attack leading to serious injuries and death. They cite precedents such as Hem Raj and Others vs. State of Haryana and Shivasharanappa vs. State of Karnataka.

Petitioner argued that the fight was provoked by the respondent and that the respondent should be held responsible.

Petitioner argues that the evidence against Shantappanavara Basappa and his relatives is insufficient to establish their involvement in the incident.

Petitioner argues based on precedents like Kenchanagoudra vs The State Of Karnataka and Hem Raj and Others vs. State of Haryana, emphasizing the need for bail and fair trial procedures.

Petitioner argues that there is insufficient evidence to prove his involvement in the alleged offenses. He claims that the prosecution witnesses are unreliable and their testimonies are contradictory.

Petitioner argues that the accused broke into the house and caused injuries, seeking justice for the victim.

The prosecution claims that the incident occurred at 12.00 a.m., and the evidence includes the wound certificate and the post-mortem report. They argue that the accused assaulted the deceased, Kamaraj, and his family members.
arguments_respondent:
Respondent argues that the absence of an independent witness undermines the credibility of the prosecution's case.

In a situation where a mob of 75-100 persons entered into a clash with the complainant party it could not have been possible for any of the witnesses, who would naturally be concerned with their own safety and to save themselves from the assault, to see as to who had inflicted what type of injury either on the deceased or on the injured witnesses. In view of such omnibus and vague statements given by the witnesses, the Court below acquitted as many as 21 accused persons on the ground that there is no evidence on record to implicate them in the offences alleged

The defense contends that the evidence of PW 7 is unreliable due to the delay in reporting and the lack of corroborative evidence, including the failure to conduct a test identification parade and prove the blood group of the deceased with the bloodstains found on the alleged weapon used in the crime.

The High Court has lightly brushed aside the inconsistency between the medical evidence and the prosecution version. The question of the time of occurrence having been shifted from 8.00 p.m. to 6.30 p.m. has been blindly believed as also the evidence regarding the production of the weapons by the accused. In view of these striking circumstances, we should have expected the High Court to have approached this case with much more care and caution that it has, particularly when a death sentence was involved.

The defense contended that the evidence of PW 5 Smt Veero is inconsistent with the medical evidence, as no incised wounds were found on the body of the deceased despite claims of multiple blows. Additionally, PW 6 Anokh Singh's evidence was deemed unreliable as he stated he did not see Piara Singh receiving any injury from the accused. The defense also noted that PW 4 Murta Singh did not witness the incident directly and his account was not corroborated by the first information report.

The trial court has considered all the aspects in proper and required manner. The judgment of conviction and order of sentence is proper and correct and does not require any interference. The delay in the FIR reaching the Court is explained on account of the P.C. having attended to his work and taken a bus to the Magistrate Court. Therefore, there is no infirmity arising out of the said delay.

Respondent's counsel contended that the accused were involved in a premeditated act of violence and presented evidence to support this claim.

The defense argues that there is insufficient evidence to prove the involvement of the accused in the alleged crimes. They question the credibility of the witnesses and the chain of evidence, citing cases like Eknath Ganpat Aher vs. State of Maharashtra and State of Uttar Pradesh vs. Om Pal.

Respondent argued that the fight was initiated by the petitioner and that the petitioner should bear the consequences.

Respondent argues that the evidence presented by the prosecution sufficiently establishes the involvement of Shantappanavara Basappa and his relatives in the incident.

Respondent argues against bail citing serious nature of offenses under Sections 149 and 148, and the potential risk to public safety.

Respondent argues that the evidence presented by the prosecution, including witness testimonies and physical evidence, is sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused. They claim that the petitioner was part of a group committing the offenses.

Respondent argues that there is insufficient evidence to prove the break-in and the extent of injuries.

The defense suggests that the incident occurred at an earlier point of time and that the accused were traveling towards their grain thrashing yard when they were assaulted by the deceased and his family members. They argue that the prosecution's evidence is contradictory and lacks independent witness testimony.
reasoning_text:
The medical evidence regarding the deceased is suspicious. Ex.P.7-wound certificate was issued at 11.00 p.m. by Dr.Raju stating the deceased was assaulted in his house, while Ex.P.9-postmortem report states a different wound size. There is no evidence on record to establish the incident at 12.00 midnight. The complaint has been manipulated and modulated to suit the requirements of the complainant.

The court examines the reliability of the testimonies provided by related witnesses and the legal implications of the absence of an independent witness.

The court noted that natural human behavior is unpredictable and varies from individual to individual. The behavior of witnesses or their reactions would differ from situation to situation and individual to individual. The court emphasized that the expectation of uniformity in the reaction of witnesses would be unrealistic but the court cannot be oblivious of the fact that even taking into account the unpredictability of human conduct and lack of uniformity in human reaction, whether in the circumstances of the case, the behavior is acceptably natural allowing the variations. The court also considered the fear factor and its impact on the witnesses' actions, noting that maintaining silence for two days is contrary to normal behavior.

The court notes that the principles stated in the judgments of Joseph v. State of Kerala and State of Haryana v. Inder Singh require that the testimony of a sole eyewitness must be confidence inspiring and beyond suspicion, leaving no doubt in the mind of the Court. The court further observes that the quality of the evidence, rather than the quantity, is crucial for placing credence on the statement.

The court analyzed the evidence of PW 5 Smt Veero and found it inconsistent with the medical evidence regarding the injuries on the body of the deceased. The court also noted that PW 6 Anokh Singh's evidence was unreliable and PW 4 Murta Singh did not witness the incident directly. The court concluded that the evidence of PW 5 casts a great doubt on the commission of any offense by the appellants.

The statements of PW 25 Mirza Majid Beg and PW 24 Mohamed Shakir were recorded after 3 days of the occurrence. No explanation is forthcoming as to why they are not examined for 3 days. It is also not known as to how the police came to know that these witnesses saw the occurrence. The delay in recording the statements casts a serious doubt about their being eye-witnesses to the occurrence. It may suggest that the investigating officer was deliberately marking time with a view to decide about the shape to be given to the case and the eye-witnesses to be introduced.

The High Court observed that even if the F.I. R. was not immediately sent to the Court of the Magistrate, it is of no consequence, since the F.I. R. had been lodged within 30 minutes of the occurrence and the said F.I. R. clearly described the basic prosecution case.

The appellants are before this Court challenging the judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the III Additional District and Sessions Judge, Ballari sitting at Hosapete (for brevity, 'trial Court') in S.C.No.89/2011 dated 28.03.2016. By way of the said judgment, the appellants/accused were convicted of the offences punishable under Sections 148, 448, 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal code (for brevity, 'IPC') and they were acquitted for the offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 504, 324, 326, 323, 506 read with Section 149 of IPC.

On 25.07.2010, at about 7.00 p.m., there was a quarrel between PW.13/CW.17-Eshwara Gouda and accused No.3-Kantesh and accused No.1-Kenchanagoudra Basavarajappa for mixing water in the milk. At around 12.00 midnight on the same day, all the accused formed an unlawful assembly in front of the house of the complainant PW.4/CW.1-Kadlenni Basappa, committed rioting by holding sticks, stones, axe, abused them in indecent words, insulted them and provoked them to break the public peace, threatened them with life and criminally trespassed into the house of PW.4/CW.1-Kadlenni Basappa. The deceased Kamaraj @ Honnappa died on 01.08.2010 at 2.20 p.m. due to the said injuries. The complainant PW.4/CW.1-Kadlenni Basappa filed a complaint before PW.20/CW.32-Shadakshari Patil, ASI of Police, Holalu on 26.07.2010 at 1.00 a.m. in the night. The Committal Court took cognizance of the offences. Charges were framed, read over and explained to the accused in a language known to them i.e. Kannada. The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. There are several inconsistencies in the events as narrated by the complainant, as such the evidence of the complainant ought to have been discarded. There is no clear and clinching evidence regarding the incident alleged to have taken place in the evening as also in the night. The prosecution alleges that the incident occurred inside the house of PW.4/CW.1- Kadlenni Basappa. In State of H.P. v. Mast Ram[(2004) 8 SCC 660], it has been stated that there is no set rule that one must react in a particular way, for the natural reaction of man is unpredictable. Everyone reacts in his own way and, hence, natural human behaviour is difficult to prove by credible evidence. It has to be appreciated in the context of given facts and circumstances of the case. Similar view has been reiterated in Lahu Kamlakar Patil and anr. v. State of Maharashtra[AIR 2013 SC (Cri) 441]. Thus, the behaviour of witnesses or their reactions would differ from situation to situation and individual to individual. Expectation of uniformity in the reaction of witnesses would be unrealistic but the court cannot be oblivious of the fact that even taking into account the unpredictability of human conduct and lack of uniformity in human reaction, whether in the circumstances of the case, the behaviour is acceptably natural allowing the variations. In the case at hand, PW-9 was given a threat when her mother was forcibly taken away but she had the courage to walk in the night to her grandmother who was in her mid-fifties. After coming to know about the incident, it defies commonsense that the mother would not tell her other daughter and the son-in-law about the kidnapping of the deceased by her mother-in-law. It is interesting to note that the High Court has ascribed the reason that PW-7 possibly wanted to save the reputation of the deceased-daughter and that is why she did not inform the other daughter and son-in-law. That apart, the fear factor has also been taken into consideration. Definitely, there would have been fear because, as alleged, the mother-in-law had forcibly taken away the deceased, but it is totally contrary to normal behaviour that she would have maintained a sphinx-like silence and not inform others. It is also worthy to note that she did not tell it to anyone for almost two days and it has not been explained why she had thought it apt to search for her daughter without even informing anyone else in the family or in the village or without going to the police station. Nine persons including four witnesses belonging to the complainant party received injuries whereas as many as 14 accused persons received injuries including some who even suffered grievous injuries. Admittedly, there was a mob of about 75-100 persons who descended from the hill side to the place of occurrence by pelting stones and a melee followed. Not even a single witness including the injured witnesses could specifically state as to who had caused what injury either to the deceased or to the injured witnesses or to the accused. A very general statement has been made that the accused persons were armed with deadly weapons and caused injuries to the complainant party. In a situation where a mob of 75-100 persons entered into a clash with the complainant party it could not have been possible for any of the witnesses, who would naturally be concerned with their own safety and to save themselves from the assault, to see as to who had inflicted what type of injury either on the deceased or on the injured witnesses. In view of such omnibus and vague statements given by the witnesses, the Court below acquitted as many as 21 accused persons on the ground that there is no evidence on record to implicate them in the offences alleged.

PW 7 had witnessed the crime being committed by the accused at about 10.30 p.m. in the night and there was no electricity at the alleged scene of offence. According to PW 7, her husband also witnessed the crime, but they could not identify whether the accused were cutting into pieces the body of a dead person or an alive person. The prosecution also cited the precedent in Ram Narain Singh v. Additionally, PW 6 Anokh Singh's evidence was deemed unreliable as he stated he did not see Piara Singh receiving any injury from the accused. The defense also noted that PW 4 Murta Singh did not witness the incident directly and his account was not corroborated by the first information report.

Both the above witnesses are residents of Kota which is at a distance of about 150 kms. from Jhalawar town. The delay in the FIR reaching the Court is explained on account of the P.C. having attended to his work and taken a bus to the Magistrate Court. Therefore, there is no infirmity arising out of the said delay. The statements of PW 25 Mirza Majid Beg and PW 24 Mohamed Shakir were recorded after 3 days of the occurrence. facts_text:
These cases are heard together and are being disposed of by this common order as the issue involved in all these cases is similar. The petitioners have filed the present petition by way of Public Interest Litigation challenging the directions issued by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), dated 16.08.2018 permitting the use of Ethephon for artificially ripening of fruits. The first petitioner before this Court is a Director of College of Post Graduate Studies, Secunderabad and teaches 'sales and marketing' and the second petitioner is a retired employee of A.P.Transco and a Trade Union Leader, as stated in the writ petition. They have stated that they are public spirited persons and they are engaged in ensuring strict implementation of laws, especially those relating to safety of food.

Another application for intervention i.e., I.A.No.2 of 2021 in W.P. (PIL) No.176 of 2020 has been filed by M/s.Heighten Innovative Solutions Private Limited, which is registered under the Companies Act and is engaged in the business of applying science and technology based solutions to reduce use of synthetic chemicals, including those in the pesticides/insecticides class, to promote organic and natural food production and consumption, reduce environmental and adverse health impacts on human beings and animals, and other life forms and promote development, pursue invention and innovation in the fields of agricultural and horticultural production and environmental protection. It is stated in the affidavit accompanying the application that it produces and markets En-Ripe for ripening of the climacteric fruits and En-Ripe capsulates ethylene gas which acts as a natural phytoharmone that is need for ripening, that En-Ripe has been evaluated by the Scientific Panel of FSSAI and has been deemed to be a safe source of ethylene for artificial ripening of fruits in crates and boxes and that En-Ripe is comprised only of biologically safe ingredients and is a novel product. A counter affidavit has been filed on behalf of the respondent No.1/Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. It has been stated that various orders and regulations of FSSAI are based upon expert opinion of the Scientific Panel and Scientific Committee of FSSAI. It has been further stated that FSS (Prohibition) Regulations was published in the Gazette on 23.08.2016 and various representations were received by FSSAI with regard to implementation and clarification in respect of source of Ethylene gas, use of Ethephon to generate Ethylene gas, measurement of Ethylene gas concentration etc. It has been further stated that the Scientific Panel on Fruits and Vegetables in its 11th Meeting held on 05.01.2018 recommended that a Working Group may be considered after approval of the Scientific Committee and after great deliberations, an order was passed on 16.08.2018 regarding grant of permission for use of Ethephon for artificial ripening of fruits and in exercise of powers conferred under Section 16(5) of the Food Safety and Standards Act.

Earlier carbide gas was used for the purpose of ripening of fruits and the FSSAI after scientific study on the subject, has banned the use of carbide gas and Acetylene gas due to its potential health hazards. The FSSAI has thereafter issued a Notification after conducting scientific research to permit the use of Ethylene gas at a concentration upto 100 ppm for artificial ripening of the fruits and a Notification was issued on 23.08.2016. The Ethylene gas is used for the purpose of ripening of the fruits. It is nobody's case that the FSSAI has permitted spraying of Ethephon or the farmers/traders are spraying Ethephon over the fruits and on the contrary a very systematic activity is permitted for use of Ethephon in powder form to obtain Ethylene gas. Before the Delhi High Court, a writ petition was preferred in W.P.No.13025 of 2018 for quashment of Guideline Note No.04 of 2018 and the Delhi High Court while disposing of the aforesaid writ petition has directed the FSSAI to re-visit the guidelines with further discussion with experts and as a consequence, the matter was discussed by the 20th Panel on Scientific on 20.07.2020.

The writ petition has been filed for quashment of the Order dated 23.11.2019 issued by the Government of Telangana. In the aforesaid order, the Government of Telangana has directed the Department of Marketing to encourage the use of 'En-ripe' which is again other source of Ethylene. In Telangana, 80 % of the fruit area is occupied by climacteric fruits like mango, banana, and sweet orange which invariably have to be artificially ripened either at.

A new product 'En-Ripe' has emerged in the market using biologically safe materials encapsulating food-grade ethylene gas. It is sealed in a triple-layer pouch and can be used during transportation, at farm gates, and in market places. The product has been certified by the scientific panel of FSSAI as an innovative and biologically safe product. IIHR, Bengaluru, tested En-Ripe on climacteric fruits like mango and banana and found it effective. The Department of Marketing is instructed to encourage the use of En-Ripe and other safe sources of ethylene in market yards by facilitating demonstrations and sensitizing farmers, traders, and distributors about the dangers of using toxic chemicals for fruit ripening and degreening. The Telangana Food Standards and Safety Authority is tasked with surveying and testing fruit ripening agents to ensure they are free from harmful chemicals.
arguments_petitioner:
The petitioners have stated that Ethephon is an insecticide and is a hazardous substance. It is a corrosive phosphoric acid and an organophosphorous chemical and the Ethephon sachets, which are being sold in the market for ripening of the fruits, are highly risky. There is a possibility of leakage of Ethephon from porous sachets resulting in health hazards. Ethephon is recognised as potentially causing burns to the mouth, oesophagus and large number of deceases and therefore, as it is an insecticide, the same cannot be permitted to be used by issuing directions by the FSSAI. It has been further stated that Ethephon is registered as insecticide keeping in view Section 3(e)(i) and 3(e)(iii) of the Insecticides Act, 1968. Section 21(2) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 specifically states that no insecticide other than the registered and approved fumigants can be used directly on food. It has also been stated that the Regulation 2.3.14(1) of the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011 (hereinafter referred to as 'FSS (Prohibition) Regulations') prohibits any person from storing or exposing any insecticide like Ethephon. Therefore, the directions issued by FSSAI are in violation and ultra vires Section 21(2) of the Food Safety and Standards Act as well as Regulation 2.3.14(1) of FSS (Prohibition) Regulations.

A rejoinder has been filed by the petitioners and much reliance has been placed upon the Insecticides Act as well as Insecticides Rules, 1971. It has been argued that Rule 10C of the Insecticides Rules, 1971 prohibits manufacture, store or sale of insecticides in the same building where any articles consumable by human beings. Reliance has also been placed upon the FSS (Prohibition) Rules and much has been argued that the FSSAI does not have an authority to issue executive instructions, circulars, orders contrary to the provisions contained under the Food Safety and Standards Act.

Much has been argued before this Court that the Ethephon is a chemical substance and is used as an insecticide across the globe. It also finds place in the Schedule of the Insecticides Act read with Section 3(e) of the aforesaid Act. Reliance has also been placed upon the Rule 10C of the Insecticides Rules, which prohibits sale or storage of insecticides from the same building or place where any articles consumable by human beings are placed.

The petitioner argues that the order of the Government of Telangana does not mandate the exclusive use of 'En-Ripe' as a source of ethylene and that it only encourages its use as an alternative to existing compounds like Ethephon. The petitioner contends that the government's decision to sensitize farmers to use 'En-Ripe' does not restrict the sale or use of Ethephon, which is already in use.
arguments_respondent:
Mr. Ravinder Kumar Nagpal, an importer of Ethephon, has stated that earlier carbide gas was used for ripening of fruits and after a thorough study, the FSSAI has banned the use of carbide gas or acetylene gas due to its potential

It has been stated that Ethephon which produces Ethylene gas is used to promote fruit ripening, abscission, flower induction and other responses. It is a systematic plant growth regulator. It has been stated that Ethephon, though registered with Central Insecticide Board and Registration Committee, produces Ethylene, which is a growth hormone and is commonly used

In the present case, Ethephon is not being sold along with fruits and vegetables nor is being stored at the same place along with the fruits, which are kept for ripening. In fact, it is being kept as per the Guidelines framed by FSSAI in small sachets in powder form. The specifications of packing Ethephon provide that it has to be packed in 40-60 micron cellulose membrane paper and it generates Ethylene gas only.

The respondent states that the order of the Government of Telangana does not restrict the sale or use of Ethephon and that 'En-Ripe' can also be used. The respondent asserts that the government's decision to sensitize farmers to use 'En-Ripe' is based on research and does not interfere with the executive instructions issued by the government.
reasoning_text:
The aforesaid provision of law empowers the FSSAI to issue directions keeping in view the aim and object of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and in the present case, directions have rightly been issued and there is no conflict at all, as argued, with the statutory provisions as contained under the Insecticides Act.

The court notes that the order of the Government of Telangana does not mandate the exclusive use of 'En-Ripe' and only encourages its use as an alternative to existing compounds like Ethephon. The court further observes that the government's decision to sensitize farmers to use 'En-Ripe' is based on research and does not restrict the sale or use of Ethephon, which is already in use.
decision_text:
The petition is dismissed as the directions issued by FSSAI are found to be within their jurisdiction and do not violate the provisions of the Insecticides Act and the Food Safety and Standards Act.

The Court allowed the application for intervention and found that En-Ripe is a safe source of ethylene for artificial ripening of fruits. The Court also upheld the authority of FSSAI to regulate the use of Ethephon for fruit ripening.

This Court, in the light of the aforesaid, does not find any reason to interfere with the Order dated 18.08.2018 issued by the FSSAI nor with the Guideline Note No.04 of 2018 and therefore, the Public Interest Litigation deserves to be dismissed.

Resultantly, the WP (PIL) No.176 of 2020 and W.P.Nos.3272 and 3719 of 2021 are dismissed. There shall be no order as to costs. Miscellaneous applications, if any pending, shall stand closed.

facts_text: This Criminal Original Petition has been filed by the petitioner/A3 to quash the complaint in CC.No.131 of 2017 pending on the file of the Judicial Magistrate, Ambattur, Chennai. It is the case of the complainant that one Manna Health Mix, Southern Health Foods Pvt Ltd., is the manufacturer of the alleged health drinks and samples were lifted and the same were sent for the analysis and report was received on 10.06.2014. As per the report, the sample were found to be sub-standard, unsafe and misbranded. Thereby, the respondent/complainant had filed the private complaint against the petitioner and other accused for the offence under Sections 3(1)(zx), 3(1)(zz)(v)(x) and 3(1)(zf)(a-i) of Food Safety and Standardization Act, 2006. The subsequent samples also reveal that the product was sub-standard and unsafe.
arguments_petitioner: Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that admittedly, as per the complaint, the health mix which was subjected to test was produced by Southern Health Food Private Limited having office at AL-84, 1st Floor, 4th Street, II Main Road, Anna Nagar, Chennai - 40 and the petitioner is the nominee of the company and as per the Section 66 of FSS Act, a mandate is cast on the complainant to proceed against the company which has produced whereas in this case, the company was not impleded. The private complaint which has been filed without impleding the company is bad in law, thereby he prayed for quashing the proceedings. Further, the learned counsel would submit that in respect of a co-accused in the very same case, this Court in Crl.OP.No.19747 of 2017 dated 26.11.2021 taking into consideration that the company was not impleaded as accused, has quashed the proceedings.
arguments_respondent: The learned Additional Public Prosecutor submitted that as per the Section 66 of the Act, when the offences are committed by the company, the company has to be added as an accused. However, he would fairly concede that the company has not been added as accused in this case.
reasoning_text: Perusal of records including the complaint reveals that the health mix had been produced by M/s.Southern Health Food Private Limited. Accordingly, the entire prosecution launched against the petitioner cannot be sustained in the eye of law. Further, the continuation of the proceedings as against the petitioner is an abuse of process of law.
