facts_text:
That on 27−11−2017 at about 6.30 p.m. when the petitioner was sitting on the motor cycle KA−52−J−581 near Someshwara hotel, at Dobbaspet, at that time, driver of the KSRTC bus bearing No.KA−40−F−1168 came from Koratagere side in a rash and negligent speed and dashed to his right side of motor cycle, consequently petitioner fell down and sustained grievous injuries. That the injured was shifted to Dobbaspet Governemtn hospital and after first aid he was admitted at Sparsh hospital, Yeshwanthpur on 27−11− 2017 and was subjected for series of surgeries. That the injured/petitioner was readmitted for further surgery at Sparsh hospital on 24−1−2018 to 27−1−2018 and spent more than Rs.18 lakhs towards treatment, conveyance, nourishment and attendant charges. That due to accidental injuries, petitioner sustained permanent disability and lost his earnings.

In order to prove the above said issues, Smt.Latha/wife of the Petitioner has been examined as PW−1 and got marked Ex.P.1 to Ex.P.20 documents. One Vijay Kumar got examined as PW−2 and got marked Ex−P21. one Nandakumar R got examined as PW−3 and got marked Ex−P22 to 26. Dr.Kumaraswamy D.R. got examined as Ex.P−22. Dr.Nagaraj B.N. got examined as PW−5 and got marked Ex−P23. The respondent got examined one Ravishankar M.N.−conductor of KSRTC bus as RW−1 and got marked Ex−R1 and 2.

The incident involves a KSRTC bus bearing reg.No.KA−40−F−1168 and a motorcycle. The complainant/informant and eye witness Vijayakumar S/o Late.Hucchasiddaiah examined as PW−2. The respondent disputed the claim of the petitioner on the ground that the complaint was lodged after a one-day delay. The police registered a case under sections 279 and 337 of IPC. The alleged accident occurred near Someshwara hotel on a mud road outside the highway. The injured was taken to Dabaspet government hospital and then to Sparsha hospital, Yashavanthapura, Bangalore.

From charge sheet, police documents it clearly depicts that, the accident occurred and police have registered a case U/s 279 and 338 of IPC. From Ex−P4−wound certificate and Ex−P15− discharge summary, it is clear that, the history of the injury mentioned and the alleged accident occurred on 27−11−2017 at 22 hours. From going through the police records, it is clear that the case was registered on the basis of complaint/FIS given by PW−2 on 28−11−2017 at about 10.30 a.m. case was MVC No.4301/2018 SCCH 26 registered against driver of KSRTC bus bearing reg.No.KA− 40− F−1168. In the complaint itself vehicle number mentioned. On careful perusal of entire police records, it is clear that KSRTC bus bearing reg.No.KA−40−F−1168 and motor cycle bearing NO.KA− 52−J−851 were involved in the accident. The petitioner states that he was aged about 42 years as on the date of accident, due to the accident, he has sustained bilateral FTP, communitated fracture with hemorrhagic contusion (2) multiple fractures of left− fronto− temporo− MVC No.4301/2018 SCCH 26 parietal boni calvarium including facio maxillary bones with surroundings soft tissue edema and hemorrage, right (3) FTP SDH left fronto parietal EDH, (4) wedge compression fracture of L3 (5) fracture of right distal radius and left clavicle (6) Undisplaced fracture of left sacrum (7) fractures of second and 5th metatarsal bones with degloving skin in left foot and on other parts of body.

The petitioner, M.P.Paramesh, was involved in an accident in 2017. He was admitted to Sparsha super speciality hospital, Yashwanthpura, Bangalore from 27−11−2017 to 27−12−2017 under neuro surgical care. He was hale and healthy before the accident and was earning Rs.25,000/− p.m. from agriculture and real estate. The accident has hampered his routine work and livelihood.

Petitioner came to Sparsh hospital on 27−11−2017 with an alleged history of RTA. The patient was examined clinically, radiologically and investigated, diagnosed to have severe head injuries, bilateral FTP with hemorrahagic contusion with left FTP communited fracture, wedge compression fracture of L3, fracture of right distal radius and left clavicle, fractures of second and 5th metatarsal bones with degloving skin in left foot and on other parts.

The patient was conservatively treated and subjected to several surgeries, including wound debridement, closed reduction, pinning for displaced fractures, and tracheostomy. The patient was discharged on 27−12−2017 with advice for OPD follow-up. On 6−1−2021, the patient complained of inability to lift things with the left shoulder and grip objects with the right hand, leading to an assessment of 16% whole-body disability.

The petitioner was involved in an accident and subsequently admitted to Sparsha hospital on 27−11−2017 to 27−12−2017 as inpatient No.11887, and again on 24−1−2018 to 27−1−2018 as inpatient No.12790. He incurred medical expenses and sought compensation for various damages.

The claim petition filed by the petitioner under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The petitioner seeks compensation for various losses including medical expenses, loss of amenities of life, food, nourishment, conveyance, attender charges, and loss of income during the period of treatment. The respondent is the RC Owner of the bus involved in the incident.
arguments_petitioner:
The petition is filed by the Petitioner under Sec.166 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1989 seeking compensation for an amount of Rs.58,25,000/− for the grievous injuries sustained by him in road traffic accident. That the bus in question was on its schedule trip from Pavagada to Bangalore and the bus was being driven by its driver slowly and cautiously on the left side of the road by observing all the traffic rules and regulations and while it was so proceeding near Dobbespet close to Someshwara Idli hotel, at about 6.30 p.m. a motor cycle rider who was stated to be one M.P.Paramesh chatting on mobile placed in between the ear and shoulder by sliding his neck towards his right without wearing helmet for safety rode the motor cycle without observing the plying vehicles on the road and came in contact with the KSRTC bus on the left side and hit to the left indicator light of the bus suddenly and unmindfully.

In order to prove the actionable negligence, the wife of the petitioner i.e., natural guardian examined as PW−1 has MVC No.4301/2018 SCCH 26 entered into the witness box and filed her affidavit in lieu of examination−in−chief and document exhibited as Ex−P1 to 20. PW−1 reiterates the averments and the allegations made in the claim petition and deposed that, the accident has occurred solely due to the rash and negligent driving of the KSRTC bus bearing reg.No.KA−40−F− 1168 by its driver. The petitioner is also relied upon various copies of police documents which are produced and got marked FIR, complaint, sketch, spot mahazar, IMV report, wound certificate and charge sheet.

The petitioner claims that the KSRTC bus hit the motorcycle, causing severe injuries to the petitioner. The police have registered a criminal case against the driver of the KSRTC bus. The petitioner's wife produced FIR, complaint, sketch, spot mahazar, and IMV report before the Tribunal to evaluate the occurrence of the accident.

The petitioner has produced proper documents and evidence of PW−1 and 2 coupled with contents of documents to establish the accident occurred due to the negligence on the part of the offending KSRTC bus bearing reg.No.KA−40−F−1168. He also states that he was aged about 42 years as on the date of accident and sustained multiple injuries.

The petitioner contended that he was earning Rs.25,000/− p.m. from agriculture and real estate before the accident. He produced mutation extracts and RTC extracts to prove his income and agricultural work. He also presented medical records and testimonies to prove his disability due to the accident.

Petitioner underwent various tests including stroop test, WCST, auditory verbal learning test, complex figure test, fluency test, logical memory test, and intelligency test to assess cognitive and intellectual functions. The patient was alert, attentive, oriented about place, person, time, but not about date, month, and year. He was cooperative, understood the nature and purpose of the evaluation, and answered some questions correctly. He suffered severe memory problems due to encoding failures and severe level bilateral fronto-temporal lobe involvement, assessed cognitive disability of 75%. He is dependent on others for daily activities.

The counsel for the petitioner argued that the tribunal should assess permanent disability and award reasonable compensation based on credible evidence, even without examining the treated doctor. They cited a recent decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka supporting this stance.

The petitioner claimed compensation for medical expenses, loss of future earnings, pain and suffering, loss of amenities of life, food and nourishment, conveyance and attendant charges, and loss of income during the period of treatment.

The petitioner argues for the awarding of interest on the compensation amount based on recent decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and settled principles of law. The petitioner claims entitlement to interest at the rate of 9% per annum from the date of filing the claim petition till the date of realization.
arguments_respondent:
That the driver of the bus has controlled the bus in a very cautious manner and avoided causing serious accident. That the compensation claimed by the petitioner is highly excessive, exorbitant, imaginary and have no relations to facts and circumstances of the case. Hence prays to dismiss the above claim petition.

The respondent disputes the claim, arguing that the complaint was lodged after a one-day delay and that the bus was not involved in the accident. The respondent claims that the police colluded with the complainant and filed a false charge sheet without proper investigation.

The learned counsel for the respondent argued that the disability assessed by doctors who are not the treating doctors should not be considered, citing a decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka (circuit bench Gulbarga) that supports this position.

The counsel for the respondent objected to the medical bills produced by the petitioner, contending that the patient name mentioned in the medical bills was different from the petitioner's name stated in the petition.

The respondent did not provide specific arguments in the text provided.
reasoning_text:
Considering the above facts and circumstances of the case and on appreciation of evidence of Pw−1 and 2 coupled with contents of documents, the petitioner has proved this issue by producing proper documents. In a claim for compensation U/S.166 of MV Act, 1988, the claimant is to prove the incident only on preponderance of probabilities and the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt is not required as held by Hon'ble Apex Court in the decision reported in 2011 SAR (Civil) 319 (Kusum and others Vs. Satbir and others).

In the absence of material documents regarding the petitioner's avocation and income, the tribunal referred to the guidelines issued by Karnataka State Legal Service Authority to assess the notional income of the injured. The notional income of the injured is taken as Rs.11,000/− p.m. and the age of the injured is taken as 45 at the time of the accident.

The tribunal considered the recent decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka and meticulously perused the oral and documentary evidence placed by the petitioner. It noted that the petitioner was represented by his wife due to his inability to appear personally.

The tribunal considered the evidence presented by PW−4 and PW−5 regarding the petitioner's physical and cognitive disabilities. It also evaluated the medical bills and the genuineness of the expenses incurred by the petitioner.

The court considered the rate of interest on the compensation amount and followed the principles laid down in previous judgments. It determined that the rate of interest at 9% per annum is not on the higher side and is in line with the rate of interest on Nationalized Banks.

facts_text:
The plaintiff, M/s.BEML Limited, has filed an arbitration suit under Section 34 of the Arbitration & Conciliation Act, 1996 against M/s Veer Engineering Works and Hon'ble Mr.Justice (Retd.) Veeeranna G.Tigadi. The suit seeks to set aside an impugned award passed by the learned Sole Arbitrator in A.C.No.01/2019. The claimant, M/s Veer Engineering Works, has been providing maintenance and repair services for heavy equipment since 1986 and has worked with the respondent, a Central Government Public Sector Undertaking under the Ministry of Defence, for over 30 years. A Work Order was issued on 25.11.2013 and a Maintenance and Repair Contract was executed on 24.12.2013 for a period of one year, renewable for four years, at SAIL Rajhara (Dalli and Rajhara Mines).

As per the terms and conditions of MARC, the claimant was required to produce and deploy labor at the work site of the respondent. The claimant applied for and obtained the requisite labor license dated 23.09.2015 issued by the office of the Deputy Chief Labor Commissioner (Central), Ministry of Labor and Employment, Government of India. The aforesaid license was subsequently renewed by the claimant till 22.09.2017.

The claimant was misled by the respondent and made payments totaling €.22,75,003/- under protest, which were credited to workers' accounts and/or to the concerned departments. The respondent issued a letter to the Punjab National Bank to hold the process of bank guarantee invocation. The respondent responded to the claimant's notice seeking arbitration by referring the dispute to the Karnataka Arbitration Centre. The claimant requested the respondent to pay €.50,77,062/- due to increased rates and penalties. The respondent ignored the claimant's pleas. The claimant received a summons from the Court of Authority under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, for paying less wages to 89 workers, quantifying the deficit payment at €.21,85,636/-. The claimant invoked the Arbitration Clause, and the respondent negated the claimant's claims and referred the disputes to the Karnataka Arbitration Centre. The claimant clarified that disputes should be adjudicated under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

The claimant has suffered financial and emotional distress due to the respondent's failure to address wage discrepancies with SAIL. The claimant made payments directly to workers and faced summons for allegedly paying less than minimum wages. The claimant attempted to comply with governmental notifications and revised wage rates, incurring significant losses.

The respondent is a Government of India Undertaking under the Department of Defence Production Ministry of Defence. The respondent is a Heavy Engineering Industry inter-alia engaged in the manufacture and marketing of equipment and components used for Mining and Constructions, Defence and Aerospace, Rail and Metro, Dredging, etc. The respondent entered into Memorandum of Understanding dated 12.05.2008 and 26.08.2011 with SAIL for the supply and maintenance of heavy earth moving equipment at SAIL's Dalli and Rajhara Mines. On 10.05.2013, the respondent invited tenders for the Full Maintenance Repair Contractor for various equipment at SAIL Rajhara. The claimant was the successful bidder and the respondent sub-contracted the work to the claimant. A work order dated 25.11.2013 was issued to the claimant for a period of 1 year renewable for 4 years.

The claimant and respondent entered into a Maintenance and Repair Contract on 24.12.2013. This contract is for the period of one year renewable for four years. The contract stipulates the obligations of the contractor including the obligations to pay Minimum Wages to its laborers in accordance with the Statute. The contract was renewed from time to time, the last being from 01.12.2016 to 30.11.2017. The MARC was again extended for one month from 01.12.2017 to 31.12.2017. SAIL issued an Office Order dated 27.06.2017 regarding the course of action to be taken in view of the revision of Minimum Wages.

Despite the situation, the respondent endeavored to persuade the claimant to pay the labor. A meeting was held on 19.09.2017, where the claimant agreed to pay the difference in wages for June 2017 in September and July 2017 in October. Another meeting was conducted on 19.07.2018, where the claimant agreed to clear the pending payments of about ₹22,10,262 towards wages. On 30.10.2017, the Labor Enforcement Officer inspected the establishment at Mines Dalli Mines, BSP SAIL, and made a report against the claimant and the Mines Manager, alleging non-payment of minimum wages to 89 workers.

The respondent had performed its entire contractual obligations and the payment of Minimum Wages, as revised, was not the obligation of the respondent. The claimant requested the respondent to make the payment of Minimum Wages, but the respondent repeatedly approached SAIL to consider payment of the revised wages, which SAIL refused. The claimant agreed to pay the arrears effective from 19.01.2017 as per G.O. The respondent advised the claimant to pay the Minimum Wages to the Contract Laborers at the earliest. The claimant delayed the payment of Minimum Wages, leading to proceedings under the Minimum Wages Act.

The claimant made payments towards Minimum Wages after the proceedings were initiated. No compensation has been levied or paid by the claimant as on the date of filing of the claim statement. The claimant had issued notice invoking arbitration requesting the respondent to suggest impartial, fair and unbiased arbitrators. The respondent had replied to the said notice. The claimant and respondent entered into a contract with specific clauses regarding the payment of wages as notified by the government. The Labor Enforcement Officer has initiated proceedings against the claimant and SAIL which is pending.

arguments_petitioner:
The plaintiff argues that the impugned award dated 11.08.2020 and 17.10.2020 passed by the learned Sole Arbitrator in A.C.No.01/2019 should be set aside. They contend that the claimant, M/s Veer Engineering Works, has been diligently performing its duties under the Maintenance and Repair Contract since its inception, despite delays and rate reductions during negotiations.

On 16.01.2016, the claimant requested the respondent to consider increasing the basic rates of the equipment by 20% w.e.f., from April, 2016 due to an unprecedented increase in labor rates by about 30%. The claimant informed the respondent about the frequency of breakdowns in the equipment and the difficulty being suffered due to the increase in the cost of labor owing to the increase in Minimum Wages by the government. The claimant also raised concerns about the sudden spurt in capital costs and the financial hardships affecting them. The claimant sought payment of an amount of €.49,23,000/- against the pending statutory payments to be paid to the workers.

The claimant argued that the liability to pay for the surge in the Minimum Wages was to be borne by the respondent as per the work order. The claimant had already made payments amounting to INR 22,75,003/- directly to the workers' accounts and to concerned departments. The claimant also clarified that disputes should be adjudicated under the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

The claimant seeks a sum of €.50,77,062/- against the respondent for increased rates and penalties due to a drastic wage hike. Despite numerous attempts to resolve the issue, the respondent did not address the wage differences with SAIL, leading to additional costs for the claimant. The claimant also seeks expenses incurred in arbitration proceedings and interest on claims.

The claimant prays for an award for the following reliefs: (A) Directing the respondent to pay an amount to the appropriate authority as sought vide notice/summons dated 15.11.2018 issued by the Court of Authority under Minimum Wages Act, 1948 and Regional Labor Commissioner (C), Raipur; (B) Directing the respondent to pay an amount to the claimant towards increased rates due to unprecedented increase in variables during the execution of the MARC and towards damages and penalty of EPF on arrear salary; (C) Directing the respondent to pay an amount to the claimant on account of the expenses incurred/to be incurred by the claimant in the present arbitration proceedings; (D) Towards interest at 18% p.a. on each and every claim as enlisted above from the date of accrual till its realization; (E) Holding that the fee payable to the Hon'ble Arbitral Tribunal be solely paid by the respondent; and (F) Any further orders/directions as this Hon'ble Tribunal may deem fit in the interest of justice.

The claimant requested the respondent to write to SAIL for an amendment to the Work Order to enable payment of wages as per revised rates. The respondent wrote to SAIL on 05.07.2017 and again on 09.08.2017 requesting amendment of the Work Order. The respondent addressed several letters to SAIL requesting for a revision in the charges to enable payment of Minimum Wages at the revised rates.

The claimant argues that the respondent is liable and responsible for any increase or revision in the rates of wages and that the respondent is to compensate for any increase or revision in the rate of Minimum Wages. The claimant asserts that the rates were downsized by 30% and the contract was performed with monetary loss.

The claimant argues that the non-consideration of the request for payment of difference in wages is contrary to the statutory provisions. The claimant asserts that the respondent had committed to making the payment if SAIL approved it. The claimant also states that they admitted their liability towards the Minimum Wages and requested the respondent to stop the invocation of the bank guarantees.

The claimant contends that the respondent is liable to pay an amount towards deficit wages quantified by the Regional Commissioner, along with interest at 18% p.a. from the date of accrual of claim till the date of actual payment.

The Claimant argues that the respondent is liable to pay an amount towards increased rate of wages during execution of MARC, damages and penalty on EPF on arrears of salary with interest. Additionally, the Claimant seeks payment for expenses incurred in the present Arbitration proceedings.

The Arbitral Tribunal failed to recognize that wherever the parties envisaged for an additional claim of any statutory payments like taxes, levies etc., they have specifically provided so in the MARC or the Work Order. However, no such additional claim clause exists in relation to payment of the enhanced wages.

The Claimant has reiterated the averments made in its claim statement and written submissions filed before the learned Arbitral Tribunal. The Claimant has stated that the present petition under section 34 of the Arbitration & Conciliation Act, 1996 does not permit re-appreciation of evidence in any manner, since this is not an appeal on facts. The Claimant has prayed the Court to dismiss the petition with exemplary costs.

arguments_respondent:
The respondent, M/s Veer Engineering Works, asserts that it has been in the business of maintenance and repairs of heavy equipment since 1986 and has maintained a working relationship with the respondent for over 30 years. They argue that the contract was awarded after a delay of nine months, leading to a reduction in quoted rates by 30%. The claimant also issued two Bank Guarantees for performance and security deposits as per the terms of MARC.

The respondent issued a letter on 28.09.2018 shifting the entire liability of payment of wages to the workers on enhanced rates unto the claimant. The respondent also requested the invocation of the two bank guarantees amounting to €.14,39,760/- as were issued by the claimant in favor of the respondent.

The respondent negated the claimant's claims and absolved itself from all liabilities, shifting the onus on the claimant. The respondent intended to refer the disputes between the parties to the Karnataka Arbitration Centre.

The respondent filed statement of objections contending that the claim under reply has no basis in law or on facts and is therefore liable to be dismissed. The claim towards payment of Compensation of €.2,18,56,360/- quantified by the Regional Labor Commissioner (Claim No.1) is hypothetical and is also beyond the scope of authority of the Tribunal. The respondent is not a party to the proceedings under Minimum Wages Act, 1948 and Regional Labor Commissioner (Central) Raipur in Claim Application No: MWA-35/2018. The claimant postponed the payments leading to the initiation of the proceedings by the Labor Enforcement Officer against the claimant and SAIL being the Principal employer for which the respondent cannot be made liable. There is no contractual obligation on the respondent to reimburse the penalty if any, imposed by the authority for the claimant's failure to meet a statutory requirement. The claim for compensation is one for reimbursement of a penalty which may be imposed on the claimant for violation of a statute and does not arise out of the said work order. This claim is therefore beyond the scope of authority of this Hon'ble Tribunal.

The respondent submits that under the work order, MARC, and in law, the respondent has no liability towards the payment of wages to the labor employed by the claimant. The claimant is required to ensure payment of Minimum Wages as notified from time to time. The principal employer, SAIL, has refused to pay the revised Minimum Wages, and the claimant has not taken any action against SAIL. Therefore, the claimant cannot have any claim or cause of action against the respondent.

The respondent contends that the claimant has not produced the registered partnership deed to maintain its claim and is put to strict proof of the averments. The respondent states that the claimant accepted the terms and conditions of the work order and entered into the MARC with the respondent, thus has no locus standi to contend that the rates were downsized by 30%. The respondent asserts that the responsibility to pay the Minimum Wages to workers lies with the claimant, not the respondent.

The respondent argues that the obligation to pay Minimum Wages to the employees of the claimant is with the claimant itself, as per the terms of the contract. The respondent denies any assurances or commitments beyond the terms of the contract and work order. The respondent also states that they repeatedly informed the claimant about the non-payment of Minimum Wages and the potential consequences under the Minimum Wages Act.

The respondent denies the claimant's contention and reiterates that it is the claimant's responsibility to pay the Minimum Wages as notified from time to time. facts_text:
On 29.03.2012, the In-charge District Inspector, Legal Metrology, Warangal-II inspected the premises of M/s. Reliance Fresh Limited, Hanamkonda, Warangal District, along with his staff. On verification of different products, he found two retail packages in violation of the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011. Those two packages pertain to Modern Milk Classic Milk Bread. The net weight of the products is 400 grams. The Maximum Retail Price is shown as Rs.18/- (inclusive of all taxes) with a further mention 'Use by date: 3-4-12'. The said Inspector found that the manufacturer failed to declare the month and year of packaging on the said Milk Bread packages. On that, the said products were seized under a cover of panchanama. The act of violation was informed to the petitioner-accused No.1 through a notice. The appeal was preferred by the petitioner-accused No.1 on 25.10.2012 under Section 50 of the Legal Metrology Act, 2009.

Two Retail packages of Modern Milk Classic Milk Bread, Net Weight: 400 grams. M.R.P. Rs.18=00 (incl. of all taxes), Use by date: 3-4-12. The manufacturer has failed to declare the month and year of packing on the Modern Milk Class Milk Bread Packages.

As per the version of the respondents, the petitioner-accused No.1 has violated Section 18 of Legal Metrology Act, 2009 read with Rule 4 and Rule 6 (1) (d) of Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011. The appeal was preferred on 25.10.2012. On 26.10.2012, a letter was addressed by the Controller, Legal Metrology, Hyderabad, to accused No.2 that the case was booked as per the provisions of Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 and therefore, he may approach the District Inspector and pay the compounding fee within the time limit. On 01.11.2012, the Controller, Legal Metrology, Hyderabad addresses a letter to the petitioner-accused No.1 that the appeal was examined and the contention of the firm was rejected.

In the case on hand, the appeal was preferred on 25.10.2012, and the decision was taken on the very next day. The learned counsel for the petitioner projects that no such opportunity was given to the petitioner, violating the principles of natural justice. The complaint was filed by the respondents in a routine manner, and the learned Magistrate took cognizance of the offence without going through the contents of the complaint to observe whether the provisions of law mentioned therein are applicable to the facts of the case.

By the discussion that went on supra, it is clear that the provisions of Legal Metrology Act, 2009 and Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 are not applicable to the deviations as projected by the complainant who has filed the complaint. However, cognizance was taken.

In the case on hand, if the Magistrate had scrutinised the material produced by the complainant to satisfy himself whether the complaint stands to test of application of law, the result would have been otherwise, but the Magistrate did not do so. Before that, the Department of Legal Metrology ought to have examined the matter after lifting of samples to verify whether it has got the power to initiate proceedings in the light of the deviations noticed, but the Department did not do so.
arguments_petitioner:
The petitioner-accused No.1 through letter dated 04.09.2012 informed that the provision of law mentioned in the notice is not applicable to the seized products and instead Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the Rules made thereunder are applicable. He requested to give an opportunity of personal hearing.

Neither the provisions of Legal Metrology Act, 2009 nor the Rules regarding the Packaged Commodities are applicable to the facts of the case. The violation as projected, will not fall within the purview of the provisions of Legal Metrology Act, 2009. Without following the principles of natural justice, the appeal was dismissed and therefore, the complaint lodged is not maintainable. Though a complaint was lodged by the Department of Metrology, the learned Magistrate ought to have applied his mind while taking cognizance of the offence projected in the complaint, but without doing so, in a routine manner, he had taken cognizance of the offence and therefore, the said act of taking cognizance and issuing summons to the petitioner-accused No.1 are liable to be quashed.

Learned counsel for the petitioner-accused No.1 submits that when an appeal was preferred by the petitioner, an opportunity of hearing ought to have been accorded to him to submit his contentions and to explain the legal position, but without doing so, on the very next day of preferring the appeal, orders were passed, which is unjustifiable and which is in violation of the principles of natural justice. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that this act of the respondents is in violation of Section 50 of Legal Metrology Act, 2009.

Learned counsel for the petitioner argues that the principles of natural justice were violated as the personal hearing was lost, making the continuation of proceedings unsustainable. They rely on the decision of the Honourable Apex Court in the case between DHARAMPAL SATYAPAL LIMITED vs. DEPUTY COMMISSIONER OF CENTRAL EXCISE, GAUHATI AND OTHERS1, which emphasizes the importance of procedural fairness and the right to a fair hearing. The learned counsel also submits that the Magistrate ought to have gone through the contents of the complaint to observe whether the provisions of law mentioned therein are applicable to the facts of the case before taking cognizance of the offence.

Taking cognizance and summoning of the accused without application of mind is improper. The Magistrate must apply his mind to the facts of the case and the law applicable thereto. The Magistrate has to carefully scrutinise the evidence brought on record and may even himself put questions to the complainant and his witnesses to find out the truthfulness of the allegations or otherwise and then examine if any offence is prima facie committed by all or any of the accused.

When the petitioner-accused No.1 has preferred an appeal, the Controller of the Department of Legal Metrology, before whom the appeal is preferred, at least ought to have given an opportunity to the petitioner to project his contentions. This is the basic principle of natural justice and though it is reiterated under Section 50 of Legal Metrology Act, 2009, such an opportunity was not given. If such an opportunity was afforded, the petitioner ought to have projected his version, as projected before this Court.
arguments_respondent:
Accused Nos.2 and 3 responded to the notice issued and they accepted to compound the offence departmentally, but they did not do so.

The petitioner and other accused ought to have compounded the offences when an opportunity was accorded, but they did not do so and therefore, continuation of proceedings against them is desirable.
reasoning_text:
In the light of the aforementioned factual scenario, the point that emerges for consideration is: Whether there exists any justifiable grounds to invoke the powers granted under Section 482 Cr.P.C and to quash the proceedings that are pending against the petitioner-accused No.1 through C.C.No.7 of 2013, which is pending on the file of the Court of VI Additional Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Warangal, as prayed for.

Legal Metrology Act, 2009, as could be seen from the statements and objects, is an Act to establish and enforce standards of weights and measures, regulate trade and commerce in weights, measures and other goods which are sold or distributed by weight, measure or number and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. Thus, the main object and purpose of the Act is to enforce the standards of weights and measures and to regulate trade and commerce in weights and measures. Rule 6 (1) (d) of the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, which envisages the declarations to be made on every package, states that the month and year in which the commodity is manufactured or pre-packed or imported shall be mentioned in the package. Provided that for packages containing food articles, the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the rules made thereunder shall apply.

Before holding that the violation is covered under Rule 6 (1) (d) of the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, the District Inspector of the Department of Legal Metrology or the Controller of the Department of Legal Metrology ought to have gone through the proviso to the said Rule, which clearly envisages that for the alleged violation which was noticed by the District Inspector, the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 alone are applicable. When a specific mention is made that the provisions of another legislation apply, it implies that the said legislation, where such mention is made, does not apply.

The well-settled principle of law is that the procedure followed by the Courts of Law or the quasi-judicial authorities must be just, fair, and reasonable. The law as projected in Section 50 (3) of the Legal Metrology Act, 2009 envisages hearing before disposal of the appeal. The doctrine of procedural fairness is time and again enunciated by different Courts of law starting from the Honourable Apex Court.

By the bare reading of the provisions of law under which the complaint is filed, it is clear that the said enactments are not applicable to the facts of the case. Had the learned Magistrate gone through at least the provisions of law, which as per the version of the complainant, applies prima facie to hold that the accused have committed offences, the decision of the learned Magistrate would have been otherwise.

Having regard to all these aspects, this Court is of the view that there exist justifiable grounds to invoke the power of this Court to prevent abuse of process of law and ultimately to quash the proceedings, as sought for by the petitioner-accused No.1.
decision_text:
This Court is of the view that the case need not be permitted to continue as taking cognizance of the offence is due to non-application of mind.

Resultantly, the Criminal Petition is allowed. The proceedings that are pending against the petitioner-accused No.1 in C.C.No.7 of 2013 before the Court of VI Additional Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Warangal, are hereby quashed.

The appeal was preferred by the petitioner-accused No.1 on 25.10.2012 under Section 50 of the Legal Metrology Act, 2009. The petitioner-accused No.1 through letter dated 04.09.2012 informed that the provision of law mentioned in the notice is not applicable to the seized products and instead Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the Rules made thereunder are applicable. Two Retail packages of Modern Milk Classic Milk Bread, Net Weight: 400 grams. M.R.P. Rs.18=00 (incl. of all taxes), Use by date: 3-4-12. Neither the provisions of Legal Metrology Act, 2009 nor the Rules regarding the Packaged Commodities are applicable to the facts of the case. The violation as projected, will not fall within the purview of the provisions of Legal Metrology Act, 2009. Without following the principles of natural justice, the appeal was dismissed and therefore, the complaint lodged is not maintainable. Though a complaint was lodged by the Department of Metrology, the learned Magistrate ought to have applied his mind while taking cognizance of the offence projected in the complaint, but without doing so, in a routine manner, he had taken cognizance of the offence.

As per the version of the respondents, the petitioner-accused No.1 has violated Section 18 of Legal Metrology Act, 2009 read with Rule 4 and Rule 6 (1) (d) of Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011. The appeal was preferred on 25.10.2012. On 26.10.2012, a letter was addressed by the Controller, Legal Metrology, Hyderabad, to accused No.2 that the case was booked as per the provisions of Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 and therefore, he may approach the District Inspector and pay the compounding fee within the time limit. On 01.11.2012, the Controller, Legal Metrology, Hyderabad addresses a letter to the petitioner-accused No.1 that the appeal was examined and the contention of the firm was rejected. Learned counsel for the petitioner-accused No.1 submits that when an appeal was preferred by the petitioner, an opportunity of hearing ought to have been accorded to him to submit his contentions and to explain the legal position, but without doing so, on the very next day of preferring the appeal, orders were passed, which is unjustifiable and which is in violation of the principles of natural justice. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that this act of the respondents is in violation of Section 50 of Legal Metrology Act, 2009.

In the case on hand, the appeal was preferred on 25.10.2012, and the decision was taken on the very next day. The learned counsel for the petitioner projects that no such opportunity was given to the petitioner, violating the principles of natural justice. The complaint was filed by the respondents in a routine manner, and the learned Magistrate took cognizance of the offence without going through the contents of the complaint to observe whether the provisions of law mentioned therein are applicable to the facts of the case. Learned counsel for the petitioner argues that the principles of natural justice were violated as the personal hearing was lost, making the continuation of proceedings unsustainable. By the discussion that went on supra, it is clear that the provisions of Legal Metrology Act, 2009 and Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 are not applicable to the deviations as projected by the complainant who has filed the complaint. However, cognizance was taken. Taking cognizance and summoning of the accused without application of mind is improper. The Magistrate must apply his mind to the facts of the case and the law applicable thereto. The Magistrate has to carefully scrutinise the evidence brought on record and may even himself put questions to the complainant and his witnesses to find out the truthfulness of the allegations or otherwise and then examine if any offence is prima facie committed by all or any of the accused. The petitioner and other accused ought to have compounded the offences when an opportunity was accorded, but they did not do so and therefore, continuation of proceedings against them is desirable. facts_text:
The petitioner is a Proprietor of a Wholesale Distributing Agency operating from the premises in APMC Yard, Vijayapura and is engaged in the distribution of various products, including instant noodles manufactured by the ITC Limited under the brand name of "Sunfeast Yippee! Noodles". Sunfeast Yippee! noodles has got different flavours namely "Classic Masala", "Magic Masala" and "Chinese Masala". Each pack of the instant noodles contain noodle pack with a sachet of masala mix with cooking instructions provided on the pack label. The noodle block is made from wheat flour and the sachet of masala mix is made of spices, herbs, dehydrated vegetables etc. On 11.06.2015 the Food Safety Inspector, picked up a sample of Sunfeast Yippee! Noodles Classic Masala packet from the premises of the petitioner and issued Form VA under Rule 2.4.1(3) of the Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011. The collected sample has been sent to the Food Analyst, Belgaum for testing. On receipt of sample Food Analyst after analyzing the sample, gave a report on 23.06.2015 opining as under: "The sample conforms to the standards as per above parameters, but it is misbranded as per Rule 2.2.1(3) of rule 2.2 of Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011. Note: Due to non-availability of the facility test for lead and flavour enhancers (MSG) could not be performed. It is suggested to get the sample analysed for the same, from NABL accredited or referral laboratory."

Further, the first respondent - Food Safety Inspector orally sought information from the petitioner about the manufacturers' details from whom he purchased the product. Thereafter, petitioner provided necessary information and he received the notice on 10.8.2015 from the Additional District Magistrate - cum - Adjudicating Authority, Vijayapura stating that action has been initiated against the petitioner under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the petitioner was required to appear before the authority on 31.08.2015. Petitioner was also surprised to note that the Adjudicating Authority by order dated 11.8.2015, provided an opportunity to the petitioner to get the sample re-tested by Referral Laboratory. It is further contended that such an opportunity was extended to the petitioner only after the product has already been labeled as misbranded and the petitioner was not provided with a right to appeal the test report of the Food Analyst, before the Designated Officer as is provided under Section 46 (4) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and in conformity with Rule 4.2 of the Food Safety and Standards Rules.

It is relevant to note the instructions given by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India dated 24.09.2018 to all the States and Union Territories Commissioner of Food Safety. The order mentions that there are pending adjudication proceedings against FBOs in States/ UTs for 'mis-branding' due to the presence of the claim of 'No MSG' or 'No added MSG' on the packaging of Noodles and Pastas. The State Authorities were advised that specific enforcement / prosecution processes might not be launched against the manufacturers of Noodles / Pasta on account of presence of MSG/ Glutamic Acid unless it was ascertained that Monosodium Glutamate flavor enhancer (INS E-621) was deliberately added during the course of manufacture without required declaration on the label.

In 1998, the Prime Minister's Council on Trade and industry appointed a Subject Group on Food and Agro Industries, recommending comprehensive legislation on Food with a Food Regulatory Authority concerning both domestic and export markets. The Joint Parliamentary Committee on Pesticide Residues emphasized the need for a single regulatory body and expressed concern over public health and food safety in India. The Standing Committee of Parliament on Agriculture desired the expediting of the Food Law. The Law Commission of India reviewed Food Laws of various countries and recommended the new Food Law to promote food processing industries. The Group of Ministers approved the Integrated Food Law, named as 'The Food Safety and Standards Bill, 2005'.

The sample collected by the first respondent (Food Safety Inspector) is sent to the laboratory for testing the quality of the product. The laboratory report indicates that the food analyst was unable to find out the presence of MSG in the sample. The sample is declared as mis-branded without proper laboratory facilities to ascertain the presence of MSG. Without affording an opportunity for the petitioner, the Additional District Magistrate cum Adjudicating Authority initiates action and issues a notice for prosecution of the petitioner.

Having said thus, this court cannot turn blind eye in arresting menace of misbranded food items or substandard food items sold and consumed in the society day in and day out. In this regard, this court requested the learned Senior counsel Sri Udaya Holla and learned Senior counsel Sri Sajjan Poovaiah, who represents the petitioners in these cases to assist the court in framing proper guidelines for proper and effective implementation of provisions of Act by the Food Safety and Standard Department. Both the learned Senior counsels have promptly responded it and spent their time. They have analysed the interplay of different provisions of the Act and furnished a detailed flow chart for proper and effective implementation of the Act keeping in view of the safety of the general public at large and unnecessary hardship that would be caused to manufactures/importers as well.

The case involves the implementation of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The Food Safety Officer (FSO) is required to ensure that food samples are analyzed in laboratories accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL). It is contended that despite the absence of any method to ascertain the presence of MSG in the sample, the Food Analyst arrives at a conclusion that the product is misbranded. It is further contended that when the label mentioned that there is no added MSG, the question of misbranding the product does not arise and therefore, the further action based on the report given by the Food Analyst is contrary to the Act and Rules. It is also contended that there is no Laboratory established in Karnataka to find out the presence of MSG in a given sample. When such being the factual aspect, the report given by the Food Analyst as misbranded is per se illegal and therefore, no action should be initiated against the petitioner.

The principal ground on which the prayer is sought for, is that the presence of MSG cannot be determined with the laboratory facility available in Karnataka and further when the label of the product specifically mentions that there is no added MSG, in order to ascertain whether there was any presence of MSG which has been added to the product, a specific methodology has been prescribed and for which a laboratory report assumes great importance in arriving at a finding that there is a presence of MSG in a given product or not. Since the Food Analyst himself has clearly opined in the report that there is no facility available to ascertain the presence of MSG, launching of prosecution under the unconfirmed report that the product is misbranded has affected the rights of the petitioner and therefore, the

The globalization is taking place at a galloping pace, the food taste across the globe has also undergone a radical change since few decades. Multinational companies have catered to the needs of the general public in the form of packaged food. Practically, every house today consumes noodles. The after effects of consuming such 'fast foods' would not appear immediately and it may take some time for the people to understand the bad effects of fast foods.

The petitioner argues that the prosecution cannot be launched without providing an opportunity for the petitioner to prove contra. The department is required to establish the alleged offence by placing positive evidence on record. Expecting the petitioner to provide a report contrary to the report issued by the Food Inspector cannot be countenanced under the criminal jurisprudence.

FSO purchases samples of packaged food from a Food Business Operator for testing analysis. FSO gives Notice (in Form V-A) to the FBO, Manufacturer and Distributor Supplier, which also contains the testing parameters for the food sample. If FBO does not acknowledge the purchase of sample, witnesses have to be requested to be present for taking of samples. FSO ensures that four equal samples of packaged food are taken and sends one of the four samples to Food Analyst without opening the same by the immediate successive working day. The sample should be of the specified quantity. FSO should ensure that the sample of food is sent for analysis in a Laboratory which is notified by the Food Safety & Standard Authority of India and also accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories.

The petitioners submitted a flow chart that would meet all requirements for effective implementation of the Act. They argue that the flow chart would address the need for proper laboratory facilities and the establishment of NABL in the State of Karnataka.

There is no proper men support to implement the provisions of the Act inasmuch as atleast one person to be appointed as a Food Safety Officer in every Taluk and such an appointment has not at all taken place as per the Act and Rules. As of now, again an ad hoc arrangement is being made by deputing a person who is having necessary educational qualification from Health and Family Welfare Department in addition to discharge of work in his parent department.
arguments_respondent:
The respondent does not provide any explanation for launching the prosecution against the petitioner without providing an opportunity for the petitioner to prove contra.

The respondent submitted that the basic requirement for effective implementation of the Act is the establishment of NABL in the State of Karnataka. The department faces delays due to the lack of proper laboratory facilities and relies on private laboratories through a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). However, the acceptability of reports from private laboratories is doubtful and could lead to challenges in prosecutions.
reasoning_text:
The object of the Act is to address the multiplicity of food laws, standard setting and enforcement agencies which create confusion in the minds of consumers, traders, manufacturers and investors. The standards are often rigid and non-responsive to scientific advancements and modernisation.

The Bill aims to bring a single statute relating to food and provide for systematic and scientific development of Food Processing Industries. It proposes to establish the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India to fix food standards and regulate/monitor the manufacturing, import, processing, distribution, and sale of food. The enforcement will be through the State Commissioner for Food Safety, his officers, and Panchayati Raj/Municipal bodies. The Bill incorporates provisions of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and is based on international legislations and Codex Alimentaries Commission.

The court emphasizes the importance of public health and the duty of the state to maintain the general health of all public at large. The court also highlights the duty of the manufacturer to disclose the presence of artificial flavors or chemicals including MSG in a given product. The court relies on the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Vincent Vs. Union of India reported in AIR 1987 SC 990.

FSO should ensure that the Notice in Form V-A is also given to the Manufacturer and the Distributor or Supplier of such sample of food. FSO should also ensure that Form V-A lists out the parameters on which such sample of food will be tested/analysed. FSO should ensure that a sample of food must be taken in front of one or more witnesses and that the signature of such witnesses shall also be taken. FSO should take 4 (four) equal samples of food in accordance with Section 47(1)(b) of the FSS Act. FSO should send the specified quantity of the sample of food to the Food Analyst for analysis. If the sample of food which is sent for analysis is sold in a package, then such package should not be opened, and such sample of food should be sent by the FSO to the Food Analyst for analysis in its original condition without opening the package along with the original label. After the FSO collects the sample of food, then the FSO should send such sample of food to the Food Analyst by the immediate succeeding working day.

The court noted the difficulties faced by the department in effectively implementing the provisions of the Act due to the lack of proper laboratory facilities. The court emphasized the importance of establishing necessary laboratories for testing samples under the Act and highlighted the potential issues arising from relying on private laboratories.

Admittedly, such deputed staff is required to carry out the work of Health and Family Welfare Department as well as work under the Act. How far, such a person would be effectively discharging the duty is again doubtful and it acts as a hindrance in properly implementing the provisions of the Act.
decision_text:
The court allowed the writ petition filed by M/S Itc Limited against the Food Safety Inspector, holding that the petitioner was not provided with a right to appeal the test report of the Food Analyst before the Designated Officer as per the provisions of Section 46(4) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and Rule 4.2 of the Food Safety and Standards Rules.

Therefore, the order passed by the Additional District Magistrate cum Adjudicating Authority in pending case in case number CC No. 307/037/225/2015 cannot be continued and further proceedings needs to be quashed.

ORDER (i) This Writ Petition is allowed. (ii) Consequently, the initiation of the criminal proceedings which is now pending in CC No.307/037/225/2015-16 dated 25.11.2015 passed by the Additional District Magistrate-cum-Adjudicating Authority, Vijayapura, is hereby quashed. The deposit of money in terms of the interim order is ordered to be refunded to the petitioner.

The petitioner is a Proprietor of a Wholesale Distributing Agency operating from the premises in APMC Yard, Vijayapura and is engaged in the distribution of various products, including instant noodles manufactured by the ITC Limited under the brand name of "Sunfeast Yippee! Noodles". Sunfeast Yippee! noodles has got different flavours namely "Classic Masala", "Magic Masala" and "Chinese Masala". Each pack of the instant noodles contain noodle pack with a sachet of masala mix with cooking instructions provided on the pack label. The noodle block is made from wheat flour and the sachet of masala mix is made of spices, herbs, dehydrated vegetables etc. On 11.06.2015 the Food Safety Inspector, picked up a sample of Sunfeast Yippee! Noodles Classic Masala packet from the premises of the petitioner and issued Form VA under Rule 2.4.1(3) of the Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011. The collected sample has been sent to the Food Analyst, Belgaum for testing. On receipt of sample Food Analyst after analyzing the sample, gave a report on 23.06.2015 opining as under: "The sample conforms to the standards as per above parameters, but it is misbranded as per Rule 2.2.1(3) of rule 2.2 of Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011. Note: Due to non-availability of the facility test for lead and flavour enhancers (MSG) could not be performed. It is suggested to get the sample analysed for the same, from NABL accredited or referral laboratory." It is contended that despite the absence of any method to ascertain the presence of MSG in the sample, the Food Analyst arrives at a conclusion that the product is misbranded. It is further contended that when the label mentioned that there is no added MSG, the question of misbranding the product does not arise and therefore, the further action based on the report given by the Food Analyst is contrary to the Act and Rules. It is also contended that there is no Laboratory established in Karnataka to find out the presence of MSG in a given sample. When such being the factual aspect, the report given by the Food Analyst as misbranded is per se illegal and therefore, no action should be initiated against the petitioner.

Further, the first respondent - Food Safety Inspector orally sought information from the petitioner about the manufacturers' details from whom he purchased the product. Thereafter, petitioner provided necessary information and he received the notice on 10.8.2015 from the Additional District Magistrate - cum - Adjudicating Authority, Vijayapura stating that action has been initiated against the petitioner under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the petitioner was required to appear before the authority on 31.08.2015. Petitioner was also surprised to note that the Adjudicating Authority by order dated 11.8.2015, provided an opportunity to the petitioner to get the sample re-tested by Referral Laboratory. It is further contended that such an opportunity was extended to the petitioner only after the product has already been labeled as misbranded and the petitioner was not provided with a right to appeal the test report of the Food Analyst, before the Designated Officer as is provided under Section 46 (4) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and in conformity with Rule 4.2 of the Food Safety and Standards Rules. The principal ground on which the prayer is sought for, is that the presence of MSG cannot be determined with the laboratory facility available in Karnataka and further when the label of the product specifically mentions that there is no added MSG, in order to ascertain whether there was any presence of MSG which has been added to the product, a specific methodology has been prescribed and for which a laboratory report assumes great importance in arriving at a finding that there is a presence of MSG in a given product or not.

It is relevant to note the instructions given by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India dated 24.09.2018 to all the States and Union Territories Commissioner of Food Safety. The order mentions that there are pending adjudication proceedings against FBOs in States/ UTs for 'mis-branding' due to the presence of the claim of 'No MSG' or 'No added MSG' on the packaging of Noodles and Pastas. The State Authorities were advised that specific enforcement / prosecution processes might not be launched against the manufacturers of Noodles / Pasta on account of presence of MSG/ Glutamic Acid unless it was ascertained that Monosodium Glutamate flavor enhancer (INS E-621) was deliberately added during the course of manufacture without required declaration on the label. The globalization is taking place at a galloping pace, the food taste across the globe has also undergone a radical change since few decades. Multinational companies have catered to the needs of the general public in the form of packaged food. Practically, every house today consumes noodles. The after effects of consuming such 'fast foods' would not appear immediately and it may take some time for the people to understand the bad effects of fast foods. The object of the Act is to address the multiplicity of food laws, standard setting and enforcement agencies which create confusion in the minds of consumers, traders, manufacturers and investors. The standards are often rigid and non-responsive to scientific advancements and modernisation.

In 1998, the Prime Minister's Council on Trade and industry appointed a Subject Group on Food and Agro Industries, recommending comprehensive legislation on Food with a Food Regulatory Authority concerning both domestic and export markets. The Joint Parliamentary Committee on Pesticide Residues emphasized the need for a single regulatory body and expressed concern over public health and food safety in India. The Standing Committee of Parliament on Agriculture desired the expediting of the Food Law. The Law Commission of India reviewed Food Laws of various countries and recommended the new Food Law to promote food processing industries. The Group of Ministers approved the Integrated Food Law, named as 'The Food Safety and Standards Bill, 2005'. The Bill aims to bring a single statute relating to food and provide for systematic and scientific development of Food Processing Industries. It proposes to establish the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India to fix food standards and regulate/monitor the manufacturing, import, processing, distribution, and sale of food. The enforcement will be through the State Commissioner for Food Safety, his officers, and Panchayati Raj/Municipal bodies. The Bill incorporates provisions of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and is based on international legislations and Codex Alimentaries Commission.

Having said thus, this court cannot turn blind eye in arresting menace of misbranded food items or substandard food items sold and consumed in the society day in and day out. In this regard, this court requested the learned Senior counsel Sri Udaya Holla and learned Senior counsel Sri Sajjan Poovaiah, who represents the petitioners in these cases to assist the court in framing proper guidelines for proper and effective implementation of provisions of Act by the Food Safety and Standard Department. Both the learned Senior counsels have promptly responded it and spent their time. They have analysed the interplay of different provisions of the Act and furnished a detailed flow chart for proper and effective implementation of the Act keeping in view of the safety of the general public at large and unnecessary hardship that would be caused to manufactures/importers as well. FSO purchases samples of packaged food from a Food Business Operator for testing analysis. FSO gives Notice (in Form V-A) to the FBO, Manufacturer and Distributor Supplier, which also contains the testing parameters for the food sample. If FBO does not acknowledge the purchase of sample, witnesses have to be requested to be present for taking of samples. FSO ensures that four equal samples of packaged food are taken and sends one of the four samples to Food Analyst without opening the same by the immediate successive working day. The sample should be of the specified quantity. FSO should ensure that the sample of food is sent for analysis in a Laboratory which is notified by the Food Safety & Standard Authority of India and also accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories. FSO should ensure that the Notice in Form V-A is also given to the Manufacturer and the Distributor or Supplier of such sample of food. FSO should also ensure that Form V-A lists out the parameters on which such sample of food will be tested/analysed. FSO should ensure that a sample of food must be taken in front of one or more witnesses and that the signature of such witnesses shall also be taken. FSO should take 4 (four) equal samples of food in accordance with Section 47(1)(b) of the FSS Act. FSO should send the specified quantity of the sample of food to the Food Analyst for analysis. The case involves the implementation of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The Food Safety Officer (FSO) is required to ensure that food samples are analyzed in laboratories accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL). The Food Analyst must complete the analysis within fourteen days and send the report to the Designated Officer (DO). If the report is adverse, the DO must provide an opportunity for the Food Business Operator (FBO) to appeal. The DO can authorize the FSO to file an application for adjudication before the Adjudicating Officer, who is notified by the State Government and is not below the rank of an Additional District Magistrate. The petitioners submitted a flow chart that would meet all requirements for effective implementation of the Act. They argue that the flow chart would address the need for proper laboratory facilities and the establishment of NABL in the State of Karnataka. The respondent submitted that the basic requirement for effective implementation of the Act is the establishment of NABL in the State of Karnataka. The department faces delays due to the lack of proper laboratory facilities and relies on private laboratories through a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). However, the acceptability of reports from private laboratories is doubtful and could lead to challenges in prosecutions.

Multiple writ petitions were filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India against the Tamil Nadu Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act 2007 (Act No. 21 of 2007) and Section 6 of the Tamil Nadu Value Added Tax Act 2006 (Act 32 of 2006). The petitions challenged the amendments made by Act 21 of 2007, which introduced changes effective from January 1, 2007, alleging unconstitutionality and violation of various articles of the Constitution of India, including Articles 14, 19(1)(g), 20, 265, 300A, 301 to 304.

The learned counsel for the petitioners contended that the impugned amendment discriminates between co-developers who use goods purchased locally and those who purchase goods from dealers outside the state, which forces dealers to purchase goods from within the state and violates rights guaranteed under Part XIII of the Constitution.

The petitioners are civil works contractors and during the course of their business, they purchased cement, blue metal, iron and steel, wood, hardware, electrical goods, sanitary wares, electrical cables, paints etc., for execution of the work entrusted to them. facts_text:
The Drug Inspector lifted sample of Prchloroperazine tablets I.P. 5 mg, manufactured by M/S Associated Pharma, from the stores of Government Hospital Gandhi Nagar on 23.10.1998. The sample was divided into 4 portions and sealed in presence of Medical Officer In-charge Government Hospital Gandhi Nagar. One portion of the sample was sent to Government Analyst CFDL, Jammu for analyses, who declared the drug in question to be not of standard quality. The drug has been purchased from M/S Narayan Das Bhagwan Das, wholesale Druggist behind State Bank of India, Bhagirath Palace Chandni Chowk Delhi. The complaint was filed on 10.02.2000 and the learned trial Court issued the process against the accused including the petitioner No. 1 herein.

From the record, it is evident that the drugs have been supplied by the petitioner No. 1 to the Government Hospital Gandhi Nagar Jammu. The petitioner No. 1 appeared through Mr. Tarun Kumar Kochar on 03.03.2004 before the trial court and submitted the bail bonds. The allegations are serious in nature and are concerned with the safety and health of the common people.
arguments_petitioner:
There is no allegation in the complaint against the present petitioners that can even remotely suggest that the petitioners have committed any offence under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940. The proceedings are required to be quashed as the petitioner No.1 has not been arrayed as accused through someone and the petitioners are facing trial for the last 12 years and still some of the accused have not been served till date.

Petitioner No. 1 contends that there is a violation of section 34 (2) of the Act and that the person from whom the sample was lifted was not arrayed as an accused. Petitioner No. 1 also argues that there has been a delay in the conclusion of the criminal proceedings due to the failure to serve accused No. 5.
arguments_respondent: Section 34 of the Act has no applicability in the instant case and merely on account of delay, the proceedings cannot be quashed. The court also observes that the person from whom the sample was lifted was not arrayed as an accused, but this does not affect the proceedings against the other accused.
decision_text: This Court deems it proper to dispose of the present petition with direction to the learned trial court to conclude the trial within the period of 6 months from the date of receipt of order of this Court and further it shall be the responsibility of the respondent No. 1 to ensure that the accused No. 5 is served and in the event, the respondent No. 1 fails to do so, the trial court shall be at liberty to proceed in accordance with law and conclude the trial within the period mentioned above.

The writ-applicant is in the business of importing food products following all the rules and regulations prescribed under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Rules framed thereunder. The writ-applicant had imported organic food products from Italy which had arrived at Mundra Port. The products were (I) Sweet Potato, Pear, Banana and Carrot Puree (ii) Blue berry, Banana and Strawberry Puree and (iii) Plums and Puree vide Bill Entry No.5235754. The authorities at the port had demanded all the products from the writ-applicant and accordingly the writ-applicant had provided all the requisite documents. Conclusively, article also violates section-22, section-23, section-26 read with section-25 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 an clause (6) of the Food Safety and Standards (Import) Regulations, 2017.

The products were fruit purees labeled '6+ M', giving the impression they are intended for infants and children. The importer clarified that the products are suitable for individuals above 6 months and not for newborns. The products were also depicted as organic and proprietary food, despite lacking necessary certifications and bilateral agreements for organic recognition between India and Italy.

The writ-applicant, M/S Nutripure Fods Private Limited, is importing organic puree products from Italy. The respondent authority issued NOC for only one product out of the three and rejected the NOC application of two other products based on the label '6+M' and the lack of Bureau of Indian Standards certification.

The writ-applicant has imported the said product from Italy. There is no existence Bilateral Agreement or Multilateral Agreement between the Ital/EU and India for certification. Further the APEDA website recognizes only organic products exported from India to Europe Commission and Switzerland. Being aggrieved by rejection of the NOC dated 1.10.2021 the writ-applicant approached the Director (Import), New Delhi by way of preferring an appeal. The said appeal came to be rejected. The writ-applicant argues that the products comply with the Regulation of the Food Safety and Standards (Import) Regulations, 2017 and are standardized as per Regulation 2.3.12 of the FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011.
arguments_respondent:
The respondent argued that the products violated BIS standards and could not be sold as 'organic'. They contended that the labeling did not comply with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and Import Regulations.

Mr. Devang Vyas, the learned Assistant Solicitor General, submitted that no bilateral agreement exists between India and Italy/EU for mutual recognition of organic certification. He relied on the APEDA website, stating that the NPOP standards for production and accreditation system have been recognized by the European Commission and Switzerland for unprocessed plant products as equivalent to their country standards. He also submitted that the label '6+M' gives the impression that the product is intended for infants and children.

The respondent authority submitted that one time relaxation was granted to the writ-applicant and the consignment may be considered for sampling and testing subject to rectification of the labels and conditions as stipulated in decisions communicated by emails dated 22.10.2021 and 12.11.2021 respectively.
reasoning_text: The court examined the compliance of the imported products with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Import Regulations. It considered the validity of the NOC rejection based on the absence of BIS certification and the labeling issues related to 'organic' claims.
decision_text:
In view of the above-mentioned points, it is decided that the said consignment may be considered for sampling and testing by treating it as conventional food for which the imported has to strike out the word 'organic' and 'certifications logos related to Organic' with inedible ink wherever mentioned on the product labels. Further the importer will submit an undertaking to the Authorised officer that the product will not be sold as Organic in the domestic market, in view of the point (vi) above. Further, in view of point (vii) above, the imported shall rectify the product labels by striking out the term 'Proprietary Food'

In view of the above submissions, the respondent authority had acted in a fair manner and prayers as prayed for by the writ-applicant be declined.

In view of the above, this Court is not inclined to interfere with in the impugned orders and no case is made out to exercise extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, more particularly in view of the C/SCA/19953/2021 ORDER DATED: 10/02/2022 regulation which do not provide for import of organic products without re-certification. The present writ-application stands disposed of.
