facts_text:
The petitioner had imported a consignment of Bamboo Sticks and filed a Bill of Entry No.7512692 on 24.04.2020. Since the import pertains to plant, the import could be cleared on production of “No Objection Certificate (NOC)” from the Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage Department as per the Clause 3(16) of the Plant Quarantine (Regulation of Import into India) Order, 2003. The NOC was issued on 14.05.2020 but not uploaded in the ICEGATE server until 29.05.2020, leading to detention and demurrage charges.

The Government has enacted several laws to regulate importation of food items, livestock products, plant materials and other agricultural commodities into the country. The import of plants and plant materials is regulated as per the Plants, Fruits and Seeds (Regulation of Import into India) Order, 1989 issued under the Destructive Insects and Pests Act, 1914 to prevent introduction of exotic pests and diseases into the country. The Customs has a pivotal role to play because, it is the agency stationed at the border to enforce the rules, regulations and orders issued by various administrative Ministries.

The petitioner had filed Bill of Entry on 24.04.2020 and Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage Department had processed the “No Objection Certificate (NOC)” on 14.05.2020. The “No Objection Certificate (NOC)” was however not uploaded for the reasons not known to the petitioner. Therefore, the petitioner kept sending representations to Help Desk of the Customs ICEGATE. Ultimately, “No Objection Certificate (NOC)” dated 14.05.2020 was uploaded only on 25.05.2020.
arguments_petitioner:
The petitioner argues that the delay in uploading the NOC was due to technical issues and not their fault. They request a Detention Certificate to claim refunds for the detention and demurrage charges incurred.

The learned counsel for the petitioner has drawn attention to Circular No.9/2015 - Cus., dated 31.03.2015 of the Central Board of Excise & Customs. The learned counsel for the petitioner submits that entire process is seamless after the issue of above circular and a specific reference was made to Paragraph No.3(ii), (v), (vi) & (vii) from the said Circular. It is submitted that there is no question of approaching any of the department to whom a sample of consignments was sent for testing or for obtaining a “No Objection Certificate (NOC)”. All that is required is to upload the Bill of Entry and once the Bill of Entry is uploaded, the system itself will not directly communicate with the respective departments.

The petitioner has asked for a “Detention Certificate” for the period from 15.05.2020 to 25.05.2020. The method of filing of Bill of Entry and Exchange of information for assessment is online in the ICEGATE. Therefore, the delay on account of any technical glitches / error in uploading the relevant information document by the concerned Department cannot saddle an importer with liability unless the delay was itself on account of the importer.
arguments_respondent:
The respondent argues that the delay is due to the petitioner's failure to ensure the NOC was uploaded in the ICEGATE server. After 2011, all documents for assessment have been filed online under the Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration) Regulations, 2011.

The learned Senior Panel Counsel for the respondent further submits that the petitioner has not followed the procedure under the provisions of the Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration and Paperless Processing) Regulations, 2018 and thus there was a delay in uploading of the “No Objection Certificate (NOC)” from the Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage Department. The learned Senior Panel Counsel further submits that non-availability of “No Objection Certificate (NOC)” from Plant Quarantine did not fall under the instruction dated 01.12.1976 quoted by the petitioner as is clear on perusal of the same.

The respondent vide impugned Communication has rejected the request of the petitioner stating that there is no provision to issue “Detention Certificate” due to the “Technical Error” in ICEGATE and therefore, the “Detention Certificate” cannot be issued as prayed for by the petitioner.
reasoning_text: The clarification of the Central Board of Customs in C.B.E.C.F.No.501/9/75-Cus.VI, dated 01.12.1976 is still relevant. The benefit of the said clarification will enure to the petitioner mutatis mutandis in the context of assessment of Bill of Entry under the Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration and Paperless Processing) Regulations, 2018. An importer cannot be denied “Detention Certificate” if the delay was not on account of any fault of the importer, but on account of the technical glitches in the system.
decision_text: In view of the above, this Writ Petition is allowed by quashing the impugned order and by directing the respondent to issue Detention Certificate to the petitioner within a period of thirty (30) days from the date of receipt of a copy of this order. No cost. Consequently, connected Miscellaneous Petition is closed.

facts_text:
This petition has been filed to quash the private complaint filed in S.T.C.No.643 of 2017 for the offences under Sections 55, 58, 59(1) and 63 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. On 22.08.2015 at 11.00am the Food Safety Officer conducted inspection in a shop belonging to the first accused and seized four packets of Cool Lip Filter Tobbaq and sent the same for analysis. From the report of the Analyst, it was found that the sample contains Nicotin, which is unsafe and thereafter on 24.11.2016, a letter was sent to the Central Food Safety Officer to give the name of the manufacturer and after receipt of reply, the present prosecution has been launched.

The charge against the petitioner indicates that some tobacco products were seized from A1, who is not connected with the present petitioner. The prosecution does not claim that the product was supplied for sale in Tamil Nadu by the manufacturers. The sale and manufacture of such products are not totally prohibited in some states. The referral lab report indicates that the seized products are only tobacco products and not food products.
arguments_petitioner: The petitioner is only the manufacturer and the petitioner Company has also been registered with Tobacco Board. The petitioner is no way responsible for the sale of the product in Tamil Nadu and his area of operation is only Haryana. The product seized by the Food Safety Officer is a Tobacco product and it is not a food product and only when the tobacco is mixed with any food product, the same can be construed as an offence. The referral lab report also clearly indicates that the Tobacco is not a food product and it falls only under the category of tobacco products.
arguments_respondent: The report of the Food Analyst clearly shows that the sample sent for analysis contains Nicotin, which is unsafe to use. When the petitioner himself has admitted that he is the manufacturer, he is also liable to be prosecuted.
reasoning_text:
Normally, this Court would be reluctant to interfere with the complaint, but at the same time when the materials relied upon by the prosecution, in the considered view of the Court, do not constitute any offence against the person and continuation of the prosecution is a sheer waste of resources.

This Court finds that there is no nexus between the sale and supply by the manufacturer and the manufacturing of the product is permitted in other states. The continuation of prosecution against the present petitioner is a mere waste of time and futile exercise.
decision_text: Accordingly, this Criminal Original Petition is allowed and the case in S.T.C.No.643 of 2017 pending on the file of Judicial Magistrate No.1, Namakkal District is quashed. Consequently, the connected miscellaneous petitions are closed.

facts_text:
The petitioner, M.Sowmiya Sundari, was appointed as a designated officer under section 36 of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 as per Order of appointment of the second respondent in R.No.961/2017/FSSA, dated 21.09.2017. She has completed in-service training and has become a regular member of service. She was given additional charge of Ariyalur District in 2018 and performed well in implementing provisions of Food Safety and Standards Act 2006. She was transferred from Perambalur District to Thiruvarur District on 26.02.2021. On 02.08.2021, she was issued a notice stating poor performance and complaints, leading to her relief from the Food Safety Department.

The Writ Petition in W.P.No.30285 of 2022 has been filed challenging the charge memo for certain poor performance of the petitioner in the month of December 2021 and she has secured only 67 marks out of 100 marks and 22 marks out of 32 marks. Further, the charge is to the effect that she has not attended the office in the third floor and she has signed files sitting in her car and she has not regularly attended the office. The charge memo also indicates that the petitioner has not shown the performance. The petitioner was appointed as a Designated Officer by an Order in R.961/2017/FSSA dated 21.09.2017 on temporary basis.

Following charges have been framed against Dr. M. Sowmiya Sundari, Designated Officer in Thiruvarur Dist., regarding poor performance in the months of June and December 2021, false activity reports, and failure to review Food Safety Officers ATP every month. Charges are vague and not specific about any misconduct. The petitioner has already been relieved to the parent Department.

The petitioner has already been relieved to the parent Department. Now enquiry under 17B of Tamil Nadu Government Servant Conduct Rules, 1973 cannot be continued by the borrowing authority. Rule 16 of the Tamilnadu Civil Service Disciplaniry Appeal Rules 1955 also makes it clear that the enquiry has to be completed and the person has to be reverted. The charge is also general in nature without any specific instances. Admittedly, all the charges relate to complete lock down period.
arguments_petitioner:
The petitioner argues that she cannot be completely relieved from the Food Safety Department as she is a designated Food Safety Officer. The Senior Counsel for the petitioner submits that the reasons in the Order will have an adverse impact on her service records.

The learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner fairly submitted that he is not challenging the relieving Order. However, his only grievance is that the adverse remarks in the relieving Order has to be expunged. According to him, without any materials, such Orders have been passed. Similarly, the charge memo has been issued for the same allegations. Therefore, the petitioner has been relieved to the parent Department and charge memo cannot be continued by the borrowing department.
arguments_respondent:
The respondents argue that the Food Safety Rules 2011 and the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 came into force after a Government Order for creating a new Department called Tamilnadu Food Safety and Drug Administration. The petitioner has not shown involvement in various activities, leading to her relief from the Department.

The learned Additional Advocate General submitted that the charge memo has been issued as the petitioner has not performed properly while working as Food Safety Officer. The contention of the learned Additional Advocate General is that the charge memo cannot be challenged.
reasoning_text:
While the petitioner was working in the Health Department as an Assistant Surgeon in the Government Hospital, she has been appointed as a Designated Officer on temporary basis. It is relevant to note that after Food Safety and Standard Act was notified, Rules also placed on the floor and the Government has sanctioned the post of the Food Safety Designated Officer to each Revenue District. However, in order to appoint the persons, the Government has also framed separate guidelines as stipulated in the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006. To fill up the post, the persons who are already in service in the Health Department have been drawn and given temporary appointment.

Rule 16 of the Tamilnadu Civil Service Disciplinary Appeal Rules 1955 states that the power to impose penalties lies with the lending authority, not the borrowing authority. The borrowing authority must complete the inquiry and revert the person to the lending authority for further action. Since the petitioner has been relieved to the parent Department, the Food Safety Department cannot impose any punishment.

Where, on promotion or transfer or recruitment by transfer, a member of a service in a class, category or grade is holding an appointment in another class, category or grade thereof or in another service, State or Subordinate, no penalty shall be imposed upon him in respect of his work or conduct before such promotion or transfer except by an authority competent to impose the penalty upon a member of the service in the latter class, category, grade or service as the case may be.
decision_text:
This Court is of the view that once, the allegation has not been established, merely on the basis some complaint such adverse Orders cannot be sustained in the absence of any proof on that regard. Therefore, this Court is of the view that the adverse remarks in the relieving Order has to be expunged.

Accordingly, the adverse remarks against the petitioner in the impugned Order of the second respondent dated 18.03.2022 is expunged and the Writ Petition in W.P.No.18749 of 2022 is disposed of. No costs. With regard to the Writ Petition in W.P.No.30285 of 2022 is concerned, the Writ Petition is allowed and the charge memo issued by the second respondent dated 18.03.2022 is quashed. No costs. Consequently, connected miscellaneous petitions are closed.

facts_text: This appeal has been filed under Section 71 (6) of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 against the judgment dated 26.11.2021 passed by Appeal Tribunal (Food Safety Appeal Tribunal)/Sessions Judge, Raigarh, District Raigarh (C.G.) in Criminal Appeal No. 67/2020 whereby the order dated 24.02.2020 passed by the Additional District Magistrate and Adjudicating Officer, Raigarh, District Raigarh (C.G.) in Case No. 39/B-121/2018-19 has been upheld. By the order dated 24.02.2020, the appellants stand convicted and sentenced of fine as under: Conviction Under Section 52 of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. One of the grounds raised by appellants in the memo of appeal is that the sample of alleged packet of semolina (Chetak Suji) was taken by respondent No.1 from grocery shop of respondent No.3 on 21.11.2017 whereas complaint was filed on 05.12.2018 which is after one year and therefore in view of Section 77 of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, the Adjudicating Authority was not justified in taking cognizance of the offence.

facts_text:
The petitioner, MAHESH GARG, has filed a Public Interest Litigation seeking implementation of provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 in the State of Madhya Pradesh, particularly regarding the establishment of Food Testing Laboratories at Indore, Jabalpur, Ujjain, and Gwalior. The petitioner is a socially active person and former Corporator of Municipal Corporation. He had previously filed PILs on issues related to the construction of 'Treasure Island' and 'Noise Pollution'.

Respondent No.1 has filed a reply without disputing the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Rules as described by the petitioner in the writ petition. A scheme for strengthening food safety norms has been approved by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and is being implemented throughout the country. This includes capacity building of Food Testing Laboratories and support for NABL accreditation of State Food Testing Laboratories.

Respondents No.2 to 5 have also filed returns by submitting that the State Government is concerned about the health and life of people at large and has taken all steps to curb the adulteration. During the Simhastha 2016, number of mobile labs were established to collect the sample and conduct the preliminary tests of the food products. These labs have also covered the interior areas of the State during that period. Respondents have filed various reports collected during Simhastha, 2016 along with the return. The State Government has now allotted a sum of Rs.12,66,442/- for construction of boundary wall of the land allotted for Food Testing Laboratory at Indore. The Food Testing Laboratory at Bhopal has also been upgraded under the Scheme of strengthening of the Food Testing System. The Mobile Units are functioning since 16.04.2018 for performing primary tests and spot tests of milk and other food products. The State Government has also notified 3 Food Testing Laboratories situated at Indore by notifying in Gazette of India dated 06.12.2016. At present Food Testing Laboratory at Bhopal and 4 private Food Testing Laboratories under NABL accreditation are working efficiently. One civil suit has been filed by Rajendra Bithre in respect of land allotted for the construction of the Food Testing Laboratories. The Civil Court has granted a stay vide order dated 25.09.2018 in respect of said property, which is delaying the construction work of the boundary wall. The Ministry of Public Health and Family Welfare Department has sanctioned new posts for Indore Food Testing Laboratories. It has been decided to establish the Food Testing and Drugs Food Testing Laboratories at Indore, Jabalpur and Gwalior in step by step manner. The establishment of Indore Food Testing Laboratories as well as Gwalior, Jabalpur Food Testing Laboratories has been expedited. The decision has been taken on 23.02.2019 by Project Screening Committee (P.S.C.).

Respondents No.2 to 5 have filed responses to the above material that several samples have been sent to agencies based in Mumbai and Anand (Gujrat). It is further submitted that vide letter dated 15.10.2019, a sanctioned has been granted to construct a Food Testing Laboratories on land survey No. 141 (4000 sqft) leaving 450 sqft area on which state has been granted by the Civil Court and thereafter the amount of Rs.433.43 lakh was sanctioned in the first phase for construction work. The Collector, Gwalior vide order dated 16.09.2019 has allotted land bearing survey No.861 area 0.408 hectares for the construction of Food and Drug Testing Food Testing Laboratory. The Collector Jabalpur vide letter dated 04.10.2019 has allotted 1 acre land of survey No.4/2, 4/3, 4/4 and 5/2 area 3.666 situated at Village Mahgawa, Tehsil Rani District Jabalpur. On 14.11.2019, this Court has directed to submit a progress report. On 06.01.2020, the Deputy Director Food, Food & Drugs Indore has submitted a progress report to the effect that State Government has allotted the fund for construction of the Food Testing Laboratories at Indore, Gwalior and Jabalpur and after which 1,50,00,000/- (Rupees One Crore Fifty Lakhs) has been released. The approval of the layout plan for the Lab at Indore has been submitted before the TNCP. Thereafter another affidavit has been filed on 16.10.2021 submitting that the Lay-out has been sanctioned on 3.02.2020 and thereafter NIT has been issued on 12.05.2020 followed by the issuance of Work order on 13.08.2020 and now the contractor has started the work from 16.08.2020 with the condition to complete up to 12.11.2021. It is submitted that because of Covid-19, the delay has been caused in the completion of work but now the contractor has been directed to complete the work on or before 12.02.2022. The contractor has been paid Rs. 3 crores for construction work. 80% of work has been completed.
arguments_petitioner:
According to the petitioner, the Government of India has enacted the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 to check the standard of food and ensure the safety of human life. The Act provides for the establishment of different authorities at Central, State, and local levels for effective implementation. The petitioner states that only one Food Testing Laboratory is functioning in Bhopal, while others in Ujjain and Indore are not operational. This leads to delays in testing, benefiting offenders.

The petitioner has filed various figures to show that number of samples are pending for testing and one lab of Bhopal is not sufficient to handle such load.
arguments_respondent:

Two food testing laboratories are to be strengthened in Madhya Pradesh, with an approximate amount of Rupees Twelve Crore to procure necessary equipment and set up a Microbiology Lab. An initial payment of Rs.50 Lakhs has been released for infrastructure renovation in Bhopal. Additionally, three mobile food laboratories are proposed to be established in Madhya Pradesh.

The State Government is concerned about the health and life of people at large and has taken all steps to curb the adulteration. The State Authority has already created 51 posts of Designated Officer and Food Safety Officer at the local level and these posts are being filled by following due process of law. The Chief Executive Officer is already deputed in the state. The Food Testing Laboratory at Bhopal is fully equipped and able to cope with the load of the sample analysis of the entire State. The State Government has sent a proposal for funds to the State for NABL Accreditation. The land to establish the lab in Indore city has been already allotted vide order dated 30.01.2016 and the DPR for the construction of the lab building is already under progress. reasoning_text: The court acknowledges the petitioner's public-spirited antecedents and decides to consider the Public Interest Litigation on its merits. The Act of 2006 establishes the Food Safety and Standard Authority of India under Section 4, which controls the overall functioning and enforcement of the Act. It also provides for the establishment of State Food Safety Authorities in each State, headed by Designated Officers and Food Safety Officers, who have powers to take samples, seize food articles, and file criminal cases.

facts_text:
The petitioners, M/s. Mangalagiri Textile Mills Private Limited and Dr. Goli Nagasaina Rao, have approached the court against the actions of The State Bank of India and its authorized officer regarding certain financial matters.

The petitioners obtained loan from the SBI. The account having become a Non-Performing Asset (NPA), the petitioners applied for One-Time Settlement (OTS), whereunder the total amount to be paid was Rs.10,36,25,840.82. The application money of Rs.52,00,000/- was paid and SBI also issued sanction letter dated 23.11.2020. Though as per the terms of OTS, the first instalment to be paid was Rs.1.04 crores by 23.12.2020, the petitioners paid only Rs.32,00,000/- on 23.12.2020. As a consequence, SBI issued letter dated 29.12.2020 informing cancellation of OTS and asking the petitioners to deposit the entire Bank dues with interest at contracted rate. The request of the petitioners by letter dated 03.01.2021 for extension of time for payment of balance amount of first instalment of Rs.72,00,000/- was rejected by the SBI vide letter dated 21.01.2021. The same is pending challenge in W.P.No.2512 of 2021, before this Court. As the petitioners had defaulted, the SBI, prior to sanctioning OTS, on 27.02.2019 had already moved before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM), Guntur, in Crl.M.P. No.201 of 2019, under Section 14 of the Act for taking physical possession of the secured asset/property.

Based on the rival contentions to which learned counsel confined their submissions, three important questions arise for consideration and determination: (a) Whether the instant writ petition ought to be entertained? (b) Whether the time-limit under Section 14 of the Act of 30 days to pass an order, extendable in aggregate to 60 days, is mandatory or directory? (c) Whether, once the time specified in the warrant had elapsed, could possession of the property in question still be taken over, under the same warrant?

(1964) 6 SCR 654] the Constitution Bench considered the question whether the High Court of Assam should have entertained the writ petition filed by the appellant under Article 226 of the Constitution questioning the order passed by the Commissioner of Taxes under the Assam Sales Tax Act, 1947.

Surely matters involving the revenue where statutory remedies are available are not such matters. We can also take judicial notice of the fact that the vast majority of the petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution are filed solely for the purpose of obtaining interim orders and thereafter prolong the proceedings by one device or the other. The practice certainly needs to be strongly discouraged.

In Raj Kumar Shivhare v. Directorate of Enforcement [(2010) 4 SCC 772], the Court examined whether the alternative statutory remedy available under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 could be bypassed and jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution could be invoked. The Court noted that a writ petition should not be entertained while ignoring the statutory dispensation when a statutory forum is created by law for redressal of grievances. In Modern Industries v. SAIL [(2010) 5 SCC 44 : (2010) 2 SCC (Cri) 280], the Court held that where the remedy was available under the Interest on Delayed Payments to Small Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertakings Act, 1993, the High Court was not justified in entertaining a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.

In Authorised Officer, State Bank of Travancore v Mathew K C, (2018) 3 SCC 85, it was held that even prior to the Sarfaesi Act, considering the alternate remedy available under the DRT Act, the High Court should not have entertained the petition under Article 227 of the Constitution and should have directed the respondent to take recourse to the appeal mechanism provided by the Act. In Satyawati Tondon [United Bank of India v. Satyawati Tondon, (2010) 8 SCC 110], the High Court had restrained further proceedings under Section 13(4) of the Act. Upon a detailed consideration of the statutory scheme under the SARFAESI Act, the availability of remedy to the aggrieved under Section 17 before the Tribunal and the appellate remedy under Section 18 before the Appellate Tribunal, it was observed that a writ petition ought not to be entertained in view of the alternate statutory remedy available. In Kanaiyalal Lalchand Sachdev v. State of Maharashtra [Kanaiyalal Lalchand Sachdev v. State of Maharashtra, (2011) 2 SCC 782], it was observed that the High Court rightly dismissed the petition on the ground that an efficacious remedy was available to the appellants under Section 17 of the Act. facts_text:
The petitioner is a partnership firm conducting business activities in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The goods exported by the petitioner from Dubai were ordered to be confiscated by the Mundra Customs Commissionerate. The petitioner requested to take back the goods as unpaid owner but was denied. Two consignments of whey protein and food supplements were involved. Orders for these goods were received from customers in Malaysia and New Delhi.

Two consignments of goods supplied by the petitioner to M/s.S.V.Industries were transported on board in vessel MV Blandine from Jabel Ali Port and offloaded at Mundra Port for the importer M/s.S.V.Industries for clearance of goods from ICD, Patparganj. The goods were covered under the Bill of Entry No.3634298 dated 13.06.2019. An inquiry was conducted by the DRI authority in respect of the consignment assessed to duties at ICD, Patparganj and the inquiry extended to Mundra Port through the office of the respondent No.2. The goods were seized at Mundra Port after the investigation by DRI Officers. The DRI recorded statements of various persons including the petitioner's representative Shri Kshitij Sharma.

Based on intelligence, a consignment of goods declared as 'Laminated Floor Covering' was imported by M/s.S.V.Industries at ICD Sonepat on 13.06.2019. The consignment was examined and instead of declared goods, the concealment of Whey Protein and other dietary supplements was noticed, for which the case was booked by the jurisdictional Customs authorities after seizure of the goods under panchnama dated 14/15.06.2019 and investigation started. Further intelligence was received that two more consignments consigned in favour of M/s.SVI were lying at Mundra Port and there is also a concealment of goods other than the declared goods. The DRI had examined the contents of two containers at Mundra Port and found concealment of goods other than the declared goods and hence, they were placed for seizure on 23.07.2019 under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962.

Summons were issued to the importer M/s.SVI and partners of M/s.SVI, but the same were returned by the postal authorities. In response to the summons by email, reply was received from Shri Vinod Sonpal Singh that someone has misused their IEC and imported the goods in their name, for which complaint had been filed by them with the police station. They avoided to make appearance in response to the summons. M/s.Jet replied that they had exported certain goods to M/s.SVI, but after the goods were shipped, they had certain dispute with the consignee in respect of the payment issues. Therefore, container line agents were taking steps to find out new buyer and in case it was not possible they were asked to recall the said consignment. On 10.09.2019 the petitioner M/s.Jet informed that it was a case of wrong shipment.

Goods imported on account of M/s.SVI are alleged to be in violation of the provisions of Section 11(1) of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 read with Rule 14 of the Foreign Trade (Regulation) Rules, 1993 and para 2.01(b), 2.03(a) of the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-2020. The goods were seized in June, 2019, show cause notice was issued in January, 2020 and order in original has been passed in July, 2021.

This is a case of mis-declaration and hiding of the food articles under the pretext of mistaken export. The petitioner had been dealing with both these products and other products and the one to be sold to M/s.Muscle Shack SDN BHD, Kualalampur, is said to have been brought to India mistakenly. A show cause notice dated 21.01.2020 was issued and the petitioner has tendered a reply. Two Additional Commissioners were transferred during the proceedings.

The petitioner, a partner conducting business in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, had goods ordered to be confiscated by Mundra Customs Commissionerate. The goods were hidden in a laminated wooden box, suggesting an attempt to evade higher customs duties. The goods were tested and found to conform to health supplement regulations but were not prohibited or banned.

The case involves 16,614 packages of whey protein and food supplements valued at Rs.3,00,26,867/- and 464 cartons of wooden laminated flooring. The goods were assessed and the issue pertains to their re-export after paying appropriate fines and duties.
arguments_petitioner:
The petitioner argues that the Mundra Customs Commissionerate does not have jurisdiction to confiscate the goods. They request an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation as per Section 125 of the Customs Act, 1962. The petitioner also seeks the release of the goods pending the final disposal of the petition.

The petitioner argued that the mix-up occurred due to the possibility of mix-up in the godown and the goods actually meant for Malaysia based customer i.e. M/s.Muscle Shack SDN BHD had been erroneously shipped to Mundra Port for M/s.S.V. Industries. There had been no deliberate mis-declaration, but the goods actually meant for Malaysia based customer had been erroneously shipped to Mundra Port for M/s.S.V. Industries.

The petitioner is the owner of the goods and there are no other claimants. The petitioner ought to be given the option to pay appropriate fine in lieu of the confiscation of the goods in question.

Shri Kshitiz Sharma appeared on behalf of M/s.Jet with authority letter dated 11.09.2019 without showing the name and designation of the signatory of the said letter. He provided a packing list dated 30.09.2019 prepared by M/s.Jet and the details found in the said packing list were different from the details declared by the petitioner before customs authorities of load port authorities. He stated that M/s.Jet had not made any communication with M/s.SVI.

The order of absolute confiscation of the goods is not legal nor authorized, but is without jurisdiction under Section 125 of the Customs Act. The petitioner being the owner of the goods in question and when there are no other claims of ownership of these goods, the petitioner ought to be given an opportunity to pay appropriate fine in lieu of confiscation of such goods in question in accordance with Section 125 of the Customs Act. The goods are taxable in nature and allowing the option to pay the fine in lieu of confiscation of such goods at the earliest would be in the interest of justice. The goods are not in the nature of prohibited goods or contraband food or banned goods for import. There was no prohibition as regard the import of goods in the nature of Whey Protein and other dietary supplements nor in respect of wooden laminated flooring. 28 representative samples were drawn from the alleged concealed consignment imported vide Bill of Lading dated 02.06.2019 which were forwarded for testing to M/s.Anaytical and Environmental Services, Vadodara and in response to the samples conformed to the general provisions laid down under Regulation 6 (Health Supplements) of the Food Safety and Standards (Health Supplements, Nutraccuticals, Food for Special dietary use, Food for Special Medical Purpose, Functional Foods and Novel Food) Regulations, 2016.

The petitioner argues that the confiscation order should be challenged under Article 226 of the Constitution of India due to the total disregard of statutory provisions. They emphasize the goods are not prohibited or banned and request the opportunity to re-export the consignment after paying a redemption fine.

The petitioner argues that the statute provides for the grant of a request once made by the petitioner and that the respondents have disregarded the provision of law which they ought to have followed.
arguments_respondent:
The respondents alleged that the goods which were actually whey protein and other dietary supplements attracting higher rate of custom duties, were deliberately mis-declared as laminated floor covering for evading the custom duties. The DRI on 21.01.2020 called upon the petitioner to show cause as to why these 16,614 packages of whey protein and food supplements should not be confiscated under Section 111(d), 111(f), 111(g), 111(m) and 111(i) of the Customs Act, 1962.

The Deputy Commissioner of the Customs Department stated on oath that based on the intelligence, a consignment of goods declared as 'Laminated Floor Covering' was imported by M/s.S.V.Industries at ICD Sonepat on 13.06.2019. The consignment was examined and instead of declared goods, the concealment of Whey Protein and other dietary supplements was noticed, for which the case was booked by the jurisdictional Customs authorities after seizure of the goods under panchnama dated 14/15.06.2019 and investigation started.

Complaints were filed against the partners of M/s.SVI in violation of the provisions of Section 174, 175 and 176 of the Indian Penal Code before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gandhidham. Shri Kshitiz Sharma appeared and his statement had been recorded. He provided the copy of purchase order and other documents to show that the goods consigned on 28.05.2019 for the export of goods declared as 'Nutritional supplement of US Origin' and other goods was 'Laminated Wooden floor of CN Origin'. There were apparent discrepancies in various kinds between the export documents, which were provided by the Liner agent and the export documents.

According to the respondents, there is a contravention of various enactments and statutory provisions for which the goods imported on account of M/s.SVI can be considered being in violation of the provisions of Section 11(1) of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 read with Rule 14 of the Foreign Trade (Regulation) Rules, 1993 and para 2.01(b), 2.03(a) of the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-2020. The petitioner is not an entity which has been incorporated under any enactments made in India seeking the protection under Article 226 of the Constitution of India is impermissible and the petition itself is not maintainable. Appealable remedy is available statutorily against the order in original. Penalties of Rs.54,00,000/- have been imposed on M/s.Jet and penalties of Rs.37,00,000/- have been imposed on Shri Kshitiz Sharma, along with testing fees of Rs.1,65,200/- under Section 145 of the Customs Act, 1962.

The authority is sought to be relied upon would have no bearing as in the instant case, there has been a concealment under the pretext of importing laminated wooden box. The whey protein had been concealed and brought to this country, it is only to evade the payment of the customs duty. There is an efficacious remedy of Appeal which cannot be permitted to be bypassed.

The respondents argue that the goods were hidden in a manner indicating an intent to evade customs duties. They sent samples for laboratory testing, which confirmed the goods did not fall into the category of prohibited or banned goods for import.

The respondents argue that the concealment of goods would preclude the petitioner from availing the opportunity to re-export the goods.
reasoning_text:
The court considers the legality of the confiscation order and the availability of alternative remedies. The court notes that the goods are not prohibited or banned and that the manner of their concealment suggests an intent to evade duties. The court also refers to the provisions of the Customs Act regarding the option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation.

The court notes that even though there is an efficacious remedy of appeal available, the statute itself provides for the grant of such a request once made by the petitioner.
decision_text:
Eventually, the respondent No.2 has adjudicated and passed order in original on 27.07.2021 and directed absolute confiscation of the goods. It held that there was non-compliance of the provisions of Clause-IV of Chapter-1A of the General Notes regarding import policy given with the ITC (HS) Classification, 2017 and there was mis-declaration of description and quantity of the goods in the import documents with an intent to evade payment of customs duty and for smuggling these 16,614 packages of whey protein and food supplements having assessable value of Rs.3,00,26,867/- for evading the payment of duties.

Accordingly, this petition is allowed. The respondents are directed to permit the petitioner an option to pay appropriate fine and other imposable duties in lieu of confiscation of the goods in question in accordance with law.

Summons were issued to the importer M/s.SVI and partners of M/s.SVI, but the same were returned by the postal authorities. In response to the summons by email

Goods imported on account of M/s.SVI are alleged to be in violation of the provisions of Section 11(1) of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 read with Rule 14 of the Foreign Trade (Regulation) Rules, 1993 and para 2.01(b), 2.03(a) of the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-2020. The goods were seized in June, 2019, show cause notice was issued in January, 2020 and order in original has been passed in July, 2021. According to the respondents, there is a contravention of various enactments and statutory provisions for which the goods imported on account of M/s.SVI can be considered being in violation of the provisions of Section 11(1) of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 read with Rule 14 of the Foreign Trade (Regulation) Rules, 1993 and para 2.01(b), 2.03(a) of the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-2020. The petitioner is not an entity which has been incorporated under any enactments made in India seeking the protection under Article 226 of the Constitution of India is impermissible and the petition itself is not maintainable. Appealable remedy is available statutorily against the order in original.

This is a case of mis-declaration and hiding of the food articles under the pretext of mistaken export. The petitioner had been dealing with both these products and other products and the one to be sold to M/s.Muscle Shack SDN BHD, Kual

The petitioner, a partner conducting business in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, had goods ordered to be confiscated by Mundra Customs Commissionerate. The goods were hidden in a laminated wooden box, suggesting an attempt to evade higher customs duties. The goods were tested and found to conform to health supplement regulations but were not prohibited or banned. The petitioner argues that the confiscation order should be challenged under Article 226 of the Constitution of India due to the total disregard of statutory provisions. They emphasize the goods are not prohibited or banned and request the opportunity to re-export the consignment after paying a redemption fine. The respondents argue that the goods were hidden in a manner indicating an intent to evade customs duties. They sent samples for laboratory testing, which confirmed the goods did not fall into the category of prohibited or banned goods for import.

The case involves 16,614 packages of whey protein and food supplements valued at Rs.3,00,26,867/- and 464 cartons of wooden laminated flooring. The goods were assessed and the issue pertains to their re-export after paying appropriate fines and duties. The petitioner argues that the statute provides for the grant of a request once made by the petitioner and that the respondents have disregarded the provision of law which they ought to have followed. The respondents argue that the concealment of goods would preclude the petitioner from availing the opportunity to re-export the goods.

facts_text:
One R.Santosh Kumar ordered Cadbury Temptation “Almond Treat” through Grofers Online Shopping but received “Cadbury Temptation rum raisins – 72 gms” instead. He found worms in the chocolate after keeping it in the refrigerator for four days. A complaint was given by the father of the buyer, Ramesh Kumar. The Food Safety Officer took a sample of the chocolate, sealed it, and sent it for analysis. The report indicated that the chocolate contained dead worms, which is unsafe food under Section 3(1)(zz)(ix) of the Food Safety & Standards Act. The analysis report was sent to the Grofers Store on 15.09.2016 and again on 20.09.2016. Sanction was accorded on 18.08.2017, and a complaint was filed for the offence under Section 59(1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act.

The alleged occurrence took place on 24.08.2016, and the offence was noted on 06.09.2016 upon receipt of the analyst report. The prosecution ought to have been initiated within one year as per Section 77 of the Food Safety and Standards Act. The report of the Analyst was received by the Food Safety Officer on 06.09.2016. The Food Analyst sought sanction only on 18.08.2017, which is against the provisions of Section 42 of the Food Safety and Standards Act.
arguments_petitioner:
The learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that the mandatory conditions provided under the Food Safety and Standards Act have not been followed while lifting the sample. The sample was not divided into four parts as mandated under the Act. Additionally, the analysis report was not sent to the manufacturer at any point of time. The prosecution was launched with an inordinate delay, and no special circumstances existed to justify the delay beyond the period of limitation. Therefore, the petitioners sought to quash the entire complaint.

The sample was not divided into four parts as required by Section 47 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, and the manufacturer was not given the opportunity to have the sample tested by an accredited laboratory. The report was never sent to the manufacturer, and the prosecution was not initiated within the prescribed time frame.
arguments_respondent:
The learned Government Advocate submits that in a special case, the sample need not be taken in four parts and that this cannot be a reason to quash the proceedings.

The Food Safety Officer took steps to find out the manufacturer and due to administrative reasons, the sanction was accorded beyond the period of one year.
reasoning_text:
The court noted that the sample was lifted on 24.08.2016 and sent to the analyst only on 30.08.2016, with a delay of six days. The analysis report was received on 06.09.2016, indicating that dead worms were found in the chocolate, making it unsafe food under the Act.

The mandatory provisions of Section 47 of the Food Safety and Standards Act require the sample to be divided into four parts, and one part should be sent to the accredited laboratory if requested by the Food Business Operator. The report of the Analyst was received on 06.09.2016, but the Food Analyst sought sanction only on 18.08.2017, violating the provisions of Section 42 of the Food Safety and Standards Act.
decision_text: This Criminal Original Petition is allowed and the proceedings in C.C.No.3867 of 2017 on the file of the XV Metropolitan Magistrate, Georgetown, Chennai is quashed.

PW-1 stated that when his daughter had regained consciousness, she had told him that she caught fire while cooking food on the gas because when she tried to pick up Masala Dani (spice container) from the almirah, the bottle of kerosene oil fell over the gas burner. PW-1 reiterated that the accused-appellant neither misbehaved with the victim nor set her on fire.

The prosecution argued that the victim caught fire due to the accidental fall of a kerosene bottle over the gas burner while the victim was cooking food. They also stated that the accused-appellant did not misbehave with the victim and did not pour kerosene on her.

The learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the reverse burden put by Sections 29 and 30 of the Pocso Act applies only when the foundational facts in respect of commission of specified offences by the accused are proved by legally admissible evidence. In absence of proof of foundational facts with regard to commission of offence punishable under the Pocso Act, the reverse burden cannot be placed on the accused to prove his innocence.

Sri Saran submitted that the recording of the dying declaration by the Magistrate concerned and the fitness certificate of the doctor concerned for its recording is neither proved nor any such witness was examined to prove the same. Further, the dying declaration, on which reliance has been placed, is not even marked an exhibit and has not been put to the accused while recording his statement under Section 313 CrPC. This is a case where even during investigation the witnesses had given their affidavits resiling from the allegations made in the FIR, and those affidavits were part of the police report. Therefore, the court ought not have treated the appellant as an accused sent for trial much less raising a presumption of his guilt under Section 29 of the Pocso Act. There is virtually no legally admissible evidence to record conviction and therefore the award of the death sentence is completely unwarranted.

The principle that a person should be presumed innocent until proven guilty is a fundamental principle in criminal jurisprudence and finds support in Article 14 (2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. But in special circumstances the legislature may put a reverse burden on the accused to prove his innocence.

The prosecution argues that the burden to prove his innocence can be cast on the accused with the aid of presumptive clause only where the prosecution succeeds in proving the basic or foundational facts with regard to commission of the offence by the accused in respect of which the presumption is available to the prosecution under the statute.

Once the foundation of the prosecution case is laid by leading legally admissible evidence, it becomes incumbent on the accused to establish from the evidence on record that he has not committed the offence or to show from the circumstances of a particular case that a man of ordinary prudence would most probably draw an inference of innocence in his favour. The accused may achieve such an end by leading defence evidence or by discrediting prosecution witnesses through effective cross-examination or by exposing the patent absurdities or inherent infirmities in their version by an analysis of the special features of the case.

Petitioners argue that the presumption under the POCSO Act imposes a burden on the accused to expose himself to cross-examination, which amounts to testimonial compulsion and breaches the right to silence. They contend that the burden of proof is heavily tilted against the accused.

It is not sufficient if the accused/ prosecution makes a facial argument that there has been a miscarriage of justice warranting a retrial. It is incumbent on the Appellant Court directing a retrial to provide a reasoned order on the nature of the miscarriage of justice caused with reference to the evidence and investigatory process.

In a challenge to the vires of one such reverse burden clause, namely, the presumptive provisions contained in section 35 and 54 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act), the Apex Court in Noor Aga vs. State of Punjab, (2008) 16 SCC 417, in paragraph 33 of its judgment, observed: 'Presumption of innocence is a human right as envisaged under Article 14(2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. It, however, cannot per se be equated with the fundamental right and liberty adumbrated in Article 21 of the Constitution of India.'

The accused argues that mere registration of a case punishable under the statute, without proving the foundational facts with regard to its commission by the accused, will not ipso facto shift the burden on to the accused to prove his innocence.

Respondent argues that the statutory provisions do not violate constitutional guarantees and that the burden on the accused is partial and justifiable on grounds of public interest. Prosecution must establish foundational facts beyond reasonable doubt before the accused is obligated to rebut the presumption.

reasoning_text:
The prosecution examined only two eye witnesses, PW-2 and PW-3, who deposed that the deceased got burnt accidentally because the kerosene oil bottle fell over the gas burner while the deceased was cooking food. PW-1, the informant, is not an eyewitness and his statement in the FIR is hearsay and cannot be considered substantive evidence.

Chapter-I of the Act includes provisions relating to title, extent and commencement of the Act as also definitions of the terms used in the Act. Chapter-II relates to sexual offences against children. Sexual offences are categorised as: (A) Penetrative Sexual Assault; (B) Aggravated Penetrative Sexual Assault; (C) Sexual Assault; (D) Aggravated Sexual Assault; and (E) Sexual Harassment. Chapter II also provides punishment for the offences specified therein. Chapter-III relates to using child for pornographic purposes and punishment therefor. Chapter-IV relates to abetment of and attempt to commit an offence and punishment therefor. Chapter-V relates to the procedure for reporting of cases. Chapter-VI relates to procedures for recording statement of the child. Chapter-VII relates to Special Courts as also presumption as to certain offences and presumption of culpable mental state including application of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC), save as otherwise provided, to proceedings before a Special Court and for appointment of Special Prosecutors. Chapter-VIII relates to the procedure and powers of special courts and recording of evidence. Chapter-IX contains miscellaneous provisions.

To obviate the burden of proving sexual intent of the offender, the Legislature in its wisdom has put Section 30 in the Act which provides that where any offence under the Act requires a culpable mental state on the part of the accused, the Special Court shall presume the existence of such mental state though it shall be a defence for the accused to prove the fact that he had no such mental state with respect to that act charged as an offence in that prosecution.

Ultimately, while upholding the vires of the provisions of Sections 35 and 54 of the NDPS Act, in paragraph 54 of the aforesaid judgment it was observed: 'provisions imposing reverse burden, however, must not only be required to be strictly complied with but also may be subject to proof of some basic facts as envisaged under the statute in question.'

To ensure that a statutory provision putting a reverse burden on the accused does not violate the mandate of Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution, it has to be interpreted in a manner that it does not lead to absurd results such as mistaken conviction on mere failure to lead satisfactory evidence in defense after submission of police report.

The concept of presumption of innocence has, in recent times, been reversed in many situations by creating statutory presumptions like under sections 113A, 113B or 114A of the Evidence Act shifting the burden on the accused to prove his innocence. Section 29 of the POCSO is, therefore, a species of such exception to the ordinary rule of presumption of innocence and must be borne in mind while appreciating the evidence of prosecution witnesses in a trial under the POCSO Act.

The court evaluates the judicial pronouncements and finds that statutory provisions excluding mens rea or imposing strict liability are not uncommon and do not make such provisions unconstitutional. The burden on the accused should be partial and not shift the primary duty of prosecution to establish foundational facts.

Foundational facts in a POCSO case include proving the victim is a child, the incident occurred, the accused committed the offence, and physical injury is established with medical evidence. The prosecution must lay foundational facts with legally admissible evidence, and the accused must rebut it by establishing from the evidence that he has not committed the offence. The presumptive provisions of section 29 of the Pocso Act are applicable only to the offences specified therein and would not apply to prove an offence of murder punishable under section 302 IPC.

For proper appreciation of oral testimony, the testimony has to be read in its entirety. Picking up a stray sentence, out of context, and coming to a conclusion is not permissible. Neither the recording Magistrate nor the doctor, who certified the mental and physical condition of the victim, has been examined. The I.O. (PW-7) states that he came to know about the dying declaration having been recorded on 01.05.2019, the day the victim died. PW-8 does not proceed to record statement of the recording magistrate and does not enlist him as a witness. The dying declaration (Paper No.39 Ka/1) is on record but has not been exhibited and it has also not been put to the accused while recording his statement under Section 313 CrPC.

The principles that emerge from the decisions of this Court on retrial can be formulated as under: The Appellate Court may direct a retrial only in 'exceptional' circumstances to avert a miscarriage of justice; Mere lapses in the investigation are not sufficient to warrant a direction for re-trial. Only if the lapses are so grave so as to prejudice the rights of the parties, can a retrial be directed; A determination of whether a 'shoddy' investigation/trial has prejudiced the party, must be based on the facts of each case pursuant to a thorough reading of the evidence;

We examined whether we should summon the magistrate concerned to get the alleged dying declaration exhibited. We decided it would not be appropriate to summon the magistrate due to several reasons: the alleged dying declaration implicates three persons, out of which only one is named without proper identification; there is no forensic evidence such as DNA profiling to connect the appellant to the crime; there is no application moved by any party to summon the recording magistrate or the doctor to prove the alleged dying declaration; and the witnesses of fact have not supported the prosecutio
decision_text:
The trial court found the victim to be a minor and relied on the provisions of Section 29 of the Pocso Act to cast the burden on the accused to prove his innocence and, thereafter, by relying on the dying declaration and the statement of PW-2, held that the prosecution was successful in proving the charge against the appellant. Consequently, the trial court recorded conviction and awarded punishment.

On the question of sentence, learned counsel for the State submitted that since it is a case of rape of a minor and, thereafter, the minor was brutally burnt, which resulted in her death, death sentence awarded to the accused-appellant is not unwarranted, therefore, the appeal be dismissed and the death penalty be confirmed.

In absence of admissible evidence to prove the foundational facts of commission of penetrative sexual assault, or sexual assault, on the victim by the accused, the presumptive provisions of Section 29 of the Pocso Act would not get attracted as against the accused-appellant and, therefore, the judgment of the trial court is vitiated by a wrong approach in law.

Consequently, we have no hesitation in holding that the conviction recorded by the trial court is unsustainable and is liable to be set aside.

In view of the discussion above, as we have found that there is no worthwhile evidence on record to prove the charges against the accused-appellant, and that in the absence of proof of foundational facts with regard to the commission of specified offences punishable under the Act, the benefit of presumption would not be available to the prosecution under section 29 of the Act, we have no hesitation in allowing the appeal and rejecting the reference. The appeal is therefore allowed. The judgment and order of the trial court is set aside. The reference to confirm the death penalty is rejected. The appellant is acquitted of the charges for which he has been tried. He shall be released forthwith unless wanted in any other case subject to compliance of the provisions of section 437-A CrPC to the satisfaction of the trial court below.

The petitioner is the distributor of various food products in the district of Madhubani including non-alcoholic beverages. The prosecution case in this instance has been instituted on the written complaint dated 21.10.2020 of one Jitendra Kumar Singh, posted as Additional Station House Officer in Pandaul police station of Madhubani on the instructions of Madhubani Town police station (Madhubani Town P.S. Case No. 265 of 2020 dated 14.10.2020), he seized the stock from the petitioner's shop bottles of non-alcoholic drink viz. Kingfisher Ultra, Heineken and Warrior Strawberry, which was sent for chemical examination to the Chemical Examiner of the Excise Department of Government of Bihar on 15.10.2020. It was claimed that in the report of the Chemical Examiner dated 21.10.2020, it was found that in the sample there was fermented liquor having Ethyl Alcohol content of 0.8% v/v and 0.07% v/v respectively. It was thus alleged that the accused persons including the petitioner were manufacturing and selling alcohol mix drinks under the garb of selling non-alcoholic drinks. During the pendency of this writ application charge-sheet has been submitted against the petitioner on the basis of which cognizance has been taken against him under Sections 272, 273, 465 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code and Sections 30(a) and 35(e) of the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016.

It is well known that alcohol may occur naturally in a beverage. Scientific studies show that the content of Ethyl Alcohol in beverages is likely to change with change in climatic conditions, temperature, sunlight and other external factors and natural processes. In the State of Kerala and others vs. Unni and another (2007) 2 SCC 365, the Supreme Court while considering Rule 9(2) of the Kerala Abkari Shops (Disposal in Auction) Rules, 2002 in respect of toddy, it found that toddy fermented automatically after sunrise. If it were permitted to be sold within a short time after it is tapped, the content could be measured. But it was difficult to fathom as to at what point of time precisely, the Ethyl Alcohol content in such toddy would exceed the base standard. The climatic conditions also would be the reason for change in the measurement and that also is required to be factored in.

There appears to be only a minor excess of 0.8% in content of Ethyl Alcohol in the sample. The fact that same batch of seized NAB product, when tested by the same Chemical Examiner in the same Excise Laboratory, there was difference in the measurement which is a clear indicator of such analysis being prone to mistakes. Since there are two conflicting test reports, the benefit must be given to the accused. There is no prohibition on sale of non-alcoholic beverage. The object of the Prohibition Act is to enforce, implement and promote complete prohibition of liquor and intoxicants in the State of Bihar. A minor infraction would not make a non-alcoholic beverage and alcoholic drink.

A reference has been made by the counsel for the petitioners of a judgment of Courts of Appeal for the Tenth Circuit in Adolph Coors Company V. Nicholas Brady. In the aforesaid case, testimony had been given during Federal Alcohol Control Administration Hearings confirming that the disclosures of the alcohol content in some of the malt beverages were misleading and therefore they could be subjected to misuse. It was found that it was difficult to exactly measure the alcohol content as the content changed with the atmospheric pressures and varying temperatures. It was thus suggested there that some percent error of margin has to be provided for while measuring the content of alcohol in such drinks. It has been urged on behalf of the petitioners that for the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016 to be workable, the tolerance limit prescribed by the FSSAI (under Regulation 1.3.2) of its regulations which provides for a tolerance limit of ± 0.3% up to 20% has been prescribed for content of Ethyl Alcohol in a beverage.

The prosecution of the petitioner in the instant case is on a finding that some of the samples which were seized contained more ethyl alcohol than the tolerance limit. If the articles, so seized, were not sold as intoxicants or could be consumed as intoxicants, it would not fall under the category of liquor which is prohibited under the Act. A margin of error is inherent in such strict legislation. The facts of this case thus does not warrant the prosecution of the petitioner. There does not appear to be any intention on the part of the petitioner to breach the Excise Law.

The petition is allowed, and the tolerance limit prescribed by the FSSAI under Regulation 1.3.2 is applicable for the measurement of Ethyl Alcohol content in beverages under the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016.

For the reasons aforestated, the subject FIR viz. Pandaul P.S. Case No. 270 of 2020 is, hereby, quashed. The order of cognizance dated 08.02.2021 also is quashed. facts_text:
These cases are heard together and are being disposed of by this common order as the issue involved in all these cases is similar. The petitioners have filed the present petition by way of Public Interest Litigation challenging the directions issued by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), dated 16.08.2018 permitting the use of Ethephon for artificially ripening of fruits. The first petitioner before this Court is a Director of College of Post Graduate Studies, Secunderabad and teaches 'sales and marketing' and the second petitioner is a retired employee of A.P.Transco and a Trade Union Leader, as stated in the writ petition. They have stated that they are public spirited persons and they are engaged in ensuring strict implementation of laws, especially those relating to safety of food.

Another application for intervention i.e., I.A.No.2 of 2021 in W.P. (PIL) No.176 of 2020 has been filed by M/s.Heighten Innovative Solutions Private Limited, which is registered under the Companies Act and is engaged in the business of applying science and technology based solutions to reduce use of synthetic chemicals, including those in the pesticides/insecticides class, to promote organic and natural food production and consumption, reduce environmental and adverse health impacts on human beings and animals, and other life forms and promote development, pursue invention and innovation in the fields of agricultural and horticultural production and environmental protection. It is stated in the affidavit accompanying the application that it produces and markets En-Ripe for ripening of the climacteric fruits and En-Ripe capsulates ethylene gas which acts as a natural phytoharmone that is need for ripening, that En-Ripe has been evaluated by the Scientific Panel of FSSAI and has been deemed to be a safe source of ethylene for artificial ripening of fruits in crates and boxes and that En-Ripe is comprised only of biologically safe ingredients and is a novel product. A counter affidavit has been filed on behalf of the respondent No.1/Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. It has been stated that various orders and regulations of FSSAI are based upon expert opinion of the Scientific Panel and Scientific Committee of FSSAI. It has been further stated that FSS (Prohibition) Regulations was published in the Gazette on 23.08.2016 and various representations were received by FSSAI with regard to implementation and clarification in respect of source of Ethylene gas, use of Ethephon to generate Ethylene gas, measurement of Ethylene gas concentration etc. It has been further stated that the Scientific Panel on Fruits and Vegetables in its 11th Meeting held on 05.01.2018 recommended that a Working Group may be considered after approval of the Scientific Committee and after great deliberations, an order was passed on 16.08.2018 regarding grant of permission for use of Ethephon for artificial ripening of fruits and in exercise of powers conferred under Section 16(5) of the Food Safety and Standards Act.

facts_text: This criminal petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is filed seeking quash of F.I.R. in Crime No.945 of 2020 of Pattabhipuram Police Station, Guntur Urban District, registered for the offences punishable under Sections 420, 272, 273 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short "I.P.C."), under Sections 57(1), 58 and 59 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (for short "F.S.S. Act") and under Section 34(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Excise Act, 1968 (for short "the Excise Act").
arguments_petitioner: This is a covered matter in view of the earlier common order passed by this Court in Criminal Petition Nos.5421 of 2019 and batch and recent common order passed by this Court in Criminal Petition Nos.2966 of 2021 and batch, whereby the F.I.Rs. registered for the similar offences based on identical facts, were quashed for the offences punishable under Sections 420, 272, 273 of I.P.C. and under Sections 57(1), 58 and 59 of F.S.S. Act. Therefore, the petitioners, who are similarly placed, are also entitled for quash of the F.I.R. relating to the said offences.
arguments_respondent: However, the present case is not covered by the aforesaid earlier common orders of this Court relating to the offence punishable under Section 34(a) of the Excise Act. So, the F.I.R. relating to the said offence cannot be quashed.
decision_text: Resultantly, in view of the aforesaid earlier common orders of this Court and for the reasons stated therein, this Criminal Petition is partly allowed quashing the F.I.R. registered only for the offences punishable under Sections 420, 272, 273 of I.P.C. and under Sections 57(1), 58 and 59 of F.S.S. Act. However, the investigation shall go on in respect of the offence punishable under Section 34(a) of the Excise Act. Miscellaneous Petitions, if any pending, in this Criminal Petition, shall stand closed.

facts_text: The Petition relates to an e-tender issued under a notice dated 18th March 2021 by the State of Maharashtra for transportation of rice from Food Corporation of India godowns and for the supply of other food grains, pulses, oil, spices and condiments to schools under the mid-day meal scheme in Nashik District. The tender was for one year and was to cover 3983 schools. The estimated cost was Rs.36.92 crores. Technical bids were opened on 30th September 2021. Commercial or financial bids were opened on 22nd November 2021. The Petitioner itself says in paragraph 10 that it obtained the documents submitted by the 3rd Respondent from the online portal. It noticed several discrepancies that allegedly rendered 3rd Respondent ineligible.
arguments_petitioner: Mr Dhakephalkar raises at least three points of ineligibility, emphasizing that one of these is fundamental. That is the requirement that, as on the date of opening of the technical bids, 30th September 2021, every tenderer must have had a valid license under the Food Safety and Standard Act ("FSSAI license"). The 3rd Respondent did not have a license till as late as 25th November 2021. The challan submitted by the 3rd Respondent was dated 16th June 2021 for registration under the FSSAI Act. But the online status of the challan showed that the 3rd Respondent's application had been rejected.
arguments_respondent: Mr Kakade confirms that as of today no tender has yet been issued. He seeks time to file a proper Affidavit. He also states that the Affidavit of the tendering authority will be filed and served on or before 31st January 2022.
reasoning_text: In a pre-bid meeting, in response to queries raised by bidders, the tendering authority clarified that since the process of obtaining FSSAI licenses was time-consuming, and since there were lockdowns in various districts, a receipt or a challan evidencing an application for registration should be submitted and would suffice.
decision_text: Having regard to these circumstances, we are of the view that Respondents Nos. 1 and 2/tendering authority should not proceed with the award of the tender until a further order of this Court.

facts_text: The Applicant, apprehending his arrest, in connection with investigation of Crime No.19/2022 of Police Station Rajgad District Pune, under Section 188, 269, 273, 328 of IPC and Section 26(2)(i), 26(2)(ii), 27(3)(c), 27(3)(e) and 59 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and Section 2, 3 and 4 of the Epidemic Diseases Act, is seeking anticipatory bail.
arguments_petitioner: The learned counsel for the Applicant submitted that the only section which is non-bailable is Section 328 of IPC. The learned counsel has placed reliance on the decision of the Supreme Court in Joseph Kurian & Anr. Vs. State of Kerala and the order dated 30 September 2021, passed in a batch of Anticipatory Bail Applications No.944 of 2020 and others, at the Aurangabad Bench, in order to submit that in similar circumstances, it has been held that Section 328 of IPC may not be attracted as there was no attempt to administer any intoxicant or stupefying substance by the Applicant with an intention to commit an offence.
arguments_respondent: Learned APP seeks time to examine and go through the judgments on which the reliance is placed on behalf of the Applicant and then to make appropriate submissions to further assist the Court.
reasoning_text: Prima facie, it appears that the learned Single Judge sitting at Aurangabad Bench, has taken a view that Section 328 of IPC may not apply in such a case. The contrary view taken by the Coordinate Bench at Mumbai is subject matter of challenge before the Supreme Court in which interim protection has been granted.
decision_text: In the event of his arrest in connection with investigation of Crime No. 19/2022 of Police Station Rajgad, District-Pune, the Applicant be released on bail on executing a P.R. Bond in the sum of Rs.25,000/- with one or two solvent sureties in the like amount.

facts_text:
The seminal question involved in these cases is: whether it is open to the District Magistrate or the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate to appoint an advocate and authorise him/her to take possession of the secured assets and documents relating thereto and to forward the same to the secured creditor within the meaning of Section 14(1A) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002. The High Court of Judicature at Bombay vide judgment and order dated 6.11.2019 in Writ Petition (L) No.28480 of 2019 opined that the advocate, not being a subordinate officer to the CMM or DM, such appointment would be illegal. On the other hand, the High Court of Judicature at Madras vide judgment and order dated 18.3.2020 in C.R.P. No.790 of 2020 has taken a contrary view while following earlier decision of the same High Court on the reasoning that the advocate is regarded as an officer of the court and, thus, subordinate to the CMM or the DM.

In each case, the CMM/DM appointed an advocate under Section 14(1A) of the 2002 Act. In the Bombay High Court cases, the borrowers challenged the appointment of an advocate by the ACMM, arguing the overburdened CMM/DM had inadequate subordinate staff. In the Madras High Court case, the Bank took symbolic possession of the property and later sought the CMM's intervention to appoint an Advocate Commissioner, which was challenged by the borrowers.

The issue concerns the power of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate to appoint an Advocate Commissioner for taking possession of secured assets and documents under Section 14(1A) of the 2002 Act. The High Court of Kerala in Muhammed Ashraf23 and subsequent cases supported the appointment of an Advocate Commissioner. The Madras High Court in S. Chandramohan29 also upheld the power of the Magistrate to authorize an officer subordinate to them to take possession of the assets and documents.

The Advocate Commissioners appointed by the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate is in tune with Section 14(1-A) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002. As per Section 14 of the Act, the secured creditors can approach the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate/District Magistrate to take possession of the assets and documents of the secured creditor. The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, instead of personally visiting the spot to take possession of assets and documents, can very well appoint the Advocate Commissioner to visit on his behalf, as in the case of issuing of commissions under the Civil Procedure Code, as it is not possible for the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate/District Magistrate to visit personally to take possession.

The case involves a dispute regarding the appointment of advocates as receivers under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002. There is a conflict of opinion between the Bombay High Court and the High Courts of Kerala, Madras, and Delhi. The Bombay High Court took a strict interpretation of the statute, while the other High Courts allowed for more flexibility.

The expression 'any officer subordinate to him' has been used in several legislations enacted by Parliament/State Legislature. Similar expressions have been used in Articles 53, 154, and 311 of the Constitution of India and other legislations with slight variations to further the intent of the concerned enactment.

This Court has had occasion to deal with identical provision in the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, in the case of A. St. Arunachalam Pillai vs. M/s. Southern Roadways Ltd. & Anr. Even in that case, the Court had to resolve the conflicting views of the Full Bench Sections 23 and 24 and Section 37 of the Chemical Weapons Convention Act, 2000; Section 80 of the Bihar Reorganisation Act, 2000; Section 81 of the Uttar Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2000; Section 26 of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005; Section 22 of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007; Section 54 of the Legal Metrology Act, 2009; Section 43 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013; Section 86 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014; Section 5 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017; Section 45 of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017; Section 100 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.

The underlying purpose of the 2002 Act is to empower the financial institutions in India to have similar powers as enjoyed by their counterparts, namely, international banks in other countries. One such feature is to empower the financial institutions to take possession of securities and sell them. The same has been translated into provisions falling under Chapter III of the 2002 Act. Section 13 deals with enforcement of security interest. Sub-Section (4) thereof envisages that in the event a default is committed by the borrower in discharging his liability in full within the period specified in sub-Section (2), the secured creditor may take recourse to one or more of the measures provided in sub-Section (4).

After taking over possession of the secured assets, further steps to lease, assign or sale the same could also be taken by the secured creditor. However, Section 14 of the 2002 Act predicates that if the secured creditor intends to take possession of the secured assets, must approach the CMM/DM by way of an application, in writing, and on receipt of such request, the CMM/DM must move into action in right earnest. After passing an order thereon, he/she (CMM/DM) must proceed to take possession of the secured assets and documents relating thereto for being forwarded to the secured creditor in terms of Section 14(1) read with Section 14(2) of the 2002 Act.
