facts_text:
The petitioner married respondent No.2 on 16.05.2010. Out of their wedlock three children begotten, who at the time of preferring this petition were 2 years and 11 months (twins Tarun Singh and Paurush Singh) in the year 2017 when she was moved an application. The children were born in New Zealand. The respondent No.2 had taken the petitioner to New Zealand in October, 2010 and the she became a permanent resident of New Zealand since 2012. The husband has been living and working in New Zealand since 2002 and is also a permanent resident of New Zealand. On 06.08.2015 the petitioner was sent to India for the purpose of attending the marriage of the sister of the respondent No.2 and after reaching India, she was denied to attend the marriage and was forced to keep elder son with her mother in law-Laxmiben Gehlot in India and the husband told her that the twin kids are too small therefore, he would bring the elder son to New Zealand from India which never happened after 23.11.2015. She returned back to New Zealand with the twins. He, in the meantime, got her son admitted in the local school of India, although he was already enrolled in the Kindergarten at New Zealand.

On 15.11.2017, the respondent husband took all the children and left the wife. He refused to return the children and filed a petition for custody and divorce. The petitioner-wife filed a complaint with the commissioner office and informed the matter to the New Zealand and Indian embassies. On 24.12.2017, she was informed by the Ahmedabad Police that her children were admitted to Divine Public School in Mehsana. She was initially denied access but later allowed to meet the children for 10 minutes. She was forced to write that she would not take the children with her. The father admitted the children to the school stating they did not have a mother. She filed an application under Section 97 of the Code of Criminal Procedure seeking a search warrant, but the Chief Judicial Magistrate directed the matter to the Competent Family Court. On 25.02.2018, the petitioner returned to New Zealand and filed a custody petition in the New-Zealand High Court.

Petitioner, a citizen of New Zealand, seeks custody of her three children aged 6 and 5 years, who were taken to India by the husband. The New Zealand High Court has ordered the return of the children to New Zealand. The Family Court in India rejected the husband's petition for custody. The petitioner has been granted citizenship of New Zealand and plans to live with her children there.

The petitioner, Sapna Gehlot W/O Devendra Singh Gehlot, filed a petition for custody of her children. The respondent, Devendra Singh Gehlot, denied all averments and raised a preliminary objection on the ground that the custody of the children is with the biological father and cannot be construed as illegal or unlawful. He had filed divorce proceedings before the Family Court at Ahmedabad. The elder son Leon is in India since August, 2015, and the younger twins are in India since October, 2017. The respondent alleged that the petitioner was not taking good care of the children and her cruelty had crossed the limit.

The petitioner filed an application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code and the Family Court allowed the said application on 02.11.2018. Aggrieved respondent No.2 challenged the same by preferring First Appeal No.2 of 2019 and First Appeal 3 of 2019 against the divorce and custody of the children petition respectively. They were withdrawn with a liberty to file fresh proceedings before the concerned Family Court. The respondent No.2 preferred Family Suit No.830 of 2019 and this order of 25.02.2019 passed by the Family Court is in challenge before this Court and the divorce petition is part and parcel of the affidavit dated 25.02.2019 filed by the respondent No.2 before the New-Zealand High Court. The petitioner-wife has preferred an application for restitution of conjugal rights before the Family Court at Rajasthan. The said matter was dismissed for default on 19.07.2018. She had also preferred a complaint under the provision of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act and the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Ahmedabad entertained the application.

The children of the petitioner and the respondent No.2 are in India where the eldest one is taken since August, 2015 and the twins since October, 2017. The allegation of the petitioner mother that they have been removed from New-Zealand and retained in India by her husband without her consent, with a deliberate plan to lure her and the children to India has been extensively considered. The High Court of New-Zealand made an interim guardian's order on 20.02.2019, meaning thereby that the children were under the guardianship of the High Court of New-Zealand from 20.02.2019. The Court also directed the respondent No.2 to take all reasonable steps to ensure the children promptly return to New-Zealand.

The Court considered the evidence of the social worker and psychologist appointed to report on the children's welfare and best interests. The Court also noted the reports and evidence given by Oranga Tamariki Social Worker and the court-appointed psychologist. arguments_petitioner:
The petitioner seeks an order of return of minor children in consonance with the guardianship order dated 04.10.2019 passed by the High Court of New Zealand in SG vs. GSG, (2019) NZHC 2523 and other order dated 11.10.2019 on the ground that the children's removal and retention in India by the respondent Nos.2, 3 and 4 is completely illegal and wrong.

The petitioner argues that the children were illegally detained and seeks their return to New Zealand, citing her financial capability and employment status. She also mentions that the children were removed from the Divine Public School due to ongoing litigation between the spouses.

The petitioner argues that the husband is avoiding the implementation of the New Zealand High Court's order and that she has been deprived of her children. She requests issuance of a writ of habeas corpus to ensure the children are produced before the court and returned to New Zealand.

According to the petitioner, hurting of these allegations and casting stigma on her is only a plot to succeed in legal battle without any semblance of truth in it.

The petitioner emphasizes the need to implement the order of the New-Zealand High Court and highlights the unlawful removal of the children from New-Zealand by the respondent No.2. facts_text:
On 02.02.2019, the petitioner Ram Avtar was going to G.B Pant Hospital for his treatment from his house and when he was crossing the road at about 7:30 AM from MCD Parking JLN Road towards Gate No.7 of the G.B. Pant Hospital, then suddenly the offending motorcycle bearing registration No. DL−5S−CA−4634 which was being driven by its driver with two other pillion riders, at a fast speed, rashly and negligently, in a zig−zag manner, in complete contravention of traffic rules and regulations, without carrying for the other traffic on the road, and in the process hit the petitioner Ram Avtar. As a result of the impact, the petitioner fell down on the road and sustained multiple grievous injuries on his body including severe head injury. After the accident, the injured became unconscious and he was taken to Lok Nayak Hospital, Delhi where his MLC was prepared. Thereafter, the injured was shifted to Max Super Specialty Hospital, Patparganj, Delhi where he was treated till 10.02.2019. During treatment, the doctor diagnosed head injury and fracture in right leg of the petitioner.

The injured Ram Avtar was removed to Max Super Specialty Hospital, Patparganj, Delhi by his relatives where he remained admitted till 10.02.2019. He was diagnosed with B/L Temporal Haemorrhage contusion, right frontal hemorrhagic contusion with right temporoparietal SDH and fracture of 5th metatarsal right foot. Petitioner's family consists of himself, his wife, and a minor son aged about 16 years. His monthly family expenses are about Rs.20,000/- per month.

arguments_petitioner:
Ram Avtar testified that there was no zebra crossing and a traffic signal at the place of the accident. He had seen the vehicle before the accident and had already crossed more than half of the road. He denied negligence and stated he became unconscious after the accident. He also denied filing false documents.

According to the petitioner, the accident in question had taken place on account of the negligence of the respondent no.1 Shivam who was driving his motorcycle in a rash and negligent manner with two pillions at a high speed in a zig−zag manner. In this regard, the petitioner Ram Avtar has examined himself as PW1.

Petitioner Ram Avtar admitted in his cross-examination that there was no zebra crossing on the road where he was crossing. He was guilty of Contributory Negligence to some extent.

Petitioner claims he spent Rs.3,50,000/- towards his medicines, treatment, special diet, conveyance, and attendant charges. He also claims financial losses due to inability to continue his job as a labourer.

Petitioner claims he spent about Rs.30,000/- towards Conveyance and Rs.50,000/- for Nursing/Attendant Charges. He also claims a loss of income of Rs.1,50,000/- due to the accident. At the time of the accident, he was working as a labour on daily wages and was earning Rs.15,000/- per month.

Ram Avtar claimed compensation for the expenses incurred on medical treatment, conveyance, special diet, nursing/attendant, loss of earnings, and non-pecuniary losses such as mental and physical shock, pain and suffering.

The petitioner argues that the respondents are liable to pay compensation due to the violation of terms and conditions of the Insurance Policy and provisions of Motor Vehicles Act/Rules.
arguments_respondent:
The respondent no.1 Shivam and the respondent no.2 Shankar have not filed their written statement/ reply despite grant of sufficient opportunity. The Insurance Company has conceded that the offending vehicle i.e. motorcycle No. DL−5SCA−4634 was insured in the name of respondent no.2 Shankar. It is pleaded that the liability of the respondent no.3 Insurance Company is subject to the compliance of the terms and conditions of the Insurance Company as well as the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act by the respondent no.2 insured. It is further pleaded that during police investigations, it has been revealed that the respondent no.1 Shivam was not holding a valid and effective driving license authorizing him to drive the insured vehicle and according, he was also challaned by the police under Section 3/181 of M.V. Act as he was driving the motorcycle alongwith two other persons i.e. his mother Smt. Anuradha and his brother Sh. Sunder. It is also pleaded that the respondent no.2 owner of the vehicle in question has violated the terms and conditions of the Insurance policy issued by the respondent no.3 by allowing the respondent no.1, who is his son, to drive the insured vehicle without holding a valid and effective driving license.

Respondent no.3, ICICI Lombard General Insurance Co. Ltd., submitted that the vehicle was insured and a notice was sent to the owner, Shankar, to produce the insurance policy and driving license, which were not provided.

The respondent no.1 Shivam claimed that the accident in question had taken place on account of negligence of the petitioner himself who suddenly appeared in front of his motorcycle while crossing the road.

Respondent no.1 Shivam stated in his statement under Section 165 of Evidence Act that the accident occurred due to the negligence of the injured himself who suddenly came in front of his motorcycle. He was not aware of the traffic rules and regulations.

Insurance Company argues that there is a violation of terms and conditions of the Insurance Policy since the driver did not have a driving license at the time of the accident.

The insurance company argued against certain claims and raised issues regarding contributory negligence.

The Insurance Company argues that since there is a willful violation of terms and conditions of the Insurance Policy and provisions of Motor Vehicles Act/Rules on the part of the owner/insured as well as the driver, the Insurance Company is not liable to pay any compensation to the petitioner.
reasoning_text:
The Tribunal noted that a claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal is neither a criminal case nor a civil case. The standard proof required is much lower than in a criminal or civil case. The Tribunal must have some material on the basis of which it can decide things necessary for awarding compensation. The principle involved is preponderance of probability.

The petitioner has placed on record the original medical documents/bills which are Ex.PW1/2 (running into 32 pages). The last page of Bill Summary shows that the dates as well as receipt numbers have been specifically mentioned showing that different amounts have been deposited on different dates.

Petitioner has not placed any documents in the form of bills issued by the transporter to show that any amount towards conveyance has been paid by him. Only a vague and non-specific averment has been made by the petitioner regarding nursing/attendant charges. No document has been placed on record to show the employment details of the petitioner/injured and his income at the time of the accident.

The tribunal considered the evidence presented by both parties, including medical records and financial statements, to determine the appropriate compensation.

The court considered the arguments and documents on record. It was found that the driver was driving without a valid driving license, which amounted to a violation of the terms and conditions of the Insurance Policy. The owner was not supposed to allow the driver to operate the vehicle without a valid license.
decision_text:
By application of the above principles, I hereby hold that the respondent no.1 Shivam was negligent in driving the offending vehicle and the injured Ram Avtar was himself guilty of Contributory Negligence. The interest of justice requires that 15% be deducted from the entire compensation amount on account of the contributory negligence on the part of the injured.

The petitioner is entitled to the compensation to the tune of Rs.2,52,845/- towards medical expenses. A notional amount of Rs.10,000/- is awarded for special diet expenses.

A notional amount of Rs.10,000/- is awarded for conveyance. The petitioner is not entitled to any compensation under the head of Nursing/Attendant Charges. The minimum wages for an unskilled worker prevailing at the time of the accident (i.e., Rs.14,000/-) is taken as the monthly income of the injured. The petitioner is entitled to the loss of income for two months i.e., Rs.14,000 X 2 = 28,000/- (Rupees Twenty Eight Thousand only).

The tribunal awarded a total compensation of Rs. 2,81,500/- after deducting 15% towards contributory negligence. Interest was also awarded at 6% per annum up to the date of the award.

Issue No.3 is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents. The respondent no.3 ICICI Lombard General Insurance Co. Ltd. is directed to deposit a sum of Rs.2,81,500/− with interest @ 6% per annum from the date of filing of DAR i.e. 04.09.2019 till realization with the Civil Nazir of this Tribunal within 30 days under intimation to the petitioner.

Only the oral evidence of R.W.1 and 2 that the petitioner No.1 is suffering from mental illness cannot be considered without any qualified doctors report or opinion. As such, I am of the opinion that the respondent has failed to prove his allegations that the petitioner No.1 is suffering from mental illness and due to the said mental illness she is behaving in improper manner with him as alleged by him in the objection statement as well as in the evidence.

The court discusses the lack of substantial evidence provided by the respondent to prove the mental illness of the petitioner and the absence of documentary proof regarding maintenance payments. The court also notes the absence of any documents showing that the petition for restitution of conjugal rights filed by the petitioner No.1 came to be dismissed.

The definition of domestic violence is wide enough to cover many instances as domestic violence. The explanation No.2 to Sec.3 of the said act provides that for the purpose of determining whether any act, omission, commission or conduct of the respondent constitute domestic violence under the section, the over all facts and circumstances of the case shall be taken into consideration. The over all facts and circumstances of the case before the trial court as discussed above clearly goes to show that the petitioner No.1 was subjected to mental, verbal and emotional and economic abuse by the respondent which amounts to domestic violence u/Sec.3 of the PWDV Act. In case of the allegation of domestic violence, the corroboration of any witnesses cannot be expected since domestic violence would take place within the four corners of the wall, when the aggrieved person lived with the respondent in domestic relationship. As such, the evidence of the victim or the aggrieved person has to be believed except in rare cases and in cases where the respondent has made out specific case that the aggrieved person is deposing falsely. In this case there are no sufficient grounds to believe that the petitioner No.1 is deposing falsely against the respondent.

The bar of limitation under 468 of Cr.P.C. is applicable to the offence which are punishable under Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act. The offences which are punishable under Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act is provided u/Sec.31 of the said act. A breach of protection order or an interim protection order by the respondent shall be an offence under the act and the said offence is punishable with imprisonment for one year u/Sec.31 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act. But in the case before the trial court, the petitioner No.1 has not alleged that the respondent has violated interim protection order or and he has committed breach of protection order. The petitioners have not alleged that the respondent has committed the offence u/Sec.31 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act. Further the petition is not filed by the petitioners before the trial court u/Sec.31 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Krishna Bhattacharjee's case and the judgment of the Hon'ble Delhi Court and Karnataka High Court have held that non-payment of maintenance amount is a continuous cause of action. The application filed under Sec.12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act cannot be dismissed only on the ground that the aggrieved party was not residing with the respondent in a shared household as on the date of filing of the petition.

The petition filed by the petitioners before trial court is deserved to be allowed. Similarly the present appeal filed by the appellants is also deserved to be allowed in terms of the prayer sought for by the petitioners before trial court.

The remaining portion of the suit property is being used by the peitioner as her residence wherein she resides with her two sons. It is stated that at present the petitioner is not doing any business or job and has to depend upon the rental income and the interest accrued in the banks against the FDs. The petitioner has a family consisting of her two sons namely Master Tarun Kochhar (aged about 17 years) and Master Bhumit Kochhar (aged about 13 years) who are studying. It is stated that the income received via rent and interest from the FDs is approximately Rs.17,000/- which is not sufficient for managing the household expenses and ensuring proper upbringing of children of the petitioner. reasoning_text:
The Supreme Court had in 'Inderjeet Kaur Vs.Nirpal Singh', [2000]Supp 5 SCR 707, laid down the following guidelines to be followed by the Courts while deciding the applications for leave to contest filed by the tenants under Section 25(4) of the Delhi Rent Control Act,1958. At a stage when the tenant seeks leave to defend, it is enough if he prima facie makes out a case by disclosing such facts as would disentitle the landlord from obtaining an order of eviction. It would not be right approach to say that unless the tenant at that stage itself establishes a strong case as would non-suit the landlord leave to defend should not be granted when it is not the requirement of Section 25B(5). A leave to defend sought for cannot also be granted for mere asking or in a routine manner which will defeat the very object of the special provisions contained in Chapter IIIA of the Act, Leave to defend cannot be refused where an eviction petition is filed on a mere design or desire of a landlord to recover possession of the premises from a tenant under Clause (e) of the proviso to Sub-section (1) of Section 14, when as a matter of fact the requirement may not be bona fide.

The court discusses the principles of natural justice and the importance of providing a tenant with an opportunity to defend against an eviction petition. The court notes that a triable issue must be raised to grant leave to defend, and that the burden is on the landlord to establish their case affirmatively.

The imperfectness of the title of the premises cannot stand in the way of an eviction petition under section 14 (1) (e) of the DRC Act, neither the tenant can be allowed to raise the plea of imperfect title or title not vesting in the landlord and that too when the tenant has been paying rent to the landlord. Section 116 of the Evidence Act creates estoppels against such a tenant. A tenant can challenge the title of landlord only after vacating the premises and not when he is occupying the premises.

In order to lay to rest, the ambiguity attached with the word 'dependent' it is critical to appreciate the intent of the legislature behind the design of section 14 of the Act. From perusal of the Act itself it is evident that the aforesaid was not intended to be against the requirement of a landlord or to act in any way as an antilandlord provision but was designed to protect the interest of the tenant that is to provide him with a safety net in case an eviction was sought either out of sheer mischief or in hope of higher monetary gains. It is trite law that the rent control law does not envisage or confer a better right than the landlord, on the tenant with respect to the bonafide enjoyment of the tenanted premises. The same is reflected from the judgment of this Court in Punjab State Cooperative Supply and Marketing Federation Limited Vs. Amit Goel and Another; 204(2013)DLT

The court notes that the landlord is entitled to seek eviction of tenanted premises not only for themselves but also for other dependant family members. The court cites precedent where the requirement of a landlord to settle down a son and help him become economically independent was found to be genuine and bonafide.

Requirement is not a mere desire. The degree of intensity contemplated by 'requires' is much more higher than in mere desire. The phrase 'required bonafide' is suggestive of legislative intent that a mere desire which is the outcome of whim or fancy is not taken note of by the rent control legislation. A requirement in the sense of felt need which is an outcome of a sincere, honest desire, in contradistinction with mere pretence or pretext to evict a tenant, on the part of the landlord claiming to occupy the premises for himself or for any member of the family would entitle him to seek ejectment of the tenant.

In considering the availability of alternative accommodation, not availability merely but also whether the landlord has the legal right to such accommodation has to be considered. The landlord has been living in Defence Colony locality for more than 35 years. The first floor which was let out to the tenant in the year 1978 as being an accommodation surplus with the landlord has with the lapse of time become a necessity for occupation by the landlord and his family members. The need as pleaded and proved by the landlord is undoubtedly natural sincere and honest and hence a bona fide need. There is no material available on record to doubt the genuineness of such need.

The court considered the petitioner's explanation regarding her financial situation and concluded that there is nothing cogent on record to disbelieve the petitioner. The court also noted that the grounds for eviction under Section 14 (1) (a) and Section 14 (1) (e) of the DRC Act being different, filing of petitions under these provisions simultaneously or one after the other does not mean that the requirement is not bonafide. The court further stated that once the facts which are alleged to have been concealed have come before the Court and the Court has had occasion to consider the same and after considering the same finds in favor of the landlord, the petition for eviction cannot be dismissed on the ground of concealment.

The Court allows the petition and holds that the tenant cannot challenge the title of the landlord or successor-in-interest. The transfer of the landlord's title is valid, and the lease continues. The petitioner's requirement of the premises for her son's grocery shop is deemed bona fide.

This submission of the respondent is also without any merits and is dismissed.

Thus, a transferee of the landlord's rights, steps into the shoes of the landlord with all the rights and liabilities of the transferor landlord in respect of the subsisting tenancy. The possession of a tenant cannot be adverse to his landlord. Parents and children are considered to be a part of the family and dependent on each other for the need of the property. Admittedly, Tarun, son of the petitioner was a minor at the time of filing of the present petition and also studying and is definitely dependant upon the petitioner mother for his needs. The fact that the rate of rent are high in Delhi is not disputed. The landlord argues that the requirement is genuine and bonafide, citing various precedents where similar requirements were upheld. The petitioner argues that the requirement of the landlord to settle down her son and help him establish a business is genuine and bonafide. The son, Tarun, was to turn 18 in October 2019, and there is no embargo that a 17-year-old cannot run a grocery store. The respondent contends that Tarun, being 17 years old and studying, cannot run a shop being underage and without any experience. The respondent questions the legitimacy of the landlord's requirement.

facts_text:
On 21.02.2016 at about 7.30 p.m., while the claimant was standing on the side of the road near NH-69, Gangavaram Mandal, Chittoor District, Andhra Pradesh, a lorry bearing registration No.HR-55-G-3073 driven by its driver came with high speed in a rash and negligent manner so as endanger human life and safety, dashed against the claimant, due to the impact, the claimant fell down and sustained multiple injuries which are grievous in nature. Thereafter, the claimant was shifted to R.L.Jalappa Hospital, Kolar where he underwent surgery for fracture and injuries. Due to the accident, the Police have registered a criminal case against the driver of offending lorry as mentioned above. As on the date of occurrence of accident, the claimant was aged 28 years and he was working as computer mechanic and earning monthly income of Rs.20,000/-. It is stated that due to the injuries sustained in the accident, the claimant is permanently disabled and he is unable to carry out work and profession as he was able to do prior to the occurrence of accident. It is further stated that due to this accident, he has sustained loss of future earning capacity which has diminished his ability to work for higher income.

On 21.02.2016 at 7.30 p.m., while the claimant was standing on the side of the road near NH-69, a lorry came in a rash and negligent manner and dashed against the claimant who was just a bystander. The claimant has produced Exs.P1 to P5 which are the Police records. The claimant was aged 28 years as on the date of occurrence of accident and was working as a computer mechanic. The tribunal has assessed the income at Rs.9,000/- per month.

The claimant suffered comminuted intra-articular inter condylar fracture of right femur and comminuted lateral condyle fracture right tibia. He underwent surgeries including ORIF + Long LCP fixation and ORIF with 2cc screw fixation. The claimant was inpatient for 32 days and has undergone multiple fractures to his leg.

The claimant is seeking compensation for pain and suffering, loss of future earnings, medical expenses, conveyance, nourishment, and loss of amenities of life. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Bengaluru, had previously awarded Rs.4,46,521/- in compensation.
arguments_petitioner:
The claimant got himself examined as PW.1 and also examined the Doctor as PW.2 and got marked documents as Exs.P1 to P11, whereas, the contesting respondents examined its official as RW.1 and got marked documents as Exs.R1 and R2.

The tribunal has not appreciated the material evidence both oral and documentary while passing the impugned judgment and award and has committed a serious error in awarding meager compensation. The tribunal has not awarded any compensation for loss of income during laid up period, despite the fact that the claimant was inpatient for a period 32 days and suffered multiple fractures. The tribunal has erred in not computing the proper income on the basis of avocation and the Legal Services Authority chart. The tribunal has not considered the evidence of Doctor-PW.2 for assessment of disability which is opined by the Doctor at 21% and taken disability at 15%. The compensation awarded by the tribunal is on the lower side.

The Doctor-PW.2 has assessed the physical permanent disability due to fracture injuries to an extent of 63.79% to the right lower limb and 21% of the whole body. The tribunal should have taken 21% as physical permanent disability of the claimant for future earning capacity.
arguments_respondent:
Respondent No.2-Insurance Company has filed his objection statement denying the claim made by the claimant and pleaded that the offending vehicle i.e. lorry has been falsely implicated in the case by the Police colluding with the claimant only with malafide intention to make wrongful gain by the claimant. On this basis, he has sought for dismissal of claim petition.

The impugned judgment and award passed by the tribunal is in accordance with material evidence both oral and documentary placed before the tribunal and same does not call for interference by this Court. The tribunal has rightly awarded the compensation which is commensurate to the material placed before the tribunal and also taking notional income as there is no material document and also on the basis of medical bills. The loss of income during laid up period cannot be awarded more than what is awarded for the period of treatment which the claimant was inpatient in the Hospital for a period of 32 days in the present case.
reasoning_text:
The tribunal has assessed the income at Rs.9,000/- per month, which is on the lower side and calls for interference by this Court. For the accident year 2016, the notional income chart prescribes Rs.9,500/- per month as income. The appropriate multiplier would be '17' as per the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Sarla Verma (Smt) and others vs. Delhi Transport Corporation and another reported in (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121.

The tribunal has assessed the disability to an extent of 15% as functional disability. The court agrees with the learned counsel for the claimant that the court should not impose its own opinion on disability other than what is stated by the Doctor as courts are not experts in the field of medicine.
decision_text:
After considering the evidence both oral and documentary and after hearing the parties, the tribunal has awarded compensation of Rs.4,46,521/- with interest at 6% p.a. from the date of petition till deposit. The liability was fixed on respondent No.2-Insurer. Being dissatisfied with the compensation awarded, the appellant-claimant is before this Court seeking enhancement of compensation.

The claimant is entitled for marginal indulgence in the matter for enhancement of compensation.

In view of the above discussions, the claimant is entitled for the loss of future earning capacity of Rs.4,06,980/- (Rs.9,500/- x 12 x 17 x 21%) as against Rs.2,75,400/- awarded by the tribunal.

i) The appeal is allowed-in-part; ii) The judgment and award passed by XXI Additional Small Causes Judge and the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Bengaluru in MVC.No.7066/2016 dated 13.11.2018, is modified; iii) The claimant is entitled for total compensation of Rs.6,63,101/- as against Rs.4,46,521/- awarded by the tribunal;

facts_text:
Petitioner is running a hotel and stated that he has bitter experience with the supply of water, as water is not potable and adverse to the Food Safety Standards. According to the petitioner, water is extracted from private wells and transported in tanker lorries. There are many persons engaged in extraction, transportation and sale of ground water. The petitioner has referred to a news item published regarding unauthorized extraction of groundwater within the jurisdiction of Aluva Municipality.

In the case on hand, there appears to be a personal interest in filing the writ petition, as the petitioner is stated to be an owner of a hotel, and aggrieved by the supply of water, which is not potable. There are general averments as regards extraction of water, transportation & sale, without due permission from the competent authorities.

Kerala Water Authority has no power to take appropriate action against illegal extraction of ground water, transportation and sale thereof. The directions issued by this Court in W.P.(C) No.31390 of 2018, squarely apply to the facts of this case.
arguments_petitioner: Petitioner seeks to call for the entire records pertaining to the facts pleaded in the writ petition and issue a writ of mandamus, any other writ, order or direction, directing the respondents to curb the transportation, supply and sale of underground water, extracted from wells, quarries and ponds for human usage otherwise than through the 2nd respondent Kerala Water Authority. The petitioner claims there is a public interest involved in this writ petition and refers to Exhibit P1 letter dated 10.12.2018 written by a Member of the Legislative Assembly to the Chief Secretary, State of Kerala.
arguments_respondent:
The Kerala Water Authority, represented by the Chairman - respondent No.2, submits that it is not dealing with illegal extraction, transportation, supply and sale of groundwater. It is for the authorities under the Kerala Ground Water (Control and Regulations) Act, 2002 and the Rules made thereunder, to take appropriate action against illegal extraction of groundwater, transportation and sale.

Earlier taking note of the extraction of ground water, without permission from the appropriate authority and the provisions of the Kerala Ground Water (Control and Regulations) Act, 2002 and the Rules made thereunder, this Court vide judgment dated 10th November, 2021, in W.P.(C) No.31390 of 2018, has issued directions. The directions issued in W.P.(C) No.31390 of 2018 would govern the facts of the case and the reliefs sought for.
reasoning_text: The State as well as District Authorities & the local bodies are duty bound to ensure that commercial establishments are not exploiting groundwater to an unprecedented level and establish such units for withdrawing groundwater without adequate NOC from the statutory authorities. Under the Kerala Panchayat Raj Act, 1994, Kerala Municipality Act, 1994 and the Building Rules issued thereunder, in order to construct any well, a permit is required from the Secretary of the local body. These provisions and others specifically covered under the laws discussed above make it clear there shall be a proper and adequate mechanism in place so as to effectively control, regulate and manage the entire affairs in respect of withdrawing groundwater.
decision_text:
The writ petition is disposed of with the above directions and observations.

Accordingly, instant writ appeal is disposed of, in terms of the judgment in W.P.(C) No.31390 of 2018 dated 10th November, 2021.

According to the petitioner, water is extracted from private wells and transported in tanker lorries. There are many persons engaged in extraction, transportation and sale of ground water. The petitioner has referred to a news item published regarding unauthorized extraction of groundwater within the jurisdiction of Aluva Municipality. Petitioner seeks to call for the entire records pertaining to the facts pleaded in the writ petition and issue a writ of mandamus, any other writ, order or direction, directing the respondents to curb the transportation, supply and sale of underground water, extracted from wells, quarries and ponds for human usage otherwise than through the 2nd respondent Kerala Water Authority. The petitioner claims there is a public interest involved in this writ petition and refers to Exhibit P1 letter dated 10.12.2018 written by a Member of the Legislative Assembly to the Chief Secretary, State of Kerala. The Kerala Water Authority, represented by the Chairman - respondent No.2, submits that it is not dealing with illegal extraction, transportation, supply and sale of groundwater. It is for the authorities under the Kerala Ground Water (Control and Regulations) Act, 2002 and the Rules made thereunder, to take appropriate action against illegal extraction of groundwater, transportation and sale.

In the case on hand, there appears to be a personal interest in filing the writ petition, as the petitioner is stated to be an owner of a hotel, and aggrieved by the supply of water, which is not potable. There are general averments as regards extraction of water, transportation & sale, without due permission from the competent authorities. Earlier taking note of the extraction of ground water, without permission from the appropriate authority and the provisions of the Kerala Ground Water (Control and Regulations) Act, 2002 and the Rules made thereunder, this Court vide judgment dated 10th November, 2021, in W.P.(C) No.

Kerala Water Authority has no power to take appropriate action against illegal extraction of ground water, transportation and sale thereof. The directions issued by this Court in W.P.(C) No.31390 of 2018, squarely apply to the facts of this case.

facts_text:
The petitioners are various printing presses and associations in Patna, Bihar. They challenge the process adopted by the respondents, including the Union of India and the State of Bihar, for procuring educational material through a centralized process and short-listing the lowest tenderer. The petitioners argue that this process is arbitrary and irrational, and that it affects public interest.

This case involves the procurement of educational materials through a tender process initiated by the Department of Education, Government of Bihar, for the implementation of the Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FL&N) scheme. The Court previously issued directions in CWJC No.7124 of 2020 regarding the provision of nutritious food and digitizing education processes during the pandemic.

The Ministry of Education (Department of School Education & Literacy) Government of India launched the Integrated Scheme for School Education- Samagra Shiksha in 2018 by subsuming the erstwhile Centrally Sponsored Schemes of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA); Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan (RMSA); and Teacher Education (TE). The Scheme treats school education as a continuum with the Sustainable Development Goal for Education (SDG-4). The Scheme provides support for the implementation of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) and is also aligned with the recommendations of National Education Policy, 2020 (NEP). The object is to ensure that all children have access to quality education with an equitable and inclusive classroom environment, taking care of their diverse background, multilingual needs, different academic abilities and making them active participants in the learning process. The RTE Act mandates the appropriate Government to provide free and compulsory elementary education to every child of the age 6 to 14 years in a neighbourhood school. Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Samagra Shiksha, financial assistance is provided as per the fund sharing pattern as decided by the Ministry of Finance. The Scheme is implemented as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme through a single State Implementation Society (SIS) at the State level. The annual plans are prepared by the States and UTs based on their requirements and priority as reflected in their Annual Work Plan and Budget (AWP &B) Proposals. These plans are then appraised and approved/estimated by the Project Approval Board (PAB) in the Department of School Education & Literacy, Government of India in consultation with the States and UTs as per the programmatic and financial norms of the Scheme, and physical and economic progress of the State for approved interventions. The details of funds released under Samagra Shiksha to the State of Bihar during the last three years, as of 17.2.2022, are provided.

This mission has been launched under the aegis of the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Samagra Shiksha, which focuses on providing access and retaining children in foundational years of schooling; teacher capacity building; development of high quality and diversified Student and Teacher Resources/Learning Materials; and tracking the progress of each child in achieving learning outcomes. The petition filed on 13 January 2022 challenged the terms upon which Request For Proposal (RFP)/Tender was issued. With the selection of the successful bidder, Telecommunication Consultants India Limited, the challenge expanded to four vital issues: the condition of the tender being tailor-made to oust the petitioners from the process of bidding, favoring the shortlisted tenderer, the process of short-listing of the tenderer(s) and selecting the successful tenderer being vitiated on account of ineligibility, malice and favoritism, and whether the Authority exceeded its jurisdiction in undertaking the process of tender.

The first meeting of the State Steering Committee held on 16 September 2021, headed by Additional Chief Secretary, Education Department, Government of Bihar, took certain decisions for implementing FL&N Mission, and minutes was circulated vide communication dated 06 October 2021. The State Project Director, BEPC, with whom the Central Government was interacting, took over the reins and convened meetings for effective implementation of FL&N Mission. Meetings were held on 04 October 2021, 09 November 2021, and 16 November 2021, where several issues were deliberated upon, and consensus arrived on the basic structure for making available the course material for implementing the FL&N mission.

Petitioner No.1 (Bihar Offset Printers Association) communicated on 03 January 2022 to the Bihar State Textbook Publishing Corporation Ltd. (BSTPC) to intervene, ensuring the tendered work is split into two components. The State Project Director, BEPC, was requested to reconsider the decision. Petitioner no.3 (Patna Offset Press) and Petitioner No.4 (New Ratan Priya) also communicated with the State Project Director, BEPC, seeking changes in the tender terms. The pre-bid meeting on 06 January 2022 involved 20 bidders, including petitioners, and resulted in a Corrigendum dated 11 January, 2022.

The Technical Evaluation Committee reviewed the FL&N Sample Evaluation Committee report and the documents submitted by the parties. In evaluating the technical bid, all the three bidders were declared to be duly qualified, competent, and fully compliant. Concerning one item, i.e. bidder's quality certification: ISO Mark, the committee, while awarding 10 out of 20 marks each to two out of three bidders, left the final decision to be taken by the Purchase Committee. Another issue, namely setting up of library etc., was also left for the Purchase Committee to decide.

The proceedings dated 01 February, 2022 of the Purchase Committee are reproduced as under:- Letter No.: Quality/ 193/ 2021-22/ 537 Date: 01/02/2022 Proceedings of the purchase committee meeting held on dated 01 February 2022 at 10:00 AM under the Chairmanship of State Project Director, Bihar Educa
arguments_petitioner:
The petitioners argue that the process adopted by the respondents for procuring educational material through a centralized process and short-listing the lowest tenderer is arbitrary and irrational. They contend that no responsible authority acting reasonably and following relevant law could have reached such a decision. Additionally, they assert that this process adversely affects public interest.

The petitioners argue that the acts of the Additional Chief Secretary and the Director, Primary Education, in finalizing the policy for the FL&N scheme by calling a tender are illegal. They also contend that the conditions laid down in the Request for Proposal (RFP) are tailored to oust them or favor others, making the action mala fide. Additionally, they claim that the terms and conditions of the tender are manifestly unreasonable and arbitrary.

The petitioners argue that the tender conditions were tailored to exclude them from the bidding process, which was illegal, malafide, arbitrary, unreasonable, and against public interest. facts_text:
The accused was charged for offences under Sections 16(1)(a)(i), 7(i), and 2(ia)(m) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The accused was acquitted by the Court of Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Andole at Jogipet, through judgment in C.C.No.42 of 2003, dated 19.01.2006. The State has preferred this appeal against the judgment of acquittal.

The Food Inspector of Medak District inspected the shop of the Accused and seized the adulterated sweets, which were kept for sale. After following all the required formalities, the sweets were sent for analysis and the Analyst gave a clear finding that the sweets are adulterated and do not conform to the standard. A complaint was filed before the Court and during the course of trial, the prosecution examined the Food Inspector as PW.1, the Attender as PW.2, and the Mediator as PW.3, and produced all the documents, including the Analyst Report. The trial Court acquitted the Accused based on trivial lacunae in the evidence produced.

In the light of the above provisions, it has to be seen whether the Accused was accorded his justifiable opportunity to get the sample analyzed through the Central Food Laboratory. Though the Analyst submitted his report on 17.10.2002, the Prosecution for the reasons best known, could not file the complaint till 04.08.2003. After filing of complaint, notice, as required under Section 13(2) of the Act, was issued on 11.09.2003. There is delay of about 11 months in according opportunity to the Accused for getting the sample analyzed through the Central Food Laboratory. The condition of the sweets, which were seized might have become so worse that they could not be subjected for analysis, even if they were sent.

The prosecution asserts that the accused was found selling adulterated sweets, which were not fit for human consumption, and the Public Analyst confirmed this through his report.

The learned Assistant Public Prosecutor contended that the judgment of the trial Court is erroneous. The prosecution established its case beyond all reasonable doubt, but the trial Court acquitted the Accused based on trivial lacunae in the evidence produced. The Accused has committed an offense affecting the health and safety of the public at large and should have been convicted by the trial Court.

No convincing reason is given as to why the complaint could not be lodged for such a long period. Furthermore, no steps were taken for arraying the Manufacturer of the alleged sweets as an Accused. The alleged mediator, who was examined as PW.3, failed to support the case of the prosecution. The evidence of PW.2 also becomes doubtful in the light of his statement during the course of cross-examination that the Food Inspector always cites him as one of the panchas.

reasoning_text:
The trial Court examined the evidence of PWs.1 to 3 and Exs.P-1 to P-29 and concluded that the prosecution failed to establish its case beyond all reasonable doubt, leading to the acquittal of the accused.

The relevant events and dates are essential to determine whether the Accused lost his valuable opportunity of sending the seized product to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. The legal provisions enumerated under the Act prescribe the procedure to be followed by the Food Inspector and the duties of the Public Analyst. The Local (Health) Authority shall, after institution of prosecution, forward a copy of the report of the result of the analysis to those persons informing them that if they desire, they may make application to the Court within a period of 10 days from the date of receipt of the copy of the report to get the sample of the article of food kept by Local (Health) Authority, analyzed by the Central Food Laboratory.

The delay of about 11 months in according opportunity to the Accused for getting the sample analyzed through the Central Food Laboratory casts a cloud of suspicion regarding the veracity of the prosecution's version. The valuable right of the Accused to have the sample analyzed in the Central Laboratory has been denied by a series of defaults committed by the prosecution.
decision_text: This Court holds that the judgment of the trial Court does not suffer from any infirmity as projected by the appellant. Thus, the ultimate conclusion of this Court is that the appeal lacks merits and deserves to be dismissed.
input_text:
The accused was charged for offences under Sections 16(1)(a)(i), 7(i), and 2(ia)(m) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The accused was acquitted by the Court of Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Andole at Jogipet, through judgment in C.C.No.42 of 2003, dated 19.01.2006. The State has preferred this appeal against the judgment of acquittal. The prosecution claims that the ingredients of the offence under Sections 16(1)(a)(i), 7(i), and 2(ia)(m) of the Act have been established. They argue that the reasons assigned for the acquittal of the accused are erroneous and that the conclusion arrived at is unjustifiable. The prosecution asserts that the accused was found selling adulterated sweets, which were not fit for human consumption, and the Public Analyst confirmed this through his report.

The Food Inspector of Medak District inspected the shop of the Accused and seized the adulterated sweets, which were kept for sale. After following all the required formalities, the sweets were sent for analysis and the Analyst gave a clear finding that the sweets are adulterated and do not conform to the standard. A complaint was filed before the Court and during the course of trial, the prosecution examined the Food Inspector as PW.1, the Attender as PW.2, and the Mediator as PW.3, and produced all the documents, including the Analyst Report. The trial Court acquitted the Accused based on trivial lacunae in the evidence produced. The learned Assistant Public Prosecutor contended that the judgment of the trial Court is erroneous. The prosecution established its case beyond all reasonable doubt, but the trial Court acquitted the Accused based on trivial lacunae in the evidence produced. The Accused has committed an offense affecting the health and safety of the public at large and should have been convicted by the trial Court. The learned counsel for the Accused submitted that the alleged mediator, who was examined as PW.3, failed to support the case of the prosecution. Nothing was seized in the presence of the mediator and no recovery panchanama was drafted in his presence. The procedure followed is in clear violation of the principles of natural justice, as no reasonable opportunity was accorded to the Accused to send the alleged seized sweets for analysis to the Central Food Laboratory. The prosecution has to state why the Manufacturer of the sweets is not arrayed as an Accused in this case.

In the light of the above provisions, it has to be seen whether the Accused was accorded his justifiable opportunity to get the sample analyzed through the Central Food Laboratory. Though the Analyst submitted his report on 17.10.2002, the Prosecution for the reasons best known, could not file the complaint till 04.08.2003. After filing of complaint, notice, as required under Section 13(2) of the Act, was issued on 11.09.2003. There is delay of about 11 months in according opportunity to the Accused for getting the sample analyzed through the Central Food Laboratory. The condition of the sweets, which were seized might have become so worse that they could not be subjected for analysis, even if they were sent. No convincing reason is given as to why the complaint could not be lodged for such a long period. Furthermore, no steps were taken for arraying the Manufacturer of the alleged sweets as an Accused. The alleged mediator, who was examined as PW.3, failed to support the case of the prosecution. The evidence of PW.2 also becomes doubtful in the light of his statement during the course of cross-examination that the Food Inspector always cites him as one of the panchas. As rightly projected by learned counsel for the respondent/Accused, the condition of the sweets, which were seized might have become so worse that they could not be subjected for analysis, even if they were sent. One could take notice through common sense, that any edible object, that too, the things like sweets, would get damaged, becomes inedible and unfit for chemical or scientific examination by passage of considerable time.

facts_text:
The vessel m.t. GP ASPHALT I was owned by one GP Asphalt Shipping Inc. Swedish Club was the Protection and Indemnity Club with which the vessel was entered. The vessel was arrested on 22 December 2020 by the 1st Respondent in Commercial Appeal No. 108 of 2021 ("V8 Pool Inc."). On 22 December 2020, after receipt of emails from the crew informing that the vessel supplies were running low, FTI Consulting, the company undertaking restructuring of the owner of the Defendant vessel, arranged for enough supplies to last a month. On 7 January 2021, the crew addressed an email to Swedish Club informing them that the salaries for November and December were overdue and that arrangements would have to be made for food and water.

Swedish Club filed Interim Application No. 2062 of 2021, stating that the vessel had been abandoned and relying on the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 ("MLC"), seeking leave of the Ld. Single Judge to make certain payments in respect of maintenance of the vessel and well-being of the crew. The Crew Members had also filed Interim Application No. 1395 of 2021, seeking that their wages accrued post-arrest be treated as Sheriff's expenses and paid out immediately from the sale proceeds. Both Swedish Club and the Crew Members appealed from the respective orders.

Mr. Narichania relies on Rule 1084 of the Bombay High Court (Original Side) Rules and states that Swedish Club had approached the Ld. Single Judge under this Rule for leave, as per established admiralty law, to make payment of the crew wages which had accrued during the period of arrest through the Sheriff. Rule 1084 reads as follows, '1084. Sheriffs expenses --In the event any expenses are required to be incurred by the Sheriff during the period of the arrest for the safety and preservation of the ship and its crew, the Sheriff shall make a report to the court and the court, shall after hearing the parties direct payment of such sums as the court may deem fit by any party the Sheriff for incurring such expenses, which shall be treated as Sheriffs expenses.'

Swedish Club approached the Ld. Single Judge to discharge its humanitarian obligations under the MLC after the vessel's abandonment. The Ld. Single Judge considered that because Swedish Club was obliged to make such payments, it could not ask for these payments to be treated as Sheriff's expenses. The Ld. Single Judge referred to the P&I Club's obligation to make payment but did not appreciate the significance of Regulation 12 of Standard A2.5.2.

The application for such payments to be treated as Sheriff's expenses in the case of Irwin Edmond Sequeira v m.v. Karnika (Colabawalla, J.) was filed by the crew, but the actual payment was made by the P&I club. The MLC under which the P & I Club came forward to make such payment and to thereafter stand in the shoes of the crew was not brought to the attention of the Court in that case. The crew were constrained to remain on board the vessel from its arrest until its sale and to take care of the vessel for no fault of theirs. A P&I Club who paid the post arrest wages to the crew was also entitled to make such payment after taking leave of the admiralty court and claim it as Sheriff's expenses.

The Ld. Judge's orders dated 21 June 2021 and 11 March 2021 disallowed Swedish Club's application for reimbursement of post arrest expenses incurred by it for wages to be treated as Sheriff's expenses. The Crew Members had been paid their wages till 28 February 2021 and this appeal was for reimbursement of wages incurred between 1st March 2021 till 20th March 2021 (when the Crew was repatriated, being to the tune of USD 11,133.31). The Crew Members were retained on board as per the minimum safe manning requirements of the vessel as per the order dated 27 January 2021 of the Ld. Single Judge.

The case involves a dispute regarding the classification of expenses incurred for the safety and preservation of a vessel and its crew after the vessel is arrested. The issue revolves around whether such expenses can be considered as Sheriff's expenses under Rule 1084.

The vessel was arrested on 22 December 2020. Owners made the last supply of provisions and fuel on 22 December 2020. Wages had not been paid since November 2020. The abandonment (which under the MLC is considered to be when the owner does not make provision for supplies or when the owner fails to pay two months' wages) was brought to the notice of Swedish Club by the crew's email of 7 January 2021. Swedish Club filed its interim application indicating its readiness to make payments for the crew's benefit and seeking leave for the same on 21 January 2021. An ad interim order was obtained on 27 January 2021 insofar as the food/water/supplies for the crew were concerned.

It appears that the Sheriff may not have been not aware of the situation on board the vessel. Given that the Sheriff did not move any application for orders relating to the maintenance and preservation of the vessel and the crew. There are several cases in which the owner abandons the vessel and the crew members are left to fend for themselves. Crew members in many cases are foreigners. Crew members who are on board a vessel, cannot be expected to expeditiously write to the Sheriff - they are more likely to air their grievances to the owner.

This Court has come across several cases where an arrested vessel has been neglected or otherwise abandoned by its owner leaving the Master and crew on board in the lurch. Often the vessel is fast running out of fuel, lubes, food and provisions. The crew are unaware of the status of the court proceedings and the steps to be taken by them. In view of the prevailing lack of clarity regarding the steps to be taken in the case of an abandoned vessel under arrest, it is necessary to frame some guidelines for the Admiralty Court to follow in such a case.

arguments_petitioner:
These appeals raise the question of whether crew wages accrued on board a vessel after her arrest by the Admiralty Court would rank as Sheriff's expenses. The further question involved is whether a party who has approached the Admiralty Court for leave to pay the crew their wages can stand in the shoes of the crew members and claim such amounts from the sale proceeds of the vessel as Sheriff's expenses and/or in priority as a maritime lien.

Mr. Narichania, on behalf of Swedish Club, submits that the payment made to the crew by Swedish Club of the amount of USD 64,663 should be considered Sheriff's expenses, being payment for wages accrued from 22 December 2020 (the date of arrest) till 28 February 2021.

Mr. Narichania further relies on the provisions of the MLC (Standard A2.5.2) which establish requirements to ensure the provision of an expeditious and effective financial security system to assist seafarers in the event of their abandonment. This includes ensuring that a financial security system meeting the requirements is in place for ships flying its flag, providing direct access, sufficient coverage, and expedited financial assistance to any abandoned seafarer on a ship flying the flag of the Member.

Mr. Narichania submits that Swedish Club promptly approached the Ld. Single Judge to discharge its humanitarian obligations under the MLC. He argues that the Ld. Single Judge erred in considering that because Swedish Club was obliged to make such payments, it could not ask for these payments to be treated as Sheriff's expenses. He submits that the Ld. Single Judge has referred to the P&I Club's obligation to make payment but has not appreciated the significance of Regulation 12 of Standard A2.5.2 which specifically provides that the P&I Club is entitled to stand in the shoes of the crew once it has made payment to the crew. He further submits that Rule 1084 does not make any distinction between voluntary payments and payments made otherwise. Any party who incurs expenses to maintain a vessel under arrest or wages to the crew during the period of arrest is entitled to recover such expenses as Sheriff's expenses, irrespective of whether it is voluntary or not. He relies on The Leoborg, [1964] 1 Lloyd's Rep 380, The Vasilia, [1972] 1 Lloyd's Rep 51 and The Berostar, [1970] 2 Lloyd's Rep 403. He submits that the Ld. Single Judge failed to follow binding precedent of this Court in (a) coming to a conclusion that crew members were not entitled to recover post arrest wages as Sheriff's expenses and (b) finding that a P&I Club was not entitled to recover wages that it had paid to the crew members for the period of arrest as Sheriff's expenses.

He submitted that the Ld. Judge erred in distinguishing the binding precedent in the case of Irwin Edmond Sequeira v m.v. Karnika (Colabawalla, J.). The application in that case, though filed by the crew, in fact sought for payments made by the P&I club to be classified as Sheriff's expenses, and this was granted. He also submits that worldwide practice is for post arrest wages to be considered as Sheriff's expenses. He relied on The Aquarius III, [2002] SGHC 138 and Credit Suisse v. Brightoil Lion (Order of the Singapore High C. Lastly, he submits that it is not necessary to file a suit to prove these expenses through trial - there can be no serious doubt about crew wages and the scrutiny is done by a competent officer of the High Court, such as the Sheriff of Mumbai or the Commissioner for taking Accounts.

The Crew Members were constrained to stay on board the vessel during the period of arrest and they were entitled to their wages. When a vessel is under arrest, the mere fact of the crew member being on board is sufficient to entitle him to his wages. Under Section 9(1)(a) r/w Section 10(1)(a) of the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, 'crew wages' are accorded highest priority after 'sheriff's expenses'.

Mr. Kamat argues that payment of wages and other employment entitlements of the crew after arrest is not the responsibility of the Sheriff unless the Sheriff considers it appropriate to employ or engage crew members. He relies on three authorities: Coromandel International Ltd. v. m.v. GLORY I, 2014 SCC Online Bom 220; Patrick Stevedores No. 2 Pty. Ltd. v. Tukarina, (1998) 154 ALR 514; and GAC Shipping (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. m.v. GOLDEN PRIDE (Order dated 17 February 2021 passed by Shriram, J.).

Mr. Narichania submits that the logic of disallowing an application by a crew member for classifying his wages as Sheriff's expenses is flawed and that this order does not have any binding value since it ignores previous orders passed by this Court where crew members have been paid their post arrest wages as Sheriff's expenses. He further submits that a lien can be transferred, but subject to leave of the court. Any purported transfer without prior leave of the court is not valid. Clause 12 of Standard A2.5.2 of the MLC provides that the rights of the crew members will be subrogated/assigned or in other manner automatically transferred to the P&I Club on making such payment.

Swedish Club filed the interim application and was open to making such payments through the Sheriff so that the court could keep a check on the payments. The club would have found itself in a position where it had made payments and been faced with other creditors' objections to recovery of such amounts on the basis that leave had not been taken.

Mr. Pratap's and Mr. Kamat's submission that Swedish Club is not entitled to the post arrest wages being considered as Sheriff's expenses on account of it being an obligation under the MLC is concerned, we are of the view that the MLC which imposes a humanitarian obligation on the P&I Club to make certain payments also gives the P&I Club the right to stand in the shoes of the crew by subrogation/ assignment/ other mode of transfer.
arguments_respondent:
Swedish Club could not claim the post arrest expenses as Sheriff's expenses. This was because Swedish Club was obliged to make payment of wages to the crew members under the MLC. It was not a volunteer and it could not seek the same benefits as a volunteer would have under such circumstances. The Ld. Single Judge was correct and justified in holding that Swedish Club was in breach of its obligations to make prompt payment under the MLC and no prior leave of the court was required for Swedish Club to comply with its obligation of payment of wages, supply of food/provision and repatriation of crew.

Mr. Pratap supports the Ld. Single Judge's impugned orders, stating that any expense required to be incurred for the safety and preservation of the vessel and its crew after the vessel is arrested can only be incurred by the Sheriff. He further submits that any expense incurred for the safety and preservation of the vessel and its crew pursuant to legal/contractual obligations will not automatically qualify as Sheriff's expenses. He relies on The Sparti, [2000] Vol. 2 Lloyd's Rep 618 [H.K. Ct.].

The Ld. Single Judge in this matter had disallowed an application by a crew member who had served on board the vessel during the period of arrest for classifying his wages as Sheriff's expenses. The Ld. Judge holds, 'If we entertain such applications, the problem will be (a) it will not be possible to ascertain whether applicant really worked on board the vessel, (b) what was he doing on board the vessel, (c) what were the terms and conditions based on which he was on board the vessel and (d) if it was a huge vessel with 50 crew members, would the Court direct the Sheriff to pay the wages of all the crew members until the vessel is sold?'

Mr. Pratap's and Mr. Kamat's submission that any such application under Rule 1084 has to come from the Sheriff is not well founded. They also contend that crew are not entitled to their post arrest wages being paid to them as Sheriff's expenses.
reasoning_text:
In The Aquarius III, the Singapore High Court observed that the post-arrest wages and disbursements were in substance sheriff's expenses. It did not matter that there was no prior order allowing the same to be treated as sheriff's expenses or that the interveners were not engaged by the sheriff himself or his agents, Gulf Agency. The sheriff had had the benefit of the interveners' presence and services to meet the regulatory requirement as a result of which the sheriff had saved on having to engage a replacement crew.

The court discusses the legal framework under Rule 1084 and the obligations of the Sheriff versus the ship owner. It also addresses the distinction between expenses incurred for the preservation and maintenance of the vessel and crew versus those incurred for the Sheriff's benefit.

Rule 1084 provides that if expenses are required to be incurred during the period of the arrest for the safety and preservation of the ship and its crew, the Sheriff should make a report to the Admiralty Court and the court shall pass appropriate orders after hearing all parties. A party putting the Sheriff in funds pursuant to such order will be entitled to recover those amounts as Sheriff's expenses. In our view, the paramount consideration is the well being of the crew members and the safety and/or preservation of the vessel and the Rule has to be construed accordingly.

Rule 1084 does not prescribe that only a Sheriff's report can be filed. It does not preclude an interim application in relation to such reliefs. A Sheriff's report can be filed pursuant to an interim application filed by a party seeking to make payments for the preservation of the vessel and the crew and orders passed in such application. The paramount consideration is the well being of the crew members and the safety and/or preservation of the vessel.

Insofar as the last bone of contention, i.e. whether pre-arrest wages paid by Swedish Club can be given the status of a maritime lien, is concerned, it appears to us that the law is that such lien is not assignable/ subrogable without prior leave of the court. However, there does not seem any blanket embargo on the transferability of such lien. If the prior leave of the court has been taken, the lien can be transferred.
decision_text:
The impugned order dated 11 March 2021 whereby the Ld. Single Judge has disallowed the crew's application for their post arrest wages to be considered Sheriff's expenses cannot, thus, be sustained.

In light of the above, both appeals are allowed. The Crew Members, the Appellants in Comm. Appeal No. 111 of 2021, is entitled to payment of USD 11,133.31 out of the sale proceeds as Sheriff's expenses, being the payment of wages for the period of 1 March 2021 till 20th March 2021 (when the Crew was repatriated). The payment on behalf of the deceased Appellant no. 3, Mr. Putta Ananda Rao, be made to his wife, Mrs. Putta Santhamani, on behalf his legal heirs (wife and 2 minor sons). Swedish Club, the Appellant in Comm. Appeal No. 108 of 2021, is entitled to payment of USD 64,663 as considered Sheriff's expenses, being payment for wages accrued from 22 December 2020 (the date of arrest) till 28 February 2021.

Swedish Club filed Interim Application No. 2062 of 2021, stating that the vessel had been abandoned and relying on the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 ("MLC"), seeking leave of the Ld. Single Judge to make certain payments in respect of maintenance of the vessel and well-being of the crew. The Crew Members had also filed Interim Application No. 1395 of 2021, seeking that their wages accrued post-arrest be treated as Sheriff's expenses and paid out immediately from the sale proceeds. Both Swedish Club and the Crew Members appealed from the respective orders. Mr. Narichania, on behalf of Swedish Club, submits that the payment made to the crew by Swedish Club of the amount of USD 64,663 should be considered Sheriff's expenses, being payment for wages accrued from 22 December 2020 (the date of arrest) till 28 February 2021.

Mr. Narichania relies on Rule 1084 of the Bombay High Court (Original Side) Rules and states that Swedish Club had approached the Ld. Single Judge under this Rule for leave, as per established admiralty law, to make payment of the crew wages which had accrued during the period of arrest through the Sheriff. Rule 1084 reads as follows, '1084. Sheriffs expenses --In the event any expenses are required to be incurred by the Sheriff during the period of the arrest for the safety and preservation of the ship and its crew, the Sheriff shall make a report to the court and the court, shall after hearing the parties direct payment of such sums as the court may deem fit by any party the Sheriff for incurring such expenses, which shall be treated as Sheriffs expenses.' Swedish Club approached the Ld. Single Judge to discharge its humanitarian obligations under the MLC after the vessel's abandonment. The Ld. Single Judge considered that because Swedish Club was obliged to make such payments, it could not ask for these payments to be treated as Sheriff's expenses. The Ld. Single Judge referred to the P&I Club's obligation to make payment but did not appreciate the significance of Regulation 12 of Standard A2.5.2. Mr. Narichania submits that Swedish Club promptly approached the Ld. Single Judge to discharge its humanitarian obligations under the MLC. He argues that the Ld. Single Judge erred in considering that because Swedish Club was obliged to make such payments, it could not ask for these payments to be treated as Sheriff's expenses. He submits that the Ld. Single Judge has referred to the P&I Club's obligation to make payment but has not appreciated the significance of Regulation 12 of Standard A2.5.2 which specifically provides that the P&I Club is entitled to stand in the shoes of the crew once it has made payment to the crew. He further submits that Rule 1084 does not make any distinction between voluntary payments and payments made otherwise. Any party who incurs expenses to maintain a vessel under arrest or wages to the crew during the period of arrest is entitled to recover such expenses as Sheriff's expenses, irrespective of whether it is voluntary or not. He relies on The Leoborg, [1964] 1 Lloyd's Rep 380, The Vasilia, [1972] 1 Lloyd's Rep 51 and The Berostar, [1970] 2 Lloyd's Rep 403. He submits that the Ld. Single Judge failed to follow binding precedent of this Court in (a) coming to a conclusion that crew members were not entitled to recover post arrest wages as Sheriff's expenses and (b) finding that a P&I Club was not entitled to recover wages that it had paid to the crew members for the period of arrest as Sheriff's expenses.

The application for such payments to be treated as Sheriff's expenses in the case of Irwin Edmond Sequeira v m.v. Karnika (Colabawalla, J.) was filed by the crew, but the actual payment was made by the P&I club. The MLC under which the P & I Club came forward to make such payment and to thereafter stand in the shoes of the crew was not brought to the attention of the Court in that case. The crew were constrained to remain on board the vessel from its arrest until its sale and to take care of the vessel for no fault of theirs. A P&I Club who paid the post arrest wages to the crew was also entitled to make such payment after taking leave of the admiralty court and claim it as Sheriff's expenses. He submitted that the Ld. Judge erred in distinguishing the binding precedent in the case of Irwin Edmond Sequeira v m.v. Karnika (Colabawalla, J.). The application in that case, though filed by the crew, in fact sought for payments made by the P&I club to be classified as Sheriff's expenses, and this was granted. He also submits that worldwide practice is for post arrest wages to be considered as Sheriff's expenses. He relied on The Aquarius III, [2002] SGHC 138 and Credit Suisse v. Brightoil Lion (Order of the Singapore High C. Lastly, he submits that it is not necessary to file a suit to prove these expenses through trial - there can be no serious doubt about crew wages and the scrutiny is done by a competent officer of the High Court, such as the Sheriff of Mumbai or the Commissioner for taking Accounts. In The Aquarius III, the Singapore High Court observed that the post-arrest wages and disbursements were in substance sheriff's expenses. It did not matter that there was no prior order allowing the same to be treated as sheriff's expenses or that the interveners were not engaged by the sheriff himself or his agents, Gulf Agency. The sheriff had had the benefit of the interveners' presence and services to meet the regulatory requirement as a result of which the sheriff had saved on having to engage a replacement crew.

The case involves a dispute regarding the classification of expenses incurred for the safety and preservation of a vessel and its crew after the vessel is arrested. The issue revolves around whether such expenses can be considered as Sheriff's expenses under Rule 1084. Mr. Kamat argues that payment of wages and other employment entitlements of the crew after arrest is not the responsibility of the Sheriff unless the Sheriff considers it appropriate to employ or engage crew members

The vessel was arrested on 22 December 2020. Owners made the last supply of provisions and fuel on 22 December 2020. Wages had not been paid since November 2020. The abandonment (which under the MLC is considered to be when the owner does not make provision for supplies or when the owner fails to pay two months' wages) was brought to the notice of Swedish Club by the crew's email of 7 January 2021. Swedish Club filed its interim application indicating its readiness to make payments for the crew's benefit and seeking leave for the same on 21 January 2021. An ad interim order was obtained on 27 January 2021 insofar as the food/water/supplies for the crew were concerned. Mr. Narichania submits that the logic of disallowing an application by a crew member for classifying his wages as Sheriff's expenses is flawed and that this order does not have any binding value since it ignores previous orders passed by this Court where crew members have been paid their post arrest wages as Sheriff's expenses. He further submits that a lien can be transferred, but subject to leave of the court. Any purported transfer without prior leave of the court is not valid. Clause 12 of Standard A2.5.2 of the MLC provides that the rights of the crew members will be subrogated/assigned or in other manner automatically transferred to the P&I Club on making such payment. The Ld. Single Judge in this matter had disallowed an application by a crew member who had served on board the vessel during the period of arrest for classifying his wages as Sheriff's expenses. The Ld. Judge holds, 'If we entertain such applications, the problem will be (a) it will not be possible to ascertain whether applicant really worked on board the vessel, (b) what was he doing on board the vessel, (c) what were the terms and conditions based on which he was on board the vessel and (d) if it was a huge vessel with 50 crew members, would the Court direct the Sheriff to pay the wages of all the crew members until the vessel is sold?'

It appears that the Sheriff may not have been not aware of the situation on board the vessel. Given that the Sheriff did not move any application for orders relating to the maintenance and preservation of the vessel and the crew.
